Executive Summary

Project Objectives

The business objective for the project is:

To understand the potential for CO2 sequestration in the Petrel Sub-basin. This business objective is supported by the following technical objectives:

Calculate elastic properties for the four 2D PSDM seismic lines through simultaneous inversion

Predict sand distributions

Estimate sand porosity

Project Overview

In order to evaluate the CO2 storage potential in the Petrel Sub-basin. CGG Jason (Australia) Pty. Ltd. were contracted by Geoscience Australia to predict sand distribution and effective porosities for 400 km of 2D seismic using simultaneous inversion.

Figure 1: Sand Index for a set of 2D lines passing through Petrel-1 and Flat Top-1. Potential sands can be identified by a positive Sand Index.

The 2D PSDM angle stacks, logs from 3 wells: Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4, and geological information were algorithmically integrated using Jason’s Simultaneous Inversion algorithm incorporating rigorous quality control procedures to create bandpass and full bandwidth volumes of P-Impedance and Vp/Vs. The simultaneous inversion results are of satisfactory quality. These outputs were combined to derive Sand Index, Sand probability and effective porosity volumes which can assist interpretation. An

example of the derived Sand Index for a set of 2D lines passing through Petrel-1 and Flat Top-1 is shown in Figure 1.

Conclusions

Based on the objectives, the data provided and the results obtained, we present the following conclusions and recommendations:

Quality of inverted bandpass P-impedance and Vp/Vs is satisfactory as demonstrated by comparisons against well logs.

Sand bodies can be delineated using Sand Index derived from full-bandwidth P-impedance and Vp/Vs compensating for trend variations. Positive Sand Index values can be used to delineate possible sands.

Sand Probability derived from Sand Index results can be used to determine the likelihood of finding sand.

Sand porosity estimations from P-Impedance shows reasonable to good match at well location for the zone of interest.

Interpretations of the inversion results need to be incorporated with other exploration evaluation studies.

Introduction

Project Scope

This project has two stages: petrophysical analysis and rock physics modelling for Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4 and 2D Simultaneous Inversion of the angle stacks.

The scope of petrophysical analysis and rock physics modelling is to petrophysically evaluate the provided logs and use the outputs (Volume of Clay , Porosity & Total Water Saturation) in rock physics modelling to check the quality of elastic logs and also to generate elastic logs where unreliable or missing.

The scope of 2D Simultaneous Inversion of the angle stacks is to invert angle stacks of seismic data to the impedance domain integrating well and other information through constrained sparse spike simultaneous inversion. The resulting impedances are to be interpreted in terms of porosity distribution. The area of interest is 400 km of 2D PSDM seismic data. Data are available from three wells (Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4). The vertical extent of the inversion comprises from ~100ms above the Turonian horizon to Top_Permian horizon. A map of four 2D lines outlining the extent of the study area is shown in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Four 2D seismic lines and well locations in the study

Project Background

This is the first reservoir characterization project undertaken by CGG Jason (Australia) Pty. Ltd. for Geoscience Australia. The main objective of this project is to predict sand distribution and effective porosities for the sand in the study area.

The most important aspects of this workflow were:

Rock physics modelling of elastic logs to derive a consistent relationship between elastic and reservoir properties.

Construction of a low frequency model combining seismic velocity and well log information updated with rock physics derived property models within the reservoir.

Extensive quality control

The main added value of this seismic reservoir characterisation project is a greater understanding of the rocks in terms of distribution of sand and porosities in the study area.

Workflow

The workflow applied in this study is a standard simultaneous inversion workflow. Multiple angle stack seismic data are integrated with well data and seismic velocity data through simultaneous inversion to produce a model of the absolute elastic properties of the reservoir and surrounding rocks. These elastic properties are then interpreted in terms of lithology and fluid distribution and reservoir properties based on a petro-elastic model derived from the well data. Summary

In this section the key findings from each step of the workflow are summarised. The technical background and quality control processes are described in greater detail in the appendices at the end of the report.

Data Loading

The data received and loaded included four 2D seismic lines, each comprising four angle stacks; an interval velocity volume; data for 3 wells including Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4 and horizon interpretations. Additional data in the form of reports on well acquisition and processing, and presentations concerning the area of interest were provided in digital form.

Data Conditioning

Seismic Data

QC checks of four angle stacks showed seismic data to be of good quality. Amplitude behaviour with offset (AVO) appears reasonable with decreasing frequency content.

Seismic Velocities

The interval velocities provided on the 6.25 m grid were found to be of good quality for use in the seismic inversion workflow. Some lateral and vertical filtering was applied to condition the data. Good trend agreements were observed with wireline P-velocity logs. Provided PSDM interval velocities contain geological information and were found to be suitable for use in this project in contributing towards building the low frequency models.

Well Data

Three wells are available for this project, i.e. Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4. There were some sections where Density and P-Sonic logs were affected by bad hole conditions and gaps were observed in the Density and P-Sonic logs. Sections which were having these issues were corrected and patched with synthesized logs. There was no S-Sonic recorded in any of the three wells.

Horizon Data

There were total of 9 horizons provided. The provided horizons were interpolated and smoothed over the study area.

Petrophysics and Rock Physics

Flat Top-1 and Petrel-1 wells were available for calibration of AVO seismic. Petrel-4 well was only used for understanding the elastic properties of the rock, this well was not used in seismic inversion as it lies 7 km away from seismic line. The well have gone through quality check, conditioning, seismic petrophysics analysis and rock physics analysis which are described in detail in the relevant Appendix section.

Seismic Petrophysics analysis were performed to obtain consistent volume of clay, porosity and water saturation for all the three wells. Volume of clay was calculated using Gamma Ray logs. Water saturation

was calculated using Modified Simandoux equation using Rw provided in the well completion reports which was derived from SP log and water sample analysis.

The missing density log from 400-1200 m for Petrel-4 was estimated through multi-linear regression using the available logs i.e. GR, Resistivity and P-Sonic. The missing S-sonic log in all three wells was generated using rock physics modeling. A S-Sonic predicted using Greenberg-Castagna (GC) equation was used as reference in the rock physics modeling.

Well Tie and Wavelets

AVA amplitude spectrum wavelets were extracted from well-seismic ties for each stack. The extractions were undertaken over zone from Valanginian (-250 ms) – Base Jurassic (+300 ms). The wavelets and well ties are of reasonable quality in the zone of interest. The conditioned logs show good to reasonable AVO match between the synthetic and seismic for key reflectors in the zone of interest.

Low Frequency Modelling

The low frequency elastic property models that contribute to the frequencies below the seismic bandwidth were built from a combination of seismic velocity, well log and rock physics information.

The ultra-low frequencies (0-2 Hz) were derived from seismic velocities and transformed into the low frequency models of P-Impedance, Vp/Vs and density through a linear relationship.

The mid low frequencies (2-6 Hz) were derived from the interpolation of well data.

Inversion

Simultaneous multiple angle stack inversion combined the information from the low frequency model with the seismic reflectivity data to produce broadband elastic property models of the reservoir and surrounding rocks. The main results are models of P-impedance and Vp/Vs with frequency content up to about 60 Hz. Key aspects of this inversion were:

The near (4-15 degrees) and Ultra-Far stack (35-45 degrees) was weighted down with respect to the other stacks.

Correlation between inverted and wireline P-impedance and Vp/Vs logs are reasonable enough indicating a good quality inversion.

Interpretation

Interpretations were conducted using full-bandwidth inversion results. The inversion results were interpreted in terms of Sand Index and sand probability. The Sand Index highlights the potential distribution of sands by estimating the distance away from a trend line defined in the elastic domain. Sands samples can fall at increasingly further distances away from the trend line, depending upon the elastic property characteristics of the reservoirs. Sands have positive Sand Index. These samples are indicative of the properties of good quality sands. Positive Sand Index values can be used to delineate sands (with associated uncertainty). In addition, the inversion results were transformed to probability for each of the identified facies or fluids. Sand probability was calculated using Sand Index. Probability is more intuitive and more quantitative for interpretation.

The P-Impedance results from inversion were used for porosity prediction. A P-Impedance vs. porosity trend was determined at well log scale and verified at inversion resolution (high cut 60 Hz filtered logs). The porosities were determined from the P-Impedance sections for the sands (as defined by the sand index) using the P-Impedance to porosity transform. Figure 4 shows the effective porosities for sand. The estimated porosities show reasonable match at the well location over the zone of interest.

Figure 4: Effective porosities for a set of 2D lines passing through Petrel-1 and Flat Top-1 derived from P-Impedance vs Porosity transform.

Appendix 2: Data conditioning

After the data are loaded they are analysed for quality and consistency. If required the data are conditioned to ensure that they are reliable as input to the inversion workflow. The quality control procedures and conditioning steps, where carried out ,are detailed below.

Seismic data

PSDM processed four angle stacks were taken through rigorous quality control procedures. The zone of interest is shown in Figure 6.

Figure 6: The figure shows main horizons and zone of interest.

QC procedures were performed for the zone of interest. Figure 7 shows PSDM angle stacks and the frequency spectrums. The alignment between four angle stacks were QC’ed before running simultaneous inversion. In the seismic processing stage event flattening across full-fold gathers were applied, however some possible misalignments were observed. The effect of these possible misalignments of seismic angle stacks on the inversion results was tested at Petrel-1 as shown in Figures 8 and 9. The time shifts were calculated between the pairs of stacks (i.e. Near-Mid, Near-Far and Near-UFar) within the common frequency bandwidths to bring the events into alignment. The time shifts were then applied to align events across stacks where correlations between the stacks were high. Simultaneous inversion was performed around Peterl-1 well to see the possible impact on the results. The results do not show conclusive improvements after the alignment therefore these additional seismic alignments were not applied on the input seismic for the final simultaneous inversion.

Well data

Good quality well log data are essential for high quality seismic reservoir characterization. In seismic reservoir characterization, well log data are routinely used for:

Wavelet estimation

Low frequency model building

Seismic velocity calibration

Time to depth conversion

Hard data in geostatistical modelling

Petrophysical interpretation

Rock physics modelling

Providing a framework for the interpretation of seismically derived elastic property volumes

This means that we require logs for petrophysical interpretation and subsequent rock physics modelling for calibration of elastic logs (density, p-sonic and often s-sonic logs) that:

Are consistent inter and intra-well

Cover the entire vertical interval of interest

Cover reservoir and non-reservoir rocks

Represent the true, undisturbed rock properties

It is often the case that the well log data do not satisfy these criteria for various reasons:

Different tool measurements

Different borehole environments

Different borehole fluids

Poor quality logging conditions

Invasion of borehole fluids into the formations

Alteration of the formation properties due to the presence of the borehole and /or borehole fluids

Missing data

Therefore well log data need to be conditioned, corrected and synthesized to provide complete and reliable input for seismic reservoir characterization. Jason has developed a workflow that ensures the highest quality well log data are available. This workflow consists of the following steps:

Data loading

Log editing and conditioning

Petrophysical evaluation

Rock physics modelling

Well tie

Analysis

At each step quality control is applied. This section of the report describes the workflow and quality control as applied to the well log data in this project.

Data loading and QC

The available data for all the three wells were loaded and merged using Jason PowerLog software. The quality, consistency, presence of the logs and ancillary data are assessed for each of the well over the inversion interval. Figure 12 shows log data for all the three wells. The Density was not logged above 1200 m and P_Sonic was missing between 1200-1400 m for Petrel-4.

Figure 12: Well log data availability for all the three wells in the study

During quality control and data merging process, the well data was checked for any borehole related problems. The overall well data quality is moderate to good. Density log was affected by the washouts in all the wells. The quality of the recorded P-Sonic logs were good except some spikes which were removed during the data conditioning phase. Figure 13 shows cross-plot of Sonic vs. Density. The data colored by differential caliper shows quality is affected in the washouts intervals. The quality of the data are access to check for the trend and similarity. The bad data points are edited during conditioning.

Figure 13: Sonic vs. Density cross-plot.

Some of the points falls out from the main trend due to Density logs are effected by washouts.

Log editing and conditioning

Log conditioning mitigates the poor quality data, generates and fills in the missing data before they are taken through to the Seismic Petrophysical analysis and Rock Physics modelling. Normally only Density, Neutron and P-Sonic logs are conditioned over the bad data while others are used to check for continuity and uniformity. Merging, depth match, splice and interpolation are applied if required. To correct the bad data, different methods are used. The most common methods are:

Adjustment by hand

Make a cross-plot of Density-Neutron with VCL in the Z-axis

Identify points in front of bad hole

Shift these points to get correct value

Regression with single log

Generate cross-plot for the log to be corrected versus the Deep Resistivity log, as this is less affected by the borehole rugosity. Poor data was identified and a regression was made over the good quality data. This relationship obtained from regression is used to replace the poor quality data

Synthetic curve generator

Using multi-linear regression techniques over good quality data, synthetic curves are generated, which are used to patch or replace poor quality data for a single or multiple wells. Normal curves used for regression are Gamma Ray, Deep Resistivity, Density, Neutron and P-Sonic.

Based on the data quality and borehole rugosity the well logs data was analysed for the bad data sections. The well log availability show there was missing Density and P-sonic data over some intervals for Petrel-4. The density log is affected by washouts for all the three wells and P-sonic data has some

spikes which were removed during conditioning. The missing Density data was synthesized from multi well regression. There were no recorded S-Sonic logs in the available wells. The S-Sonic logs were synthesized using Greenberg-Castagna as a reference for rock physics modeling. The final S-Sonic used for simultaneous inversion was estimated from rock physics modeling.

Figure 14 shows the measured and conditioned data for Petrel-4 from Top to TD. Bad data were identified and flagged using cross-plot and histogram. Multi curve regressions were performed to create synthetic curves from the other good logs - i.e. P-Sonic, Gamma Ray and Deep Resistivity. In this well, the bad Density and P-Sonic data was removed. The elastic logs were generated from rock physics modelling which is explained in the rock physics modelling section.

Appendix 3: Petrophysics Analysis

Petrophysics was carried out to provide consistent input to the rock physics modelling. Rock physics requires input in terms of volumes of minerals and fluids presents. Rock physics modelling was carried out to quality control the measure elastic property logs and to synthesize data where missing of poor quality or affected by the drilling.

Petrophysics model

The aim of a petrophysical analysis is to accurately compute the volumes of hydrocarbons (fluids) and minerals (lithologies). These data are later used as inputs to the rock physics modeling. The petrophysical phase of the workflow is carried out to provide suitable input to the rock physics stage, as well as meaningful evaluation of the petrophysical properties of the reservoir rocks. This analysis can differ from standard petrophysical evaluation in several ways. One of the biggest differences is the emphasis placed on the evaluation of non-reservoir rocks. Since the well logs are used in their entirety for processes such as wavelet estimation and low frequency modelling, ensuring high quality log data in non-reservoir rocks is just as important as in the reservoir rocks. Another significant difference can be that the rock physics modelling requires mineral volumes such as volume of clay rather than lithology volumes such as volume of shale. These differences may not necessarily change the interpretation of the reservoir but can have a significant effect for the non-reservoir rocks.

In this study, the petrophysical evaluation was carried out where complete suite of logs were available for all 3 wells. Lithology mainly consists of sand and shale. The petrophysical evaluation was carried out using Dual-Mineral models (Quartz+Clay) based on the known lithology from well completion report and mud logs. The petrophysical evaluation consists of estimation of the volumes of minerals and fluids present in the invaded and virgin zones. The volume of clay is estimated using Gamma Ray log. The porosities (effective and total) are determined by an iterating procedure of mud invasion correction based on the density log. The detailed methods are presented as follows.

Rock Physics Modelling and Fluid Substitutions

The objective of the rock physics modelling is to provide a consistent set of elastic logs at each well for wavelet estimation; to provide a link between the petrophysical properties and the elastic properties of the rocks (Vp, Vs, b). This link will allow the elastic properties of the rocks determined through seismic inversion to be interpreted in terms of reservoir properties. This link can only be achieved accurately for full bandwidth inversion results.

The methodology applied was to construct a rock physics model that was consistent with the petrophysical analysis and the elastic properties of the rocks as given by the conditioned well log data. The parameters of the rock physics model usually determined from the wells where the measured data were complete and considered to be of good quality. There was no measured S-Sonic data available is all there wells. The S-Sonic predicted from Greenberg-Castagna (GC) was used as reference in the Rock Physic modeling workflow. The model build using Petrel-4 well was then applied to other wells to generate synthetic elastic logs that were used to determine the quality of the data. Where necessary, the synthetic data were used to replace poor quality data and to supply data where they were not measured.

In this project, rock physics is carried out by using the petrophysical logs. There was no recorded S-Sonic for 3 wells in the study, therefore elastic properties of the rocks cannot be understood in detail. Processed and reliable P and S-Sonic data is very important for build a good quality rock physics model. In all three wells, S-Sonic predicted from Greenberg-Castagna (GC) was used as stating point. Appendix 5: Low Frequency modelling

A low frequency model is required to provide information below the seismic bandwidth. A correct low frequency model will remove side lobes and provide absolute values for the elastic properties that are required for quantitative interpretation. The low frequency model must be consistent with the geology and therefore often requires interpretation and iteration to achieve the desired results. For simultaneous inversion as carried out in this work a low frequency model is required for P-impedance, Vp/Vs and density.

The low frequency model is generated by combining information from seismic velocities, which control the lowest frequencies, and a geological model that represents the interpolation of well data within a stratigraphic framework.

The low frequency model is formed by the merging in the frequency domain of the very low frequency component from the seismic velocities with the geological model which has a broad bandwidth. The merge point is assigned based on the frequency content of the seismic velocity based model.The steps taken to build the models are described in some detail below.

Ultra-low frequencies

Seismic velocity data contain information about the variation in the lowest frequency range throughout the seismic volume. This information can be used to guide the construction of the lowest few Hz of the low frequency models. The workflow for this is outlined in the following steps:

Extract the seismic velocity data along the well tracks

Cross-plot the seismic velocity and the log P-impedance

Derive a simple relationship between these properties

Use this relationship to convert the seismic velocity to P-impedance

Extract this P-impedance along the well tracks

Create a calibration factor that converts the seismic P-impedance to the log P-impedance

Extrapolate the calibration factor throughout the volume within a structural framework

Apply the calibration factor to the seismic P-impedance volume

This workflow results in a P-impedance volume that is tied to the wells and follows variations in the seismic velocity. In this case the frequency content of this model was limited to 2 Hz. The same workflow was applied to calculate Vp/Vs and Density volume.

Laterally smoothed filtered interval velocities were used to build the ultra low frequency models. Figure 30 shows a seismic velocity section filtered to 2 Hz and lateral filtered at 7.5 km. The seismic velocities show a reasonable match at the well location.

The microlayering scheme can be chosen that best represents geological (structural and/or depositional) patterns as evident in the seismic. Figure 33 illustrates the solid model built. Appendix 8: Interpretation

Interpretation of the inversion results here is carried out using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. In the deterministic approach a Sand Index is created that identifies sand versus shale. In the probabilistic approach the probability of sand is estimated. Effective porosity volume was also estimated using full bandwidth P-Impedance volume.

Sand Index

The Sand Index is an attribute designed to highlight the locations where the inversion results show an increased likelihood of encountering sands and/or hydrocarbons. A full bandwidth Sand Index was therefore calculated as a distance of separation of samples from a trend line established on an elastic property cross-plot. Low P-impedance and Vp/Vs samples have positive Sand Index. These may represent good quality sands. Sand Index based interpretation is shown in Figure 47 through 47. We started with well base feasibility using high cut filter logs at 60 Hz. The trend line use to separate sand and shale. The final sand index volume shows good match at the well location.

Sand Probability

The Sand Index is strongly focused on highlighting areas of potential sand. The downside is that it is a qualitative parameter, which is not particularly intuitive. Probability is more intuitive and more quantitative. In addition, the inversion results can be transformed to probability for each of the identified facies. Sand probability was calculated using sand index volume. The probability density functions (PDFs) were designed for sands and shales. These PDFs were then converted to cumulative density functions (CDFs). The CDFs were then applied to sand index sections to get the sand probability volume. A decade of marine seismic technology development from an oil company perspective. What does the future hold?

Per Eivind Dhelie*, Vidar Danielsen & Jan Erik Lie (Lundin Norway)

Summary

The	history	of	Lundin	Norway	dates	back	to	2004	starting	with	a	handful	of	employees	with	an

overwhelming appetite for seismic data and exploration. From the very beginning until today, seismic data has been and still is the primary tool for finding and discovering new fields. This is probably not unique or very different to most other oil exploration companies, but what makes Lundin and our history a bit different is the way we see and use the data–never believing that we cannot get more out of what we already have, by constantly re-processing, re-acquiring and trying new and different tools, with a desire to find new ways of using and seeing things in the data. There is no best practice in our work,

only better practice and reprocessing is not a project from a to z, merely part of an always ongoing effort to  continuously  improve  the  seismic  images. Lundin  Norway  has  also  always  had  appetite  for  new technologies and have been in the forefront of many new seismic developments. Since the discovery of Edvard Grieg (LUNO) back in 2007, the Utsira High became a seismic laboratory both for 2D and 3D image testing. Directly following the discovery of the Luno field Lundin Norway commenced acquisition of the 1st high density OBC survey on the Utsira High, LN0803, approx. 50sqkm of 200x25m dense 4C OBC data. This dataset paved the way for several good appraisal wells and has been used to push for low frequency signal and provided a fundamental understanding of the image challenges  in  the  area.  The  dataset  is  still  today,  10  years  later,  constantly  under re-processing  and scrutinization for comparison to other new and different tools. A year later, in 2009, Lundin Norway was the first company in the world to acquire 3D dual-sensor deghosted Geostreamer data, LN0902. Over 1650km2  of new (revolutionary) technology data. Like the OBC data, this is still today, a decade later actively used every single day to explore and develop further the Edvard Grieg field and the surrounding areas. A few years later, in 2012, another contractor launched their BroadSeis combined with Broadsource full deghosting technology based on pressure only sensors. Also this time, Lundin Norway were first adopters and went ahead and acquired over 2500km2 of high density 3D data–as the first company in the world to use this technology. The desire to seek the unknown and the new, is not by luck, but by desire and understanding, and the will to go further and beyond what other companies can and are willing to do. The list of new technology embarking’s is long; MagSeis, Snake Streamer, IsoMetrix, TopSeis (2016/2017/2018), inApril, Compact small point sources (2016) (1/3 of conventional  source  outputs),  Triple  source, Hexasource  (2018,2019)  and  now  lastly  the  TopSeis  2 hexasource in addition to very recently also testing the Source Isolation technology.

This paper does not intent to recap all and everything from each and all these different technologies, but will instead shed light on the why’s, the what’s and the how’s of developing and taking part in all these new novel acquisition and processing technologies and how they have actively led to more and better discoveries. Without trying to predict the future, we will also, based on the history, try to discuss what we think the future of seismic exploration may hold, at least on the Norwegian Continental Shelf.

The first steps of Broadband seismic across the Southern Utsira High

Since the first license commitment from Lundin Norway on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, license PL338 (Luno–Edvard Grieg) in 2005, seismic data massaging and re-processing has been looked upon as a continuous process of development. There is no start and no end; Processing, re-processing and continuously investigating new ways to image and develop the understanding of the seismic data and the subsurface has been a foundation for the field development. The original seismic data used to place the discovery well on the Edvard Grieg field was ST9511. With special denoise, high cut filtering and low frequency signal boost, it was possible to see hints of the graben structures up on the Utsira High area. Following the discovery well, 16/1-8, the first OBC survey was planned and completed in 2008. The focus was to improve the low frequency content and also deghost the data using PZ summation. Only a year later the new dual-sensor streamer technology, GeoStreamer was tested in full 3D as the first commercial survey ever. Approximately 1650km2 of broadband data was collected. Lundin

Norway has always had an appetite for new promising technologies, and are rarely afraid of going “all in”. With the introduction of BroadSeis and also BroadSource, Lundin Norway followed up again in 2012 with an even larger 3D broadband survey, covering all of the Southern Utsira High area.

Along with or trailing slightly behind are processing based solutions that tries to overcome the need for special  equipment. Tendency  has  it  that  processing  can  and  will  try  to  mimic  expensive  acquisition solutions like dual-sensor, multi-sensor and broadband sources, by application of mathematical deghosting processes. This led to Lundin’s own Snake streamer test in 2015, whereby 11 different slant streamer profiles were tested to dig deeper into processing based deghosting solutions and try to determine  what  profiles  are  optimum for  processing based deghosting applications. This dataset  has been processed as trial and error by many processing contractors, both as a development tool for them and for optimization of future acquisition setups. Acquisition, reprocessing and comparison to other 3D solutions has also been performed, such as high density 3D site survey data. Pcable technology with lots of very small short offset (~50m) streamers towed extremely dense has also been acquired, processed  and  tested.  During  the  work  on  site  survey  3D  data,  along  with  the  introduction  of  more sources (more than dual source) it became necessary to investigate the general setup of typical marine seismic sources. This work led to studies of source sizes, areal source distribution, making the source both smaller and more compact to gain better focus of the seismic source wavefield. The initial trial was performed across the Edvard Grieg field in 2016 and was a direct instigator to the triple source small compact source used for the first ever commercial TopSeis survey, LN17001 in the Barents Sea. Prior to performing this survey, the field test across Utsira High in 2016, confirmed that smaller source was not just acceptable to use, but also increased the spatial resolution in the data. This was also confirmed with reprocessing of relatively old 3D site survey data using only 160 in3  across the Neiden area on the Loppa High.

The latest development of both sources and receiver setups is the TopSeis 2 Utsira Hexasource survey, CGG18003, which utilized 6 small compact sources towed over and across a 10 streamer deep-towed spread. This survey is still in processing, but fully migrated fast track images at reservoir level again reveal  that  dense sampling of the wavefield, from 6 sources shot  with only 2.5 s shot  point  interval combined with a source-over-streamer geometry is yet another step up in quality compared to any other legacy dataset.

Overcoming the image challenges across the Loppa High in the Barents Sea

Lundin Norway’s desire to really challenge the imaging problems across the Loppa High in the Barents Sea  was  driven  by  the  discoveries  of  Alta  and  Gohta  in  2013  and  2014,  respectively.  Hydrocarbon accumulations were discovered in high velocity  karstefied carbonates of Permian age. The deepest reservoirs  are  located  at  ~1700m  MSL  and  follows  the  upward  dipping  trend  towards  North  on  the Loppa ridge. The shallowest reservoirs have been found at only 700-800m. Water depth in the Barents Sea is roughly 350m and relatively constant. Due to recent Tertiary uplift of more than 1500m followed by significant erosion, the seafloor and the shallow geologic layers today consist of very dense and high velocity strata that was previously buried much deeper. The seafloor is generally very hard and iceberg have scraped along the seafloor for decades which have given rice to a very rugose seafloor topography which acts more or less as millions of diffractor points. This geologic setting can generally be split into three main geophysical challenges:

1) Shallow high velocities which bends the rays quickly and warrants the use of near offset data, simply because the further offset data ricochets away and goes critical and as such is not usable for imaging. The solution to this is to alter the acquisition setup and use a method that captures much more of the zero and near offset data

2) Rugose and hard seafloor with high reflection coefficients sets up very strong multiples and a lot of multiple diffractions plus strong interbed multiples. In order to be able to handle and remove all these strong multiples (often 10 orders of multiples) it is critical to sample them without aliasing such that they can be properly modeled and removed in processing. This is true for multiples and multiple generators in 3D, i.e. not just along the sailing direction of the seismic vessel, but in all directions. This

implies an acquisition solution that samples both shots and receivers in full 3D adequately in“both”directions,  x and  y,  or  more  correctly,  in  all  azimuths.  The  earth’s  impulse  response  does not  know which direction the seismic data was acquired in, and it should not be visible in the data either. It should be uniformly sampled and dense in all directions.

3) Relatively shallow reservoirs in carbonates of varying porosity and permeability. These carbonates have been exposed to fresh water and erosion that has given rise to caves and other permable zones. As with exposed carbonates today, we see that some areas are completely tight and without any porosity whereas other areas close by have large caves and permeable fracture zones. In order to produce hydrocarbons from such reservoirs it is important to see the areas of best porosity and permeability and place future production wells in these areas. This again warrants geophysical data with as high as possible resolution, both temporal and spatial and in full 3D (both inline and xline). Another aspect of this is signal to noise ratio (S/N). Small fractures and permeable zones must be distinguished and separated from general noise and all the diffracted multiple noise. This warrants a setup that provides high S/N level without compromising resolution. Also, because the targets are relatively shallow the stack mute is often at  less than 1000m offset. This again requires  very short  shot  point  interval  and dense trace spacing in cmp domain to obtain good stack power.

With the above challenges in mind, Lundin Norway set out on a journey to come up with new acquisition setups that would tackle as many of the above issues as possible.

With multiples, fold and high velocities in mind, it did not take long until the need for a towed marine solution  with  the  sources  placed  directly  in  the  middle  and  above  all  the  streamers  was ironed  out. However, a multi-year trial and error including testing and re-design should occupy most of 2014 and 2015,  including  also  a  number of  modeling  exercises.  Originally,  Lundin  Norway  approach  several contractors with the proposal to tow the sources in the middle of all the  receivers, but CGG was the

only one that finally decided to go ahead and try if this actually could be done. Once the 1st trail was successfully completed (in Gabon) and we knew it was feasible to acquire data like this, a more detailed investigation commenced to optimize all the acquisition parameters. 2 years later, this all culminated with the LN17001 triple-wide tow compact dithered TopSeis survey in the Barents Sea across the Loppa High area.  Results of this are now showing clear improvement  on all  the  aspects it  was designed to tackle.

What does the future of marine seismic look like for the NCS from a technical perspective?

For the towed marine seismic market there is no going back to dual source technology any more. The successful application of multisource distributed acquisition such as triple, penta and hexasource have proved itself in terms of viability and quality. When it also increases the efficiency by reducing the time it takes to acquire a dataset, this type of marine source setups will become the norm very soon, if it has not already done so. The challenge still remains with some of them to overcome the need for using two vessels, however with autonomous small extra source vessel, this hurdle may soon be overcome. There are promising tests with much longer source umbilicals too, so there may be other was to avoid mobilizing more than one vessel. For much larger areas, the normal survey could include a quarto wide tow source behind the streamer towing vessel, and one could add a second source vessel with

hexasources in “TopSeis” mode to cover a part of the survey (a field in development) to get the highest

possible image quality.

There are still a number of companies that are worried about the blending and deblending of the seismic data inside the target level. i.e. that the next shot is fired before the two-way time for the target zone. In the  North Sea and  Barents Sea, this  means typically less than  2s  (below  the  seafloor). Results  from Lundin’s own tests on deblending technology does not support this worry. Indeed when shots are fired denser and more often, the amplitude behavior is more similar so it is possible to recover the signal behind the next source before the previous (n+1 and n-1).

For Ocean Bottom Seismic, the introduction of several source boats with multiple sources happened several year ago and will eventually become the norm. The efficiency gain obvious and the sampling desire is similar to streamer seismic. In fact, the industry is more likely to try and save on the number

of receivers (or to cover larger areas) and instead use many more source than is typical today. Let us not forget permanently installed seafloor systems, where the source effort is 100% of the time. There is certainly a serious cost saving to obtain using 6 sources (hexasource) covering 3 times the amount of lines in a single pass (reducing the turnaround time by 60%.).

In order to convert a typical dual-source setup into a hexasource without increasing the inventory requires each single source to be much smaller. Typically reducing the source from ~3500 in3  down to 600-800 in3. Quite a few companies have engaged themselves in field tests and studies on the source size requirements over the last decade. Several studies have been published on detailed comparisons of source sized from very large 3 sub-arrays sources (~3500in3) down to single strings and even all the way down to single guns. The takeaway from these tests are that signal strength and low frequencies are maintained every for very small sources. Currently most single distributed sources will perform well in a NCS setting, down to around 500in3. Going below this source size the signal strength is overcome by noise at around 2-3 seconds TWT. This is of course geology dependent, but as a rule of thumb, it seems to be accepted.

There is no straightforward answer to the question of re-processing or re-acquire data. However, a new survey should be able to tackle the geologic and geophysical challenges the area requires and there is certainly a lot of understanding to be had, in terms of multiples, sampling, velocities etc. that one would learn and gain good understanding of by first going back and re-process whatever data the area has, prior to designing and choosing parameters for a new high spec high density 3D data acquisition, both in an OBS and a towed marine setting.

A Seismic Multi-Attribute SandbodyIdentification Method Based on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm

Teng-fei Ren, Zhi-bing Feng1,2,*, Ying Zhang, Xiang Zhang, Li Jiang1, Yuan-li Ning4,Jing-yi Wang1, Jian Ding1, and Zeng-shuo Qi1

Abstract: Seismic attributes encapsulate substantial reservoir characterization information and can effectively support reservoir prediction. Given the high-dimensional nonlinear between sandbodies and seismic attributes, this study employs the RFECV method for seismic attribute selection, inputting the optimized attributes into a LightGBM model to enhance spatial delineation of sandbody identification. By constructing training datasets based on optimized seismic attributes and well logs, followed by class imbalance correction as input variables for machine learning models, with sandbody probability as the output variable, and employing grid search to optimize model parameters, a high-precision sandbody prediction model was established. Taking the 3D seismic data of Block F3 in the North Sea of Holland as an example, this method successfully depicted the three-dimensional spatial distribution of target formation sandstones. The results indicate that even under strong noise conditions, the multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on LightGBM effectively characterizes the distribution features of sandbodies. Compared to unselected attributes, the prediction results using selected attributes have higher vertical resolution and inter-well conformity, with the prediction accuracy for single wells reaching 80.77%, significantly improving the accuracy of sandbody boundary delineation.

Keywords: Sandbody identification; Seismic attributes; LightGBM model; RFECV method

Introduction

Sandbodies are an important component of oil, gas, and uranium reservoirs in sedimentary basins (Feng et al., 2017, 2024; Cheng et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025). Understanding their location and shape helps in better exploration and development. Lithology, a core parameter controlling reservoir properties, directly

influences petrophysical characteristics and fluid distribution, holding significant importance for accurate reservoir description (Cheng et al., 2022; Chaki et al., 2015). Current sandbody identification methods primarily rely on seismic attribute analysis and seismic inversion techniques, which acquire lithological information by establishing statistical relationships between lithology and petrophysical parameters or inversion parameters (Garia et al., 2021). Han (2021) revealed the

Manuscript received by the Editor March 19, 2025; revised manuscript received August 31, 2025

lithofacies development pattern and predicted sandbody development zones in the Yingcheng Formation of the Xuxi area based on multi-attribute analysis. Zhang et al. (2024) analyzed the connectivity of shallow sandbodies in the Bohai Depression using seismic fusion attributes. While these methods have yielded robust outcomes in specific geological contexts, their application faces significant limitations. Conventional methods are highly dependent on data quality and inversion accuracy. Furthermore, noise interference and inversion uncertainties during actual seismic data processing often reduce prediction reliability, making it difficult to meet the demands of detailed reservoir characterization (Fan et al., 2023).

Machine learning methods, owing to their powerful data mining capabilities, demonstrate significant advantages in pattern recognition and classification prediction. By training models on known data, this approach enables reliable prediction in unknown regions (Jiang et al., 2024; Chenin et al., 2020). In hydrocarbon exploration, Othman et al. (2021) predicted reservoir properties using seismic amplitude data via a probabilistic neural network (PNN) algorithm. Xiong et al. (2021) utilized bidirectional long short-term memory neural networks for lithofacies prediction in areas with sparse well control. Extensive research shows that LightGBM, as an efficient gradient boosting decision tree framework, outperforms traditional machine learning algorithms in training speed, accuracy, and memory efficiency. The framework employs a histogram algorithm for feature parallel optimization, significantly enhancing computational efficiency. Addressing the characteristics of large seismic data volumes and high feature dimensionality, LightGBM proposes two innovative algorithms: Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB). These optimize the computational process from the dimensions of sample sampling and feature handling, respectively, substantially improving computational efficiency while maintaining prediction accuracy.

Compared to raw seismic data, seismic attributes exhibit higher sensitivity to variations in reservoir properties and lithology, effectively revealing implicit geological features within the reservoir, and hold significant application value in reservoir prediction and lithology identification. The nonlinear relationship between seismic attributes and sandbodies is the core issue in sandbody identification research (Sun et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2024). Notwithstanding, a single

seismic attribute is insufficient for accurate sandbody prediction, while combining too many attributes may introduce information redundancy, reducing model generalization. Conventional methods typically rely on cross-plot analysis of seismic attributes or elastic parameters for lithology identification, but this approach has clear limitations: firstly, elastic parameters for different lithologies often exhibit overlapping regions; secondly, cross-plot interpretation heavily relies on manual identification, which is subjective and has poor reproducibility (Yan 2022). Consequently, constructing an optimal seismic attribute subset is crucial for improving the sandbody identification accuracy of machine learning models. The RFECV algorithm effectively selects the most representative subset of features by recursively eliminating redundant ones and incorporating cross-validation to evaluate model performance. Its model-agnostic nature, not relying on any specific machine learning algorithm, enhances the stability and generalization capability of feature selection. In the context of sandbody identification, this method can effectively address the challenges posed by high-dimensional data, providing robust and interpretable feature selection results with significant practical value (Wang et al., 2019).

Consequently, we propose a solution based on the LightGBM machine learning algorithm. This method employs RFECV technology for optimized seismic attribute selection and utilizes a grid search strategy for model parameter tuning, ultimately constructing a high-precision sandbody identification model. Practical application demonstrates that this method can effectively identify sandbody distribution features in seismic sections, with prediction results showing good agreement with measured data, validating the method's practicality and reliability.

Method Principle

Well-to-Seismic Matching

Supervised machine learning algorithms require a sample set with calibrated labels for training (Silveira et al., 2024). Consequently, well log lithology data with known sandbody information is essential for machine learning-based sandbody identification. To integrate sandbody information with seismic attribute data, well- to-seismic matching is necessary. Based on the time-

depth conversion relationship obtained from well-to- seismic calibration, well log lithology data in the depth domain is converted to the time domain. Due to differing sampling rates between well log and seismic data, the well log data must be resampled according to the seismic data's sampling rate to achieve consistency in the time domain (Kumar et al., 2018; He et al., 2020). Using the inline and crossline values of the wells, multiple seismic attributes and elastic parameters are extracted point-by-

point from the adjacent seismic traces as features for lithology samples. These are combined with the time- converted and resampled well log lithology data to form the initial seismic attribute sample set. As shown in Fig. 1, the sample set is based on individual sampling points, with corresponding data including time-domain data, lithology data, seismic attributes, and elastic parameters for that point.

Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of typical well-log and seismic data matching results. On the far left is lithology, where blue represents mudstone and yellow represents sandstone. From left to right are: natural gamma, instantaneous amplitude, P-wave impedance, and 24 Hz frequency-divided energy.

Seismic Attribute Optimization

Seismic attributes refer to special measures derived through mathematical transformations, describing seismic waves in geometric, dynamic, and statistical aspects, capable of characterizing reservoir structure, properties, and lithology. They can be classified into phase attributes, amplitude attributes, absorption attenuation attributes, and frequency attributes.

Attributes like amplitude, frequency, phase, P-wave and S-wave velocity, acoustic impedance, and absorption coefficient are primarily used for lithology and reservoir characterization interpretation. A single seismic attribute is easily influenced by sand-mudstone configurations, limiting sandbody identification accuracy and often leading to ambiguity. Inputting an excessive number of seismic attributes can also degrade machine learning

performance, as not all attributes positively contribute to sandbody identification (Li et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2023). Consequently, when handling multiple seismic attribute features, it is necessary to optimize and select attributes highly correlated with sandbodies. This reduces the training data size, accelerates model training, avoids insufficient features from a single attribute, and prevents overfitting (Huang et al., 2025). Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV) is a feature selection technique combining Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) and Cross-Validation (CV), designed to automatically determine the optimal number of features. This algorithm does not require pre-setting the number of features to retain; instead, it dynamically determines the optimal feature count through cross­validation. It supports any supervised learning model that provides feature importance scores and exhibits good model generalization. Hence, the RFECV algorithm is used to optimize seismic attributes, selecting those highly correlated with sandbodies. The RFECV process can be summarized in the following steps:

Initialization: Given the training dataset X ∈ R^n*m (n: number of samples, m: number of original features) and labels y, select a supervised learning model capable of outputting feature importance, set the number of cross-validation folds k, and define the number of features to remove per iteration.

Feature Importance Calculation & Ranking: Train the base model M on the full feature set X, employing cross-validation to avoid initial overfitting. Extract feature importance scores S = {s1, s2, ..., sm} based on the model's characteristics. Rank features in descending order of importance score S, generating the ranked list F_rank = [f(1), f(2), ..., f(m)], where f(1) is the most important feature.

Recursive Feature Elimination & Cross­Validation Iteration: Starting with the full feature set, the algorithm enters an iterative loop. In each iteration, it performs k-fold cross-validation on the current feature subset: the data is divided into k parts, the model is trained on k-1 folds, and its performance is validated on the remaining fold. The average cross-validation score is computed to assess the generalization ability of the current feature subset. Based on the pre-ranked feature importance list, the least important features (a predefined number) are then removed, resulting in a smaller feature subset. This process continues until the number of remaining features reaches a preset minimum or the cross-validation score drops significantly. Throughout

the iterations, both the number of features and their corresponding scores are recorded to generate a feature­number vs. performance curve.

Optimal Feature Subset Selection: Analyze the feature-number vs. performance curve and select the feature number m_opt yielding the highest cross­validation score. If multiple feature counts yield similar scores, the principle of parsimony is followed to choose the smallest number. Ultimately, the top m_opt features from the original ranked list F_rank are retained to form the optimal subset F_final. This subset reduces dimensionality while preserving maximum predictive power, with generalization ensured through cross­validation (Xing et al., 2023).

LightGBM Principle

LightGBM is an efficient machine learning framework based on Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT), proposed by Microsoft in 2017. It is adaptable to diverse machine learning scenarios, including ranking, classification, and regression tasks, and has been widely applied in fields such as finance, medicine, and geoscience, becoming a primary method for solving classification and regression problems using data-driven models (Ke et al., 2017). The essence of LightGBM is an ensemble algorithm that transforms weak learners into strong learners. It combines numerous low-accuracy tree models, iterating continuously using gradient descent. In each iteration, the loss function is minimized by moving in the negative gradient direction of the loss function, ultimately resulting in a high-performing tree used as the prediction model. LightGBM supports three parallelization methods: feature parallel, data parallel, and voting parallel, effectively enhancing processing speed. Compared to other ensemble learning methods, LightGBM offers faster processing time and higher accuracy when handling data with high feature dimensionality and large sample sizes (Dramsch, 2020). This is primarily due to two innovative algorithms: Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) and Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS).

In high-dimensional data processing, exploding feature dimensions can significantly reduce model training efficiency. Traditional gradient boosting tree algorithms search for the optimal split point by traversing all features. Seismic sandbody identification data typically contains numerous seismic attributes (e.g., amplitude, frequency, coherence volume), often exhibiting high sparsity and partial mutual exclusivity among features

(Hampson et al., 2001; Dixit et al., 2020). LightGBM's EFB algorithm addresses computational efficiency through feature dimensionality reduction. The core idea of EFB is to merge mutually exclusive features— defined as features with near-zero correlation—into a single synthetic feature, thereby reducing the feature search space. EFB allows LightGBM to traverse only the bundled features during training instead of the original features, reducing computational complexity from O(#data × #feature) to O (#data × #bundle). In seismic sandbody identification, this method effectively compresses seismic attribute dimensions, accelerates model training, and retains key information about formation reflection characteristics.

Addressing computational bottlenecks in massive sample scenarios, LightGBM proposes the GOSS algorithm. Traditional random sampling discards high-gradient samples (i.e., samples with large model prediction errors), whereas GOSS significantly improves sampling efficiency by retaining these high-information samples. Let a denote the top samples selected based on the absolute values of the gradients, and b represent the remaining samples. By combining these two subsets of samples using the GOSS algorithm, the computational cost can be significantly reduced while maintaining the effectiveness and accuracy of model training. The theoretical time complexity is reduced to O((a + b)% × #data × #feature). In seismic sandbody identification, this method prioritizes learning sensitive features in seismic waveform anomalous zones (e.g., sandbody boundaries), avoiding overfitting to stable background regions, thereby enhancing model generalization capability.

The EFB and GOSS algorithms optimize computational efficiency from the feature space and sample space, respectively, forming a "dual dimensionality reduction" mechanism. EFB reduces feature search times, while GOSS lowers sample computation. Their combination enables LightGBM to achieve 3-5 times speedup compared to algorithms like XGBoost when training large-scale seismic data. Furthermore, the gradient focusing characteristic causes the model to pay more attention to the discrimination boundary between sand and non-sand, improving the identification accuracy of thin interbedded sandbodies. This computational efficiency characteristic is particularly significant for capturing weak reflection signals in seismic data.

Method Workflow

The seismic multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on the LightGBM-RFECV coupling algorithm mainly includes the following steps: 1. Data Processing:Identify the location and seismic reflection characteristics of the target interval. Extract seismic data and elastic parameters (including various attribute volumes like amplitude, frequency, phase) for the target interval. 2.Well-to-Seismic Matching: Combine well log data with seismic data. Extract seismic attributes and lithology data along the time domain at well locations to establish the initial sample set. 3.Seismic Attribute Optimization: Based on the RFECV method, use the initial sample set as input data to optimize the extracted seismic attributes, obtaining the subset most highly correlated with sandbodies. Apply the optimized attributes to the seismic data at well locations and combine them with well log lithology data to form the optimized sample set. 4. Class balance correction: Perform class balance on the optimized sample set to equalize the number of sandstone and mudstone samples. Use this balanced set as the input data for the LightGBM model. 5.Grid Parameter Tuning: Construct the LightGBM model. Split the input data into training and test sets in an 8:2 ratio. Utilize GridSearchCV grid search to optimize and tune the LightGBM model parameters, identifying the optimal parameter combination to maximize model performance and enhance generalization. 6.Predict SandBody Distribution in Sections: Extract seismic attributes for the target interval along seismic sections containing wells. Optimize these attributes using the selected subset. Input the optimized attributes into the trained LightGBM model to predict the sandbody distribution within the target interval of that section. The method flowchart is shown in Fig. 2.

Field Application

The data used in this study is from the publicly available OpendTect dataset for the F3 Block in the Dutch North Sea (https://terranubis.com/datainfo/F3- Demo-2023). This area exhibits a prominent large-scale S-shaped reflection on seismic data, characteristic of a river-dominated delta primarily composed of sandstone

and mudstone. Available data includes 3D post-stack seismic data, seismically inverted P-impedance data, geostatistically inverted natural gamma ray data (totaling 11 seismic attributes), and lithology data from four wells within the block.

Fig. 2 Method workflow diagram.

Software versions used: Python 3.8.19, pandas 1.3.5, scikit-learn 1.0.2, LightGBM 3.3.0.

Well-to-Seismic Matching

We performed well-to-seismic matching for the four known wells. Due to inherent differences in data acquisition physics between well logs (point measurements) and seismic survrys (volume illumination),, well log data must be converted from the depth domain to the time domain using the time­depth conversion file before prediction to establish correspondence between seismic and well log data. The known seismic data sampling rate is 4ms. Consequently, the depth-converted well log data was resampled at 4ms to ensure consistency with seismic data in the time domain. Grid data sampling was used to extract seismic data from traces adjacent to the wells. Well log data and seismic data at the same time were combined (Wang et al., 2018). As the block is primarily composed of sandstone and mudstone, only these two lithologies were retained. To ensure the input data format is recognizable by the machine learning model, mudstone was coded as 0 and sandstone as 1, constructing the initial sample set as shown in Table 1. Due to the limited number of wells with known lithology (four) and the 4ms seismic sampling rate, the number of lithology samples is relatively small.

Seismic Attribute Optimization

A single seismic attribute can lead to ambiguity, while too many attributes can adversely affect sandbody identification. Consequently, a machine learning approach was used for seismic attribute optimization. Given the limited labeled data available, the quality of features becomes far more important than their quantity, necessitating rigorous feature engineering. For this block, 11 seismic attributes were selected for analysis and optimization: natural gamma ray, P-impedance, amplitude, instantaneous amplitude, instantaneous

frequency, RMS energy, amplitude kurtosis, quality factor Q, and spectral energy at 24Hz, 44Hz, and 64Hz. After well-to-seismic matching, we combined these attributes with well log lithology data to form the initial sample set and then standardized the data to eliminate unit differences. To screen for attributes highly correlated with sandbodies, we performed attribute optimization using the RFECV method. The LightGBM classifier was selected as the base model. The RFECV recursion step size was set to 1, and cross-validation folds were set to 5. Balanced accuracy was chosen as the evaluation metric

to balance computational efficiency and result stability. We performed recursive feature elimination on the initial sample set. Feature importance was calculated in each iteration, and the lowest-ranked attribute was eliminated until all features were removed. Using 5-fold cross­validation, the model's CV score on the validation set was computed for each fold. The feature subsets' scores were compared, and the subset with the highest score was selected as the optimal combination.

Fig. 3 shows the CV scores for subsets of different

sizes. The highest score (0.664) was achieved with 8 features. Consequently, this was chosen as the optimal subset. Within this subset, attributes ranked by importance (highest to lowest) are: Natural Gamma Ray, P-Impedance, 24Hz Spectral Energy, Instantaneous Frequency, 64Hz Spectral Energy, 44Hz Spectral Energy, Instantaneous Amplitude, and RMS Energy, as shown in Fig. 4. Using this subset as the standard, the sample set was refined to retain only the optimized seismic attributes.

The natural gamma log records the radioactivity intensity of the formation, primarily produced by radioactive elements. Since pure quartz sand contains almost no radioactive elements and mudstone contains a relatively high amount of clay minerals, areas with lower natural gamma values may indicate the presence of sandbodies. P-wave impedance is the product of

density and P-wave velocity, reflecting the resistance encountered by seismic waves as they pass through a medium. Generally, the P-wave impedance of sandstone is lower than that of the surrounding rock formations. Frequency-divided energy refers to the energy level of seismic signals at specific frequencies. Different types of rocks respond differently to seismic waves of different

frequencies. Instantaneous amplitude describes how the amplitude of seismic data changes over time. The acoustic impedance difference between sandbodies and surrounding rocks causes variations in the amplitude of reflected waves, aiding in the identification of sandbody locations. This information collectively helps in distinguishing and identifying sandbodies within geological formations effectively.

Class imbalance correction

To mitigate the impact of class imbalance on the machine learning model, Synthetic Minority Over­sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to the existing sample set. This technique synthesizes minority class samples to increase their representation within the sample set, thereby improving model generalization ability (Chawla et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2020). The result of the class imbalance correction is shown in Fig. 5.

Class distribution after balancing

Fig. 5 Class imbalance correctionresult plot.

LightGBM Application

A LightGBM model was constructed to establish the mapping relationship between seismic attributes and sandbodies. To address potential issues like missing values or outliers in the seismic attribute data, the optimized sample set underwent data preprocessing, including removing invalid and outlier values. Notwithstanding, as LightGBM is a tree-based model where numerical scaling does not affect split point positions, standardization was not applied to the optimized sample set. The preprocessed, optimized sample set served as input data. Due to the limited sample size, reserving an entire well log for testing was not feasible. Instead, the entire sample set was split into training and test sets in an 8:2 ratio.

The key to model performance lies in parameter selection. This study used the sklearn API version of LightGBM combined with grid search for parameter tuning and optimization. The learning rate was set to 0.1 after sensitivity analysis, and early stopping was set to 30 rounds to expedite the tuning of other parameters. Parameters like number of boosted trees, maximum number of leaves, subsample ratio for training data, subsample ratio of features for each tree, L1 regularization term on leaf weights and L2 regularization term on leaf weights were optimized sequentially. The learning rate determines the speed at which the model converges. A smaller learning rate, combined with a larger number of number of boosted trees, can achieve better generalization performance. The maximum number of leaves directly influences the expressive power of a single tree; notwithstanding, a larger value significantly increases the risk of overfitting. Subsample ratio for training data and subsample ratio of features for each tree can reduce overfitting and improve training speed. These parameters control the fraction of data and features used for training each tree, respectively, thereby adding randomness to the training process which helps in reducing overfitting. L1 regularization term on leaf weights and L2 regularization term on leaf weights serve as regularization parameters. Lambda_l1 applies L1 regularization which can lead to sparse solutions where some feature weights are reduced to zero, effectively performing feature selection. Lambda_l2 applies L2 regularization which penalizes the square of the weights, leading to smaller and more diffuse weight values across all features, helping to prevent overfitting by discouraging the model from becoming overly complex. By tuning these parameters appropriately, one can enhance the model's ability to generalize well to new, unseen data while mitigating the risk of overfitting. Finally, we performed a grid search for the optimal learning rate based on this optimized parameter set, determining its final value based on the score, resulting in the optimal parameter set, The optimal parameter set obtained is: learning_rate: 0.03, number of boosted trees = 300, maximum number of leaves = 14, subsample ratio for training data = 0.2, subsample ratio of features for each tree = 0.9, L1 regularization term on leaf weights = 0.3, L2 regularization term on leaf weights = 0.01. The ROC curve after tuning is shown in Fig. 6. The AUC value reached 0.823, significantly better than random guessing, demonstrating good sand-mudstone discrimination capability.

The optimal parameter set was used as the parameters for the LightGBM model. The optimized seismic attribute set served as input data, and lithology data served as labels for training the LightGBM model. LightGBM training utilizes an ensemble learning approach with multiple decision trees for classification.

It first selects the feature and split point providing the highest information gain for sandbodies. Continuous features are discretized into histograms, reducing computation and supporting parallelization. Logarithmic loss (log loss) is used to measure the difference between predicted probabilities and true labels. Each tree fits the negative gradient of the previous tree, progressively optimizing the loss function. After training, sections containing known wells were selected for prediction. Based on the inline and crossline values of a well, the optimized seismic data for the target interval along that section was sliced. These optimized seismic attributes were input into the trained LightGBM model for prediction. To predict sandbodies, seismic attribute data is input sequentially into each decision tree. Based on node splitting rules, the data is directed to leaf nodes. Finally, the prediction score sums from the leaf nodes of all trees are aggregated. A Sigmoid function converts this sum into a probability, indicating the likelihood of a sample point being sandstone. After obtaining the prediction results, the probability threshold was fine­tuned based on the visual outcome to determine the best prediction effect. The prediction accuracy for single wells is highest when the probability threshold is set to 0.65. Additionally, the resulting sandbody distribution aligns well with actual geological understanding.

Consequently, a probability of 0.65 is determined as the optimal threshold for classification. Sample points with a sandstone probability ≥ 65% are classified as sandstone; those < 65% are classified as mudstone.

For the single-well section selected within the 3D volume, the predicted sand-mudstone distribution achieved a maximum accuracy of 80.77% when validated against the actual well log interpretation results from the blind well F03-4. The prediction results for all sample points along the section were integrated to generate the final predicted section.

Prediction Result Analysis

Due to the complexity of seismic data and potential errors in well log data collection and processing, overemphasizing exact agreement between prediction results and well log lithology labels may not yield the best predictive outcome. As shown in the prediction figures for well F03-2 (Fig. 7), well F03-4 (Fig. 8), and the 3D view of F03-4 (Fig. 9), the images display inline slices at the locations of wells F03-2 and F03-4, along with the seismic profile and predicted sandbody distribution in 3D around well F03-4. The original seismic data in the F3 Block contains significant noise, which impacts the prediction results. The sandbody results predicted by the LightGBM method show high consistency with the two well logs. The distribution of sandbodies between wells corresponds well with the extension of seismic reflectors. Overall, sandstone layers in this block are primarily located at the top of the target interval, mudstone layers at the bottom, with sand­mudstone interbeds in the middle. As shown in Figures 7 and 8, the prediction results for slices containing both wells exhibit this characteristic, demonstrating good stability. Unlike conventional understanding where sand­mudstone distribution is heavily influenced by seismic amplitude, the feature importance ranking (Fig. 4) indicates that distribution in this area is most influenced by natural gamma ray values: high values typically correspond to mudstone, low values to sandstone. Strong correlations also exist with other highly important attributes like 24Hz spectral energy and P-impedance, reflecting unique characteristics of this region. Compared to results using all 11 attributes, predictions using the optimized 8 attributes show finer and more precise delineation between sandstone and mudstone, and more accurate identification of subtle sandbodies, better depicting their spatial extent and location. layers predominantly located above and mudstone layers below. This is consistent with the prediction

results from a single section. It can be observed that the deltaic deposits spread in a northeast-southwest direction. This visualization helps in understanding the spatial relationship and geological structure of the subsurface, providing insights into the depositional environment and aiding in the accurate identification of potential hydrocarbon reservoirs or aquifers. Overall, the prediction results demonstrate good accuracy and continuity, showing a strong correspondence with well log lithology and aligning well with the actual distribution of sandbodies.

Conclusions

This paper proposes a seismic multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on the LightGBM- RFECV coupling algorithm. After performing well- to-seismic matching on seismic and well log data, the RFECV method is used to optimize and select the seismic attribute subset most highly correlated with sandbodies. This subset is input into the LightGBM model for training. Grid parameter tuning is employed to find the LightGBM model with optimal performance. The trained model was used to predict sandbodies in seismic sections from a field block. Results demonstrate that this method can more accurately delineate sandbody regions.

LightGBM effectively compresses seismic dimensionality, increasing model training speed while preserving key formation reflection characteristics. The RFECV method optimizes the seismic attribute set using a machine learning model; the selected attributes show high correlation with sandbodies. Using this subset as input data achieves finer prediction results. Using the seismic attribute subset as input data and sandbody information as sample labels effectively captures the nonlinear relationship between sandbodies and seismic attributes, deeply mining the underlying feature information within the data. Predicting sandbodies along sections containing two wells in the Dutch North Sea F3 Block yielded results that accurately reflect the sandbody distribution in these sections, achieving geologically reasonable predictions. This verifies the method's practicality and provides a new approach for seismic sandbody identification.
