Biofuels supply 
Supply functions for corn, non-corn grain, and cellulosic biomass feedstocks are available on an annual 
basis through 2050 for ethanol production (blended into transportation fuel). Supply functions for soy 
oil, other seed-based oils, and grease are available on an annual basis through 2050 for biodiesel, 
renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production. Available ethanol imports and 
potential ethanol exports are represented by supply and demand curves, respectively.
Corn feedstock 
Corn feedstock supplies and costs are represented in the LFMM as corn supply curves, defined using U.S. 
corn supply and cost data and corn-to-ethanol data provided by Polysys in the NEMS Renewable Fuels 
Module (RFM).8 Operating costs of corn ethanol plants are from the U.S. Department of Agriculture 
(USDA) survey of ethanol plant costs.9 Energy requirements come from a study about energy 
consumption by corn and ethanol producers.10
Biodiesel and renewable diesel feedstock 
Biodiesel and renewable diesel feedstock supplies include seed oils, yellow grease, and white grease. 
Seed oils include soybean, cottonseed, sunflower, and canola oils. All seed oil supplies, except soybean 
oils, are provided externally to NEMS. The price and supply data for soybean oil come from Polysys in 
the RFM. Based on a 2019 to 2020 estimate by USDA11 in July 2020, the LFMM assumes that 34.3% of 
the soybean oil supply is used for biodiesel. We use the soybean oil price as a proxy for defining the 
price in the seed oil supply curves. The supply data for yellow and white grease that are available for 
biodiesel production are a function of regional population, fat production, and an estimate of how much
Apil 2026
U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
19
fat is available for biodiesel production. Corresponding costs are about 67.5% of soybean oil supply 
costs.
Biomass feedstock 
The RFM in NEMS provides cellulosic (biomass) feedstock supply and costs. Initial capital costs for 
biomass cellulosic ethanol come from a research project that reviewed cost estimates from multiple 
sources. Operating costs and credits for excess electricity generated at biomass ethanol plants are from 
a survey of literature.12
Ethanol exports 
Demand curves for ethanol exports allow corn ethanol to be exported. The curve is an isoelastic demand 
curve built from an initial price, quantity, and elasticity (Po, Qo, ε=-0.4). For historical years, we estimate 
Po to be 50% higher than the historical domestic wholesale ethanol price, and Po grows 1% each 
projection year. We assume Qo to grow 2.5% from the previous year, beginning with historical 2019 
levels. Po is in dollars per barrel ($/b), and Qo is in thousand barrels per calendar day (Mb/cd).
Ethanol imports 
Ethanol import supply curves represent sugarcane ethanol available for import from Brazil. The curve is 
an isoelastic supply curve built from an initial price, quantity, and elasticity (Po, Qo, ε=0.4). For historical 
years, we estimate Po to be 2% higher than the historical domestic wholesale ethanol price, and Po 
grows 2% each projection year. We assume Qo to grow 1% from the previous year, beginning with 
historical 2019 levels (Po in $/b, Qo in Mb/cd).
Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) 
Modeling the RFS in EISA2007 required a number of assumptions:
• 
The penetration of cellulosic ethanol into the market is limited to one operational plant before 
2023. 
• 
Methyl ester biodiesel (FAME) production contributes 1.50 credits toward the advanced 
requirement. 
• 
Renewable diesel fuel contributes 1.70 credits toward the biomass-based diesel requirement. 
• 
Diesel from biomass pyrolysis and Fischer-Tropsch contribute 1.70 credits toward the cellulosic 
requirement. 
• 
Cellulosic drop-in gasoline contributes 1.54 credits toward the cellulosic requirement. 
• 
Imported sugarcane ethanol from Brazil contributes 1 credit and counts toward the advanced 
renewable requirement. 
• 
Separate biofuel waivers can be activated for each of the four RFS fuel categories. 
• 
Renewable diesel is compatible with diesel engines without significant infrastructure 
modification (either in vehicles or delivery infrastructure). 
• 
Ethanol is consumed as E10, E15, or E85 with no intermediate blends. The cost of placing E85 
pumps at the most economical stations is spread over diesel and gasoline pump costs. 
• 
To accommodate the ethanol requirements, transportation modes are expanded or upgraded 
for E10, E15, and E85, and we assume most ethanol originates in the Midwest and has nominal 
transportation costs of a few cents per gallon.
Apil 2026
U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
20
• 
For E85 dispensing stations, the average cost to retrofit an existing station or to build a new 
station is about $160,000 per station (2016 dollars). Interregional transportation is by rail, ship, 
barge, and truck, and the associated costs are included in the LFMM. 
• 
LFMM does not model all fuels and accounting items that EPA includes in the RFS requirements 
(for example, biogas, renewable heating fuel imports, renewable identification number [RIN] 
banking), which is why the LFMM models reduced RFS targets. 
• 
No small refinery exemptions are modeled for 2021 and onward.
Non-petroleum fossil fuel supply 
As of AEO2026, the LFMM no longer models domestic coal-to-liquids, gas-to-liquids, or biomass-to-
liquids facilities. These technologies have not proven to be economically feasible given recent market 
conditions, but they will be included in future versions of LFMM if economics shift.
Combined heat and power (CHP) 
Electricity consumption at refineries and other liquid fuels production facilities is a function of the 
throughput of each unit. Sources of electricity consist of:
• 
Refinery power generation 
• 
Utility purchases 
• 
CHP from other liquid fuels producers (including cellulosic ethanol, and advanced ethanol)
The LFMM linear program models power generators and CHP plants as separate units, and they are 
allowed to compete with purchased electricity. Operating characteristics for these electricity producers 
are based on historical parameters and available data. Sales to the grid or own-use decisions are made 
on an economic basis within the LP solution. The price for electricity sales to the grid is set to the 
marginal energy price for baseload generation (provided by the EMM for each NEMS model year).
Short-term methodology 
Our November 2025 Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) forecasts U.S. petroleum balance and price 
information for 2025 and 2026 at the national level. The LFMM adopts STEO results for 2025 and 2026, 
using regional estimates based on the national STEO forecasts.
Legislation and regulation
The Tax Payer Relief Act of 1997  
This law reduces excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gases and methanol produced from natural gas. 
The reductions set taxes on these products equal to the federal gasoline tax, based on British thermal 
units.
Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 (CAAA90) 
Title II of CAAA90 established regulations for oxygenated and reformulated gasoline and on-highway 
diesel fuel. The LFMM explicitly models these regulations. Reformulated gasoline represented in the 
LFMM meets the requirements of Phase 2 of the Complex Model, except in the Pacific region where it 
meets Phase 3 specifications.
Apil 2026
U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
21
EPA’s Tier 3 Vehicle Emissions and Fuel Standards 
EPA’s Tier 3 Vehicle Emissions and Fuel Standards require the average annual sulfur content of federal 
gasoline to contain no more than 10 ppm after January 1, 2017. For years before 2017, AEO2026 reflects 
the Tier 2 Motor Vehicle Emissions Standards and Gasoline Sulfur Control Requirements, which require 
the average annual sulfur content of all gasoline used in the United States to be no more than 30 ppm.
Heavy-Duty Engine and Vehicle Standards and Highway Diesel Fuel Sulfur Control 
Requirements 
All highway diesel must not contain more than 15 ppm sulfur at the pump.
Nonroad, locomotive, and marine diesel regulation (NRLM) 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requires that nonroad diesel supplies must not contain 
more than 15 ppm sulfur. For locomotive and marine diesel, these requirements established a NRLM 
limit of 15 ppm beginning in mid-2012.
Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPACT2005) 
EPACT2005 sets a number of requirements for the petroleum industry, which include removing the 
oxygenate requirement in RFG.
Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA2007) 
EISA2007 includes a number of provisions for the petroleum industry, including a Renewable Fuel 
Standard (RFS) that increases total U.S. consumption of renewable fuels. To account for the possibility 
that RFS targets might be unattainable at reasonable cost, LFMM includes a provision for purchasing 
waivers. EISA2007 specifies the price of a cellulosic waiver. The non-cellulosic LFMM RFS waivers 
function as maximum allowed Renewable Identification Number (RIN) prices. LFMM also assumes that 
EPA will reduce RFS targets as allowed by the EISA2007 statute.
EPA Mobile Air Toxics (MSAT2) 
The MSAT2 requires all gasoline products (including reformulated and conventional gasoline) produced 
at a refinery during a calendar year to contain no more than 0.62% benzene by volume. This 
requirement does not include gasoline produced or sold in California, which is already covered by the 
current California Phase 3 Reformulated Gasoline Program.
California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard 
This state law aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels in that state by 20% from 
2010 through 2030.
Oregon’s Clean Fuels Program 
This program aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels sold in Oregon by 10% by 
2025 from a 2015 baseline, followed by a 20% reduction by 2030 and a 37% reduction by 2035.
Washington’s Clean Fuels Standard 
This program aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels sold in Washington by 20% 
by 2034 from a 2017 baseline.
Apil 2026
U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
22
Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006 
The cap-and-trade program within the California Assembly Bill (AB32), the Global Warming Solutions Act 
of 2006 started on January 1, 2012, and enforceable compliance obligations began in 2013. Petroleum 
refineries receive allowances (calculated in the LFMM) in the cap-and-trade system based on the 
volumetric output of:
• 
Aviation gasoline 
• 
Motor gasoline 
• 
Kerosene-type jet fuel 
• 
Distillate fuel oil 
• 
Renewable liquid fuels 
• 
Asphalt
Suppliers of reformulated blendstock for oxygenate blending (RBOB) and Distillate Fuel Oil No. 1 and No. 
2 were required to comply starting in 2015 if the emissions from full combustion of these products were 
greater than or equal to 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) equivalent (mtCO2e) in any year 
from 2011 to 2014.
Other state laws 
Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, 
and Vermont all have laws that lower the sulfur content of all heating oil to ultra-low sulfur diesel 
(ULSD) levels over different time schedules. Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island law require a 
transition to at least 5% biodiesel content.
International Maritime Organization’s MARPOL Annex 6 
The LFMM does not explicitly represent the MARPOL Annex 6 rule that covers cleaner marine fuels and 
ocean ship engine emissions. However, the rule is reflected in the effects on transportation and 
petroleum product export demands, which are provided to the LFMM from the TDM and IEM, 
respectively, in NEMS. LFMM produces several fuels that meet marine fuel demands, including ULSD, 
low-sulfur residual fuel oil, and high-sulfur residual fuel oil (if the marine vessel has a scrubber on 
board).
Federal tax credits
The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) creates the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit for the sale and 
production of qualifying fuels from 2025 to 2027. Qualifying fuels are subject to specific emissions 
reductions and other requirements, such as the prevailing wage for employees. Total potential credits 
amount to $1.00/gal of transportation fuel or $1.75/gal of sustainable aviation fuel.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) extends the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit by two 
years through 2029, and the credit removes eligibility for imports. The OBBBA reduces the credit for 
sustainable aviation fuel from $1.75/gal to $1.00/gal starting in 2025 to match all other clean fuels.
Apil 2026
U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
23
In AEO2026, the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit is included as a $1.00/gal credit for 
domestically produced biodiesel, renewable diesel, renewable naphtha, and sustainable aviation fuel 
through 2029.
AEO2026 also includes scheduled sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. These sales, 
which occur between 2016 and 2031, are required by a number of congressional acts.13

The National Energy Modeling System’s (NEMS) Liquid Fuels Market Module (LFMM) projects petroleum 
product prices and sources of liquid fuels supply for meeting petroleum product demand. The sources of 
liquid fuels supply include:

• 
Petroleum-based fuels, such as: 
– Domestic and imported crude oil 
– Petroleum product imports 
– Unfinished oil imports 
• 
Non-petroleum-based inputs, such as:  
– Alcohols 
– Ethers 
– Esters 
– Corn 
– Biomass 
– Natural gas 
– Coal 
• 
Other liquid fuels inputs, such as: 
– Natural gas plant liquids production 
– Refinery processing gain
The LFMM also projects capacity changes and fuel consumption at domestic refineries.

To better represent policy, import and export patterns, and biofuels production, we created eight U.S. 
regions by subdividing three of the five Petroleum Administration for Defense Districts (PADDs) (Figure 
1). The LFMM also represents refining activity in the Maritime Canada and Caribbean refining region, 
which predominantly serves U.S. markets. The LFMM’s linear program (LP) represents:

• 
U.S. petroleum refining activities 
• 
Biofuels production activities 
• 
Other non-petroleum liquid fuels production activities

•

The nine LFMM regions and the import and export curves are connected in the LP model by crude oil 
and product transport links. To interact with other NEMS modules that have different regional 
representations, the module converts certain LFMM inputs and outputs from sub-PADD regions to other 
regional structures and vice versa. For example, the LP model converts end-use product prices from the 
LFMM regions (excluding the non-U.S. Maritime Canada and Caribbean region) into prices for the nine 
U.S. census divisions (Figure 2).

Key assumptions 
 
Product types and specifications 
The LFMM models refinery production for a number of products (Table 1).

The LFMM assumes no change in the state and federal specifications for the products listed in Table 1. 
The costs of producing different formulations of gasoline and diesel fuel required under current 
regulations are determined within the LP representation of refineries.

a CARB (California Air Resources Board) establishes regulations for gasoline and diesel specifications in California. 
 
 
Motor gasoline specifications and market shares 
The LFMM models production and distribution of two types of gasoline: conventional and reformulated. 
The LFMM includes several specifications to differentiate between conventional and reformulated 
gasoline blends (Table 2):

• 
Reid vapor pressure (RVP) 
• 
Benzene content 
• 
Aromatic content 
• 
Sulfur content 
• 
Olefins content 
• 
Percentage evaporated at 200°F and 300°F (E200 and E300)

The LFMM incorporates the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Tier 3 program requirement 
that the sulfur content of delivered gasoline must not be greater than 10 parts per million (ppm), 
effective January 1, 2017.1 The LFMM assumes refiners produce 5 ppm gasoline because some sulfur 
content will increase during transportation to the end user. By producing 5 ppm gasoline, the refiner 
ensures that the gasoline will meet the 10 ppm requirement by the time it gets to the end user.

PSI=pounds per square inch 
a The two values reflect sulfur levels before and after January 1, 2017, to meet the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) final 
ruling, “EPA Sets Tier 3 Motor Vehicle Emission and Fuel Standards.” The Liquid Fuels Market Module uses 5 ppm at the refinery to 
ensure sulfur contamination does not cause the specification to exceed 10 ppm at the market point.
b CARB (California Air Resources Board) establishes regulations for gasoline and diesel specifications in California.

Many areas in the United States have required reformulated gasoline (RFG) since January 1995.2 In 
1998, EPA began certifying reformulated gasoline using the Complex Model, which required refiners to 
achieve emissions reductions compared with a baseline for four categories.3 Other clean gasoline 
programs4 have currently subsumed requirements for air toxics, benzene, and nitrogen oxide emissions, 
leaving only a standard for volatile organic compounds. As an estimate of compliance with this 
remaining standard, LFMM restricts RVP to levels sufficient to achieve these reductions.

The Annual Energy Outlook 2026 (AEO2026) assumes a minimum 10% blend of ethanol in domestically 
consumed motor gasoline. Reformulated and conventional gasoline can be blended with up to 15% 
ethanol (E15) in light-duty vehicles for model years 2001 and later and with 51%–83% ethanol (E85) in 
flex-fuel vehicles (LFMM assumes an average annual ethanol content of 74% for E85 fuel). Current state 
regulations, along with marketplace constraints, limit the market share of E15 in the projection period. 
In addition, reformulated and conventional gasoline can be blended with 16% biobutanol; however, 
because no biobutanol has entered the gasoline market in recent years,5 AEO2026 assumes no 
biobutanol blends into motor gasoline. The Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA2007)

U.S. Energy Information Administration   |   Assumptions to the Annual Energy Outlook 2026: Liquid Fuels Market Module 
6

defines a Renewable Fuel Standards (RFS) schedule for blending renewable fuels into transportation 
fuels by 2025.

Although RVP limitations are in effect during the summer and typically differ by consuming region, the 
LFMM does not represent RVP at this level of detail. Instead, the LFMM assumes that the annual 
average specifications―based on summertime RVP limits, wintertime estimates, and seasonal 
weights―capture these variations in RVP.

Within the LFMM, total gasoline demand is separated into demand for conventional gasoline and 
demand for reformulated gasoline by applying assumptions about the annual market shares for each 
type. In AEO2026, the annual market shares for each region reflect actual 2015 market shares and 
remain constant throughout the projection period (Table 3).

Capacity change 
The LFMM allows for capacity expansion for all processing unit types, which include: 
• 
Distillation units, such as: 
– Atmospheric distillation unit (ADU) 
– Vacuum distillation unit (VDU) 
– Condensate splitters 
• 
Secondary processing units, such as: 
– Hydrotreating 
– Coking 
– Fluid catalytic cracking 
– Hydrocracking 
– Alkylation

Capacity expansion occurs by processing unit, starting from regional capacities established through 
historical data.

Expansion occurs in the LFMM when the value received from the sale of products that could be 
produced with new processing capacity exceeds the investment and operating costs of adding this new 
capacity, plus the cost of purchasing additional feedstock. The investment costs assume a financing ratio 
of 60% equity and 40% debt. Those costs also include an after-tax return on investment ranging from 6% 
for building new refinery processing units to more than 13% for higher-risk projects.

The LFMM models capacity expansion using a three-period (Periods 1, 2, and 3) planning approach 
similar to that used in the NEMS Electricity Market Module (EMM). The first two periods contain a single 
model year (current year and next year), and the third period represents a net present value of the next 
19 years in the projection period. The LFMM uses the second and third planning periods to establish an 
economic plan for capacity expansion for the next NEMS model year. In Period 2, product demands and 
legislative requirements must be met. Period 3 acts as leverage in the capacity expansion decision for 
Period 2, and this decision is controlled by the discount rate assumptions. Larger discount rates increase 
the net present value (NPV) of revenue and expenditures in earlier periods and decrease the NPV of 
revenue and expenditure in later periods. The LFMM uses multiple discount rates for the NPV 
calculation to represent various categories of risk. For AEO2026, the LFMM uses an 18% discount rate.

The LFMM also models capacity expansion for producing:  
• 
Corn and cellulosic ethanol 
• 
Biomass pyrolysis oil 
• 
Biodiesel 
• 
Renewable diesel 
• 
Sustainable aviation fuel

All process-unit capacity that is scheduled to begin operating in the future is added to existing capacities 
in their respective start years.

For AEO2026, the LFMM introduced an endogenous refinery retirement methodology. All eight U.S. 
LFMM refining regions are evaluated independently for retirement of petroleum refinery capacity each 
projection year after 2029.

Capacity utilization in a given region is computed as the ratio of throughput for the atmospheric 
distillation unit (ADU) to the total ADU capacity. Capacity retirements are triggered when ADU capacity 
utilization in a refining region dips below an 85% utilization threshold. For any year projected capacity 
utilization falls below this utilization threshold, a capacity reduction factor is calculated representing 
between 1% and 4% of existing capacity. As long as a refining region’s ADU capacity utilization is below 
the utilization threshold, existing capacity for all petroleum refining units in that region will be adjusted 
by the capacity reduction factor. If capacity utilization of the ADU goes above the utilization threshold 
due to retirements, refining capacity does not reduce further.

Throughput for an ADU is typically a blend of crude oils, but historically this throughput has included 
unfinished oil imports at some refineries. Therefore, historical ADU capacity utilization at these 
refineries includes both crude oil and unfinished oil imports. Because the LFMM processes unfinished oil 
imports only in secondary units, downstream from the ADU, an assumed historical percentage of the 
unfinished oils imported to the refinery was included as part of the throughput when calculating the 
ADU capacity utilization reported in AEO2026.

Biofuels supply 
Supply functions for corn, non-corn grain, and cellulosic biomass feedstocks are available on an annual 
basis through 2050 for ethanol production (blended into transportation fuel). Supply functions for soy 
oil, other seed-based oils, and grease are available on an annual basis through 2050 for biodiesel, 
renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production. Available ethanol imports and 
potential ethanol exports are represented by supply and demand curves, respectively.

Corn feedstock 
Corn feedstock supplies and costs are represented in the LFMM as corn supply curves, defined using U.S. 
corn supply and cost data and corn-to-ethanol data provided by Polysys in the NEMS Renewable Fuels 
Module (RFM).8 Operating costs of corn ethanol plants are from the U.S. Department of Agriculture 
(USDA) survey of ethanol plant costs.9 Energy requirements come from a study about energy 
consumption by corn and ethanol producers.10

Biodiesel and renewable diesel feedstock 
Biodiesel and renewable diesel feedstock supplies include seed oils, yellow grease, and white grease. 
Seed oils include soybean, cottonseed, sunflower, and canola oils. All seed oil supplies, except soybean 
oils, are provided externally to NEMS. The price and supply data for soybean oil come from Polysys in 
the RFM. Based on a 2019 to 2020 estimate by USDA11 in July 2020, the LFMM assumes that 34.3% of 
the soybean oil supply is used for biodiesel. We use the soybean oil price as a proxy for defining the 
price in the seed oil supply curves. The supply data for yellow and white grease that are available for 
biodiesel production are a function of regional population, fat production, and an estimate of how much

19

fat is available for biodiesel production. Corresponding costs are about 67.5% of soybean oil supply 
costs.

Biomass feedstock 
The RFM in NEMS provides cellulosic (biomass) feedstock supply and costs. Initial capital costs for 
biomass cellulosic ethanol come from a research project that reviewed cost estimates from multiple 
sources. Operating costs and credits for excess electricity generated at biomass ethanol plants are from 
a survey of literature.12

Ethanol exports 
Demand curves for ethanol exports allow corn ethanol to be exported. The curve is an isoelastic demand 
curve built from an initial price, quantity, and elasticity (Po, Qo, ε=-0.4). For historical years, we estimate 
Po to be 50% higher than the historical domestic wholesale ethanol price, and Po grows 1% each 
projection year. We assume Qo to grow 2.5% from the previous year, beginning with historical 2019 
levels. Po is in dollars per barrel ($/b), and Qo is in thousand barrels per calendar day (Mb/cd).

Ethanol imports 
Ethanol import supply curves represent sugarcane ethanol available for import from Brazil. The curve is 
an isoelastic supply curve built from an initial price, quantity, and elasticity (Po, Qo, ε=0.4). For historical 
years, we estimate Po to be 2% higher than the historical domestic wholesale ethanol price, and Po 
grows 2% each projection year. We assume Qo to grow 1% from the previous year, beginning with 
historical 2019 levels (Po in $/b, Qo in Mb/cd).

Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) 
Modeling the RFS in EISA2007 required a number of assumptions:

• 
The penetration of cellulosic ethanol into the market is limited to one operational plant before 
2023. 
• 
Methyl ester biodiesel (FAME) production contributes 1.50 credits toward the advanced 
requirement. 
• 
Renewable diesel fuel contributes 1.70 credits toward the biomass-based diesel requirement. 
• 
Diesel from biomass pyrolysis and Fischer-Tropsch contribute 1.70 credits toward the cellulosic 
requirement. 
• 
Cellulosic drop-in gasoline contributes 1.54 credits toward the cellulosic requirement. 
• 
Imported sugarcane ethanol from Brazil contributes 1 credit and counts toward the advanced 
renewable requirement. 
• 
Separate biofuel waivers can be activated for each of the four RFS fuel categories. 
• 
Renewable diesel is compatible with diesel engines without significant infrastructure 
modification (either in vehicles or delivery infrastructure). 
• 
Ethanol is consumed as E10, E15, or E85 with no intermediate blends. The cost of placing E85 
pumps at the most economical stations is spread over diesel and gasoline pump costs. 
• 
To accommodate the ethanol requirements, transportation modes are expanded or upgraded 
for E10, E15, and E85, and we assume most ethanol originates in the Midwest and has nominal 
transportation costs of a few cents per gallon.

• 
For E85 dispensing stations, the average cost to retrofit an existing station or to build a new 
station is about $160,000 per station (2016 dollars). Interregional transportation is by rail, ship,

• 
LFMM does not model all fuels and accounting items that EPA includes in the RFS requirements

Non-petroleum fossil fuel supply 
As of AEO2026, the LFMM no longer models domestic coal-to-liquids, gas-to-liquids, or biomass-to-
liquids facilities. These technologies have not proven to be economically feasible given recent market 
conditions, but they will be included in future versions of LFMM if economics shift.

Combined heat and power (CHP) 
Electricity consumption at refineries and other liquid fuels production facilities is a function of the 
throughput of each unit. Sources of electricity consist of:

• 
Refinery power generation 
• 
Utility purchases 
• 
CHP from other liquid fuels producers (including cellulosic ethanol, and advanced ethanol)

The LFMM linear program models power generators and CHP plants as separate units, and they are 
allowed to compete with purchased electricity. Operating characteristics for these electricity producers 
are based on historical parameters and available data. Sales to the grid or own-use decisions are made 
on an economic basis within the LP solution. The price for electricity sales to the grid is set to the 
marginal energy price for baseload generation (provided by the EMM for each NEMS model year).

Short-term methodology 
Our November 2025 Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) forecasts U.S. petroleum balance and price 
information for 2025 and 2026 at the national level. The LFMM adopts STEO results for 2025 and 2026, 
using regional estimates based on the national STEO forecasts.

The Tax Payer Relief Act of 1997  
This law reduces excise taxes on liquefied petroleum gases and methanol produced from natural gas. 
The reductions set taxes on these products equal to the federal gasoline tax, based on British thermal 
units.

Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 (CAAA90) 
Title II of CAAA90 established regulations for oxygenated and reformulated gasoline and on-highway 
diesel fuel. The LFMM explicitly models these regulations. Reformulated gasoline represented in the 
LFMM meets the requirements of Phase 2 of the Complex Model, except in the Pacific region where it 
meets Phase 3 specifications.

EPA’s Tier 3 Vehicle Emissions and Fuel Standards 
EPA’s Tier 3 Vehicle Emissions and Fuel Standards require the average annual sulfur content of federal 
gasoline to contain no more than 10 ppm after January 1, 2017. For years before 2017, AEO2026 reflects 
the Tier 2 Motor Vehicle Emissions Standards and Gasoline Sulfur Control Requirements, which require 
the average annual sulfur content of all gasoline used in the United States to be no more than 30 ppm.

Heavy-Duty Engine and Vehicle Standards and Highway Diesel Fuel Sulfur Control 
Requirements 
All highway diesel must not contain more than 15 ppm sulfur at the pump.

Nonroad, locomotive, and marine diesel regulation (NRLM) 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requires that nonroad diesel supplies must not contain 
more than 15 ppm sulfur. For locomotive and marine diesel, these requirements established a NRLM 
limit of 15 ppm beginning in mid-2012.

Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPACT2005) 
EPACT2005 sets a number of requirements for the petroleum industry, which include removing the 
oxygenate requirement in RFG.

Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA2007) 
EISA2007 includes a number of provisions for the petroleum industry, including a Renewable Fuel 
Standard (RFS) that increases total U.S. consumption of renewable fuels. To account for the possibility 
that RFS targets might be unattainable at reasonable cost, LFMM includes a provision for purchasing 
waivers. EISA2007 specifies the price of a cellulosic waiver. The non-cellulosic LFMM RFS waivers 
function as maximum allowed Renewable Identification Number (RIN) prices. LFMM also assumes that 
EPA will reduce RFS targets as allowed by the EISA2007 statute.

EPA Mobile Air Toxics (MSAT2) 
The MSAT2 requires all gasoline products (including reformulated and conventional gasoline) produced 
at a refinery during a calendar year to contain no more than 0.62% benzene by volume. This 
requirement does not include gasoline produced or sold in California, which is already covered by the 
current California Phase 3 Reformulated Gasoline Program.

California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard 
This state law aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels in that state by 20% from 
2010 through 2030.

Oregon’s Clean Fuels Program 
This program aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels sold in Oregon by 10% by 
2025 from a 2015 baseline, followed by a 20% reduction by 2030 and a 37% reduction by 2035.

Washington’s Clean Fuels Standard 
This program aims to reduce the carbon intensity of gasoline and diesel fuels sold in Washington by 20% 
by 2034 from a 2017 baseline.

The cap-and-trade program within the California Assembly Bill (AB32), the Global Warming Solutions Act 
of 2006 started on January 1, 2012, and enforceable compliance obligations began in 2013. Petroleum 
refineries receive allowances (calculated in the LFMM) in the cap-and-trade system based on the 
volumetric output of:

• 
Motor gasoline 
• 
Kerosene-type jet fuel

• 
Renewable liquid fuels 
• 
Asphalt

Suppliers of reformulated blendstock for oxygenate blending (RBOB) and Distillate Fuel Oil No. 1 and No. 
2 were required to comply starting in 2015 if the emissions from full combustion of these products were 
greater than or equal to 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) equivalent (mtCO2e) in any year 
from 2011 to 2014.

Other state laws 
Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, 
and Vermont all have laws that lower the sulfur content of all heating oil to ultra-low sulfur diesel 
(ULSD) levels over different time schedules. Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island law require a 
transition to at least 5% biodiesel content.

International Maritime Organization’s MARPOL Annex 6 
The LFMM does not explicitly represent the MARPOL Annex 6 rule that covers cleaner marine fuels and 
ocean ship engine emissions. However, the rule is reflected in the effects on transportation and 
petroleum product export demands, which are provided to the LFMM from the TDM and IEM, 
respectively, in NEMS. LFMM produces several fuels that meet marine fuel demands, including ULSD, 
low-sulfur residual fuel oil, and high-sulfur residual fuel oil (if the marine vessel has a scrubber on 
board).

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) creates the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit for the sale and 
production of qualifying fuels from 2025 to 2027. Qualifying fuels are subject to specific emissions 
reductions and other requirements, such as the prevailing wage for employees. Total potential credits 
amount to $1.00/gal of transportation fuel or $1.75/gal of sustainable aviation fuel.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) extends the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit by two 
years through 2029, and the credit removes eligibility for imports. The OBBBA reduces the credit for 
sustainable aviation fuel from $1.75/gal to $1.00/gal starting in 2025 to match all other clean fuels.

In AEO2026, the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production credit is included as a $1.00/gal credit for

through 2029.

AEO2026 also includes scheduled sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. These sales,

Characterization of Three Forks Formation Reservoir Lithofacies in 
the Williston Basin, North Dakota 
 
Adedoyin Adeyilola*1, Stephan Nordeng2, Chioma Onwumelu2, Olusegun Tomomewo2, 
1. Central Michigan University, 2. University of North Dakota 
 
Copyright 2020, Unconventional Resources Technology Conference (URTeC) DOI 10.15530/urtec-2020-3237 
 
This paper was prepared for presentation at the Unconventional Resources Technology Conference held in Austin, Texas, USA, 20-
22 July 2020.
The URTeC Technical Program Committee accepted this presentation on the basis of information contained in an abstract 
submitted by the author(s). The contents of this paper have not been reviewed by URTeC and URTeC does not warrant the 
accuracy, reliability, or timeliness of any information herein. All information is the responsibility of, and, is subject to corrections by 
the author(s). Any person or entity that relies on any information obtained from this paper does so at their own risk. The information 
herein does not necessarily reflect any position of URTeC. Any reproduction, distribution, or storage of any part of this paper by 
anyone other than the author without the written consent of URTeC is prohibited.
Abstract
The continuous demand for energy and advancement in technology has accelerated the research in the 
areas of unconventional petroleum resources. The Devonian Three Forks Formation consisting of 
carbonate and clastic sediments is an unconventional reservoir with about 3.73 billion barrels of 
technically recoverable oil. However, major gaps remain in the knowledge of how mineralogy, structures 
and fabrics within the various lithofacies have influenced the hydrocarbon storage and transport capacity. 
This work integrates petrographic (physical rock description, XRD bulk mineralogy and thin section) and 
petrophysical (Helium pycnometry and NMR) studies in characterizing the reservoir potentials of the 
Three Forks lithofacies. Physical core description and wireline logs were utilized to identify and correlate 
seven (7) lithofacies within the Three Forks Formation. They are: 1) green - grey massive mudstone; 2) 
tan massive dolostone; 3) grey - tan laminated mudstone and dolostone; 4) tan - dark brown mottled 
dolostone; 5) grey and tan mottled mudstone; 6) grey and tan mudstone conglomerates; and 7) grey and 
tan brecciated mudstone. Diverse pore types were identified within various lithofacies, with microporosity 
pores dominating the mudstone rich lithofacies and interparticle pores dominating the dolostone rich 
lithofacies. Preliminary results showed the dolostone lithofacies have relatively lower total porosities 
while the mudstone lithofacies have relatively higher total porosity values.
Introduction
The Three Forks Formation is a tight reservoir in the Bakken-Three Forks unconventional petroleum 
accumulation in the Williston basin (Lefever et al. 1991, Nordeng et al. 2010, Nesheim 2019). The 
Devonian Three Forks Formation directly underlies the Bakken Formation and overlies the Bird Bear 
Formation. It is mainly an association of tight carbonates, clastic sediments and anhydrites. The amount of 
oil in place within the Bakken- Three Forks system is estimated to be about 7.8 billion barrels with almost 
a half of it from the Bakken Formation while the other half is from the Three Forks Formation (Gaswirth 
and Marra 2015). Apart from being a thermally matured and prolific a source rock, the Bakken Formation 
has produced an appreciable amount of oil through advanced drilling, completion and stimulation
<image: Indexed(44,DeviceRGB), width: 250, height: 52, bpc: 8>
URTeC 3237
techniques (Lefever and Nordeng 2015). Oil discovery and production in the Bakken-Three Forks system 
began in 1953 from the Antelope Field with vertical wells (Lefever and Nordeng 2015).
The lithofacies and stratigraphy of the Three Forks Formation have been studied by various researchers, 
they have been subdivided into different members and units based on mineralogical composition, structures, 
and other geological features (Nordeng and LeFever, 2009; Bottjer et al., 2011; Sonnenberg et. al., 2011; 
LeFever et. al., 2013; and Sonnenberg, 2017). Mudstones have varying pore types, sizes, and distribution 
that influences hydrocarbon distribution (Slatt and O’Brien, 2011). Primary porosity develop during 
deposition, and may be influenced by compaction, cementation, and burial (Desbois et al., 2009; Milliken 
and Reed, 2010 and Loucks et al., 2012) Carbonates are known to have complex and diverse pore networks 
due to multiple factors that increase, preserve, modify or destroy pores (Norbisrath et al., 2015; Li et al., 
2016a).  Researchers have utilized helium porosimetry (Grejj et al., 1993; Chalmers et. al, 2012; Adeyilola 
et. al 2020), mercury intrusion porosimetry (Loucks et. al 2009; Li et al., 2016b), nuclear magnetic 
resonance (Brigaud et. al 2014; Gharechelou et. al 2016; Awad 2019), gas adsorption (Bustin et. al., 2008; 
Zhang et al. 2017) small angle neutron scattering (Clarkson et al., 2013), micro-CT imaging (Lawal and 
Mahmoud, 2020), Scanning Electron Microscopy image analysis (Loucks et al., 2009; Klaver et al., 2016; 
Deng et al., 2016) and thin section petrography (Choquette and Pray, 1970, Lonoy 2006, Lai et. al 2020) to 
characterize tight reservoirs. Similarly, the point-load test (Broch and Franklin, 1972), rebound hardness 
test (Aydin and Basu, 2005), micro-indentation (Su et al., 2018), scratch test (Kolawole and Ispas, 2020), 
and other geomechanical methods (Zoback et al., 1985) has been utilized in characterizing the mechanical 
properties of mudstones. The goal of this research is to provide a better understanding of the Three Forks 
Formation reservoir qualities.
Fig. 1. County Map of North Dakota showing boundary states. (Inset: Fields of interest in Divide County)

Materials and Methods
Four wells from the Ambrose (NDIC# 22809), West Ambrose (NDIC# 26745 & 28042) and Colgan 
(NDIC# 23828) fields were utilized in this study (Fig. 1). They are all located in Divide County, North 
Dakota. Polished and epoxy stained thin sections were used to identify and characterize the pores, mineral 
assemblages and other depositional features with a transmitted light microscope. X-ray diffraction (XRD) 
was used to examine the bulk mineralogical composition of samples. Crushed and pulverized samples were 
analyzed with a RIGAKU Smartlab XRD equipment and results were interpreted with a PDXL software. 
Each sample was analyzed at 5 degrees to 90 degrees, two theta (5º-90º 2θ) in order to identify the entire 
mineral assemblage and distributions. 
 
Porosity was estimated using both helium porosimetry and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). The helium 
porosimetry method uses Boyle’s law gas expansion technique and pressure differences to penetrate pores 
within samples inside its chamber. Samples were initially dried to get rid of trapped moisture, weighed and 
transferred to a 3D Laser scanner that measures the bulk volume. Core samples of known mass and bulk 
volumes were inserted into the matrix cup in the porosimeter and filled with disks of known mass to occupy 
void spaces in the matrix cup. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) was used to quality check the helium 
porosity results and characterize pore fluid distribution within the rocks. Core samples were saturated in 
300,000 ppm brine at 100 psi for 60 days to match the estimated salinity of connate water in the Bakken 
Petroleum System. The saturated samples were analyzed for total porosity and pore fluid distribution with 
an Oxford Instruments Geospec 2 core analyzer.
Results and Discussion
Lithofacies identification and description 
 
Physical core description and wireline logs wells were used to identify and correlate the Three Forks 
reservoir lithofacies (Fig. 2). They are: 1) Laminated mudstone and dolostone lithofacies; 2) massive 
dolostone lithofacies; 3) mottled dolostone lithofacies; 4) massive mudstone lithofacies; 5) mottled 
mudstone lithofacies; 6) mudstone conglomerates lithofacies; and 7) brecciated mudstone lithofacies.  
 
1) 
Laminated Lithofacies: It consists of finely interlaminated grayish-green to greenish-gray dolomitic 
mudstones and pinkish-tan silty dolostones. Laminar bedding ranges from less than 1cm up to 
approximately 15cm with no preference to mineralogy. Unidirectional and bidirectional ripples are more 
visible in the tan dolostone compared to the green mudstone. The different lithologies are mostly separated 
by a sharp contact or gradation which include both fining and coarsening upward sequences. Lithofacies 
thickness is about 2 to 5ft (Fig. 2A & 2B). 
 
2) 
Massive Dolostone: This a tan dolostone lithofacies which is mainly composed of silt and sand-
size dolomite. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the very fine sand range 
(~0.07 mm). It is composed mainly of dolomite and trace amount of quartz and clay. They also have sub-
rounded lenses that are probable deformed dolomite-filled burrows. No major sedimentary structure, they 
have massive texture and scoured surfaces. Lithofacies thickness varies from 1 to 3ft (Fig. 2C).   
 
3) 
Mottled Dolostone: Predominantly tan dolostone with interbed of green - grey mudstone. They 
contain about 20 to 40 percent thinly interbedded green mudstone that are slightly folded and deformed due 
to the soft sediment deformation. They are flaser bedded, slightly laminated and contain deformed thinly 
laminated silty dolostones. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the fine sand 
range (~0.07 mm). Thickness of this lithofacies is approximately 1 to 4ft (Fig. 2D).
URTeC 3237
4) 
Massive Mudstone: This unit is a thinly laminated green to grayish-green mudstone. They are clay-
sized, matrix supported rock with sparsely scattered, silt-sized, dolomite and quartz grains. Abundant 
burrows and crystal aggregates of variable sizes are distributed irregularly throughout this unit. The texture 
is massive with no visible sedimentary structure.  Thickness of this lithofacies is approximately 0.5 to 3.5 
ft (Fig. 2E). 
 
5) 
Mottled Mudstone: It composed of light brown dolomitic shaly siltstone and gray to dark green 
dolomitic claystone.  They are massive, slightly laminated, flaser bedded with irregular distribution of 
dolostones. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the fine sand range (~0.07 
mm). They are chaotic, slightly brecciated with thickness ranging from less than 1 to 5ft (Fig. 2F). 
 
6) 
Mudstone conglomerates: This lithofacies consists of green-grey dolomitic mudstone matrix with 
tan dolomitic clasts. The clasts range in size from 0.5 to 2 cm and the matrix are predominantly silt size 
(~0.04 mm). Moderate to well-rounded and poorly sorted. Brown in the deeper section of Middle Three 
Forks due to oxidation. The lithofacies is matrix supported with no visible sedimentary structure (Fig. 2G).  
 
7) 
 Brecciated Mudstone: Composed of brecciated layers interbedded with reddish massive dolomitic 
mudstone with clasts. The clasts are angular and poorly sorted. They are chaotic with no visible sedimentary 
structure. It is matrix supported at the top and clast supported at the base. The matrix is silt size (~0.04 mm) 
while the clasts range from <1cm to 3.5cm (Fig. 2H & 2I). 
 
Pore types
Petrographic thin sections were used to characterize the various types of pores within these lithofacies under 
a petrographic microscope with plane polarized light. The dominant pores identified and described with the 
petrographic microscopes are interparticle, intercrystalline, fracture, vuggy and micropores.
1) 
Interparticle porosity: This class of pores occurs between two or more mineral grains (Choquette 
and Pray, 1970). Interparticle porosity is formed by well sorted sand-sized carbonate grains and minerals 
with little interstitial mud as seen in the massive dolostone, mottled dolostone and brecciated dolostone 
lithofacies (Fig. 3A).  
 
2) 
Intercrystalline porosity: This class of pores occur between crystals of either primary or secondary 
origin (Choquette and Pray, 1970). They typically occur at the edges of two or more dolomite crystals where 
they are characterized by their smooth and sharp edges. They occur in medium to coarse dolomite grain 
(fine-grained sand size) with cloudy core and clear as seen in the massive and mottled dolostone lithofacies. 
(Fig. 3B & 3C). 
 
3) 
Fracture Porosity: These are laterally extensive features that occur in both macroscopic and 
mesoscopic scale within the Three Forks Formation lithofacies Fractures occurring in mudstones are widely 
distributed and relatively longer while fractures in dolostone are less abundant and relatively shorter.  
Fractures in mudstones are both mineralized and non-mineralized (Fig. 3D). 
 
4) 
Vuggy Porosity: These are secondary solution pores that cuts across grains and cements boundaries 
(Lenoy, 2006). They are relatively larger and wider than all the other pores discussed, circular to elongated 
in shape and mostly interconnected. These pores are widely distributed in the sand-sized dolostone facie 
within the highly fractured brecciated mudstone lithofacies. (Fig. 3E).   
 
5) 
Mudstone microporosity: This group of pores are characterized by their extremely small pore sizes 
(<2um), they are the smallest in size and most widely distributed within the mudstone lithofacies in the 
Three Forks Formation (Fig. 3F).  The extremely small sizes of the dolomite crystals and mudstone matrix 
makes it challenging to classify them into intercrystalline or interparticle pores (Lonoy 2006).

Porosity
Helium, NMR porosities and XRD mineralogical composition results are displayed in Table 1. The results 
from the helium porosimetry analysis include grain density, bulk density, pore volume and total porosity. 
The massive dolostone is seen to have the lowest porosity (2.32 %), highest grain density (2.82 g/ml) and 
highest bulk density (2.75 g/ml).  The relatively higher grain density is attributed to the abundance of the 
dense dolomite minerals which is 67% of the total composition. Mottled dolostone lithofacies shows a 
relatively lower porosity, grain density and bulk density (5.62%, 2.75 g/ml and 2.59 g/ml respectively). 
Again, these differences in grain density, bulk density and porosity is controlled by the mineralogical 
composition as the dolomite was observed to have decreased relatively from the massive dolostone. The 
massive mudstone lithofacies have relatively low grain density (2.67 g/ml), lowest bulk density (2.42 g/ml) 
and hence the highest porosity (9.63%). This high porosity in the massive mudstone lithofacies is attributed 
to the abundance of low density siliciclastic minerals (clay, quartz and feldspars). Overall, the bulk and 
grain densities are observed to increase from the less dense clean mudstone lithofacies with relatively higher 
porosities into the denser clean dolostone lithofacies with relatively lower porosities.  
 
The results of the NMR transverse relaxation time analysis are displayed in Fig. 4.  The results show the 
incremental porosity in percentage versus transverse time in milliseconds. The peak of the curves 
corresponds to the transverse relaxation time (T2) with the highest porosity. The peak occurs at varying 
time on the T2 time axis depending on the pore distribution within the various lithofacies. T2 distribution in 
rocks with smaller pores have a corresponding shorter relation time (faster) and rocks with larger pores 
have corresponding longer relaxation time (slower) (Kleinberg et. al 1993; Kenyon, 1997). The mudstone 
lithofacies show peaks at faster relaxation with right skewed T2 spectra (the bigger peak on the left and 
smaller peak on the right), this is interpreted as dominance of relative smaller pore sizes (mainly 
mudstone micropores). The T2 spectra in massive dolostone lithofacies is left skewed with their peak 
occurring at longer (slower) relaxation time. This confirms the dominance of larger pore sizes in the 
dolostone dominated lithofacies (intercrystalline, vuggy and interparticle porosity).
NMR porosity values are observed to be greater than the corresponding helium porosimetry values with the 
differences being less than 1% (Fig.5). This difference in porosity values from the two types of 
measurements are attributed mainly to the difference in the operating techniques of both methods. The 
NMR technique can detect both interconnected pores that make up the effective porosity and closed pores 
that host the clay bound water, while helium porosity detects mainly interconnected pores (pores accessible 
to the helium molecules). Yuan and Rezaee (2019) compared the porosity values from helium porosimetry 
and NMR T2 analysis on clay-rich and clay-poor shale samples from different basins in Australia and USA. 
The NMR porosity results were observed to be higher than the corresponding helium porosity values in the 
clay-rich shale and lesser than helium porosity values in clay-poor shales. The authors suggested the higher
URTeC 3237
NMR porosity is due to the capability of NMR technique in detecting the effective porosity and clay bound 
water (CBW) that is tightly bound to the surface area of the clay minerals. Also, Clarkson et al. (2012) 
compared total porosity in tight-gas shale samples using both Small-angle and Ultra-small-angle neutron 
scattering (SANS and USANS) and helium porosimetry method. Helium porosity was observed to be 
smaller than the corresponding neutron scattering results. The authors suggested the difference is likely 
caused by the capability of neutron scattering to measure both closed and open pores, unlike helium 
porosimetry that measures only accessible (open) pores.

Conclusion 
 
• 
The reservoir facies identified in the Three Forks Formation are 1) Laminated mudstone and 
dolostone; 2) Massive dolostone; 3) Mottled dolostone; 4) Massive mudstone; 5) Mottled mudstone 
6) Mudstone conglomerates and 7) Brecciated mudstone.  
 
• 
Five major types of porosity were identified and described. They include interparticle, 
intercrystalline, fracture, vuggy and mudstone microporosity. The interparticle and intercrystalline 
porosity are abundant in dolostone dominated lithofacies while the mudstone microporosity are 
abundant in mudstone dominated lithofacies.   
 
• 
The mudstone-rich lithofacies have relatively higher porosities while the dolostone-rich lithofacies 
have relatively lower porosities. This high porosity in the mudstone-rich lithofacies is attributed to 
the abundance of low density siliciclastic minerals (clay, quartz and feldspars). Overall, the bulk 
and grain densities are observed to increase from the less dense clean mudstone lithofacies with 
relatively higher porosity to the denser clean dolostone lithofacies with relatively lower porosity.  
 
• 
NMR porosities values are all greater that the Helium porosimetry method with a difference <1%, 
because Helium porosimetry measures mostly connected pores while NMR detect both connected 
and isolated pores.  
 
• 
Despite the low total porosity values in the dolostone lithofacies, they have the highest distribution 
of large pores sizes as seen from NMR spectra due to the crystal arrangement of the large dolomite 
grains.

a half of it from the Bakken Formation while the other half is from the Three Forks Formation (Gaswirth 
and Marra 2015). Apart from being a thermally matured and prolific a source rock, the Bakken Formation 
has produced an appreciable amount of oil through advanced drilling, completion and stimulation

techniques (Lefever and Nordeng 2015). Oil discovery and production in the Bakken-Three Forks system 
began in 1953 from the Antelope Field with vertical wells (Lefever and Nordeng 2015).

The lithofacies and stratigraphy of the Three Forks Formation have been studied by various researchers, 
they have been subdivided into different members and units based on mineralogical composition, structures, 
and other geological features (Nordeng and LeFever, 2009; Bottjer et al., 2011; Sonnenberg et. al., 2011; 
LeFever et. al., 2013; and Sonnenberg, 2017). Mudstones have varying pore types, sizes, and distribution 
that influences hydrocarbon distribution (Slatt and O’Brien, 2011). Primary porosity develop during 
deposition, and may be influenced by compaction, cementation, and burial (Desbois et al., 2009; Milliken 
and Reed, 2010 and Loucks et al., 2012) Carbonates are known to have complex and diverse pore networks 
due to multiple factors that increase, preserve, modify or destroy pores (Norbisrath et al., 2015; Li et al., 
2016a).  Researchers have utilized helium porosimetry (Grejj et al., 1993; Chalmers et. al, 2012; Adeyilola 
et. al 2020), mercury intrusion porosimetry (Loucks et. al 2009; Li et al., 2016b), nuclear magnetic 
resonance (Brigaud et. al 2014; Gharechelou et. al 2016; Awad 2019), gas adsorption (Bustin et. al., 2008; 
Zhang et al. 2017) small angle neutron scattering (Clarkson et al., 2013), micro-CT imaging (Lawal and 
Mahmoud, 2020), Scanning Electron Microscopy image analysis (Loucks et al., 2009; Klaver et al., 2016; 
Deng et al., 2016) and thin section petrography (Choquette and Pray, 1970, Lonoy 2006, Lai et. al 2020) to 
characterize tight reservoirs. Similarly, the point-load test (Broch and Franklin, 1972), rebound hardness 
test (Aydin and Basu, 2005), micro-indentation (Su et al., 2018), scratch test (Kolawole and Ispas, 2020), 
and other geomechanical methods (Zoback et al., 1985) has been utilized in characterizing the mechanical 
properties of mudstones. The goal of this research is to provide a better understanding of the Three Forks 
Formation reservoir qualities.
Fig. 1. County Map of North Dakota showing boundary states. (Inset: Fields of interest in Divide County)

Four wells from the Ambrose (NDIC# 22809), West Ambrose (NDIC# 26745 & 28042) and Colgan 
(NDIC# 23828) fields were utilized in this study (Fig. 1). They are all located in Divide County, North 
Dakota. Polished and epoxy stained thin sections were used to identify and characterize the pores, mineral 
assemblages and other depositional features with a transmitted light microscope. X-ray diffraction (XRD) 
was used to examine the bulk mineralogical composition of samples. Crushed and pulverized samples were 
analyzed with a RIGAKU Smartlab XRD equipment and results were interpreted with a PDXL software. 
Each sample was analyzed at 5 degrees to 90 degrees, two theta (5º-90º 2θ) in order to identify the entire 
mineral assemblage and distributions. 
 
Porosity was estimated using both helium porosimetry and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). The helium 
porosimetry method uses Boyle’s law gas expansion technique and pressure differences to penetrate pores 
within samples inside its chamber. Samples were initially dried to get rid of trapped moisture, weighed and 
transferred to a 3D Laser scanner that measures the bulk volume. Core samples of known mass and bulk 
volumes were inserted into the matrix cup in the porosimeter and filled with disks of known mass to occupy 
void spaces in the matrix cup. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) was used to quality check the helium 
porosity results and characterize pore fluid distribution within the rocks. Core samples were saturated in 
300,000 ppm brine at 100 psi for 60 days to match the estimated salinity of connate water in the Bakken 
Petroleum System. The saturated samples were analyzed for total porosity and pore fluid distribution with 
an Oxford Instruments Geospec 2 core analyzer.

Lithofacies identification and description 
 
Physical core description and wireline logs wells were used to identify and correlate the Three Forks 
reservoir lithofacies (Fig. 2). They are: 1) Laminated mudstone and dolostone lithofacies; 2) massive 
dolostone lithofacies; 3) mottled dolostone lithofacies; 4) massive mudstone lithofacies; 5) mottled 
mudstone lithofacies; 6) mudstone conglomerates lithofacies; and 7) brecciated mudstone lithofacies.  
 
1) 
Laminated Lithofacies: It consists of finely interlaminated grayish-green to greenish-gray dolomitic 
mudstones and pinkish-tan silty dolostones. Laminar bedding ranges from less than 1cm up to 
approximately 15cm with no preference to mineralogy. Unidirectional and bidirectional ripples are more 
visible in the tan dolostone compared to the green mudstone. The different lithologies are mostly separated 
by a sharp contact or gradation which include both fining and coarsening upward sequences. Lithofacies 
thickness is about 2 to 5ft (Fig. 2A & 2B). 
 
2) 
Massive Dolostone: This a tan dolostone lithofacies which is mainly composed of silt and sand-
size dolomite. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the very fine sand range 
(~0.07 mm). It is composed mainly of dolomite and trace amount of quartz and clay. They also have sub-
rounded lenses that are probable deformed dolomite-filled burrows. No major sedimentary structure, they 
have massive texture and scoured surfaces. Lithofacies thickness varies from 1 to 3ft (Fig. 2C).   
 
3) 
Mottled Dolostone: Predominantly tan dolostone with interbed of green - grey mudstone. They 
contain about 20 to 40 percent thinly interbedded green mudstone that are slightly folded and deformed due 
to the soft sediment deformation. They are flaser bedded, slightly laminated and contain deformed thinly 
laminated silty dolostones. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the fine sand 
range (~0.07 mm). Thickness of this lithofacies is approximately 1 to 4ft (Fig. 2D).

4) 
Massive Mudstone: This unit is a thinly laminated green to grayish-green mudstone. They are clay-
sized, matrix supported rock with sparsely scattered, silt-sized, dolomite and quartz grains. Abundant 
burrows and crystal aggregates of variable sizes are distributed irregularly throughout this unit. The texture 
is massive with no visible sedimentary structure.  Thickness of this lithofacies is approximately 0.5 to 3.5 
ft (Fig. 2E). 
 
5) 
Mottled Mudstone: It composed of light brown dolomitic shaly siltstone and gray to dark green 
dolomitic claystone.  They are massive, slightly laminated, flaser bedded with irregular distribution of 
dolostones. The predominant grain size is silt (~0.04 mm), with some grains in the fine sand range (~0.07 
mm). They are chaotic, slightly brecciated with thickness ranging from less than 1 to 5ft (Fig. 2F). 
 
6) 
Mudstone conglomerates: This lithofacies consists of green-grey dolomitic mudstone matrix with 
tan dolomitic clasts. The clasts range in size from 0.5 to 2 cm and the matrix are predominantly silt size 
(~0.04 mm). Moderate to well-rounded and poorly sorted. Brown in the deeper section of Middle Three 
Forks due to oxidation. The lithofacies is matrix supported with no visible sedimentary structure (Fig. 2G).  
 
7) 
 Brecciated Mudstone: Composed of brecciated layers interbedded with reddish massive dolomitic 
mudstone with clasts. The clasts are angular and poorly sorted. They are chaotic with no visible sedimentary 
structure. It is matrix supported at the top and clast supported at the base. The matrix is silt size (~0.04 mm) 
while the clasts range from <1cm to 3.5cm (Fig. 2H & 2I). 
 
Pore types

Petrographic thin sections were used to characterize the various types of pores within these lithofacies under 
a petrographic microscope with plane polarized light. The dominant pores identified and described with the 
petrographic microscopes are interparticle, intercrystalline, fracture, vuggy and micropores.

1) 
Interparticle porosity: This class of pores occurs between two or more mineral grains (Choquette 
and Pray, 1970). Interparticle porosity is formed by well sorted sand-sized carbonate grains and minerals 
with little interstitial mud as seen in the massive dolostone, mottled dolostone and brecciated dolostone 
lithofacies (Fig. 3A).  
 
2) 
Intercrystalline porosity: This class of pores occur between crystals of either primary or secondary 
origin (Choquette and Pray, 1970). They typically occur at the edges of two or more dolomite crystals where 
they are characterized by their smooth and sharp edges. They occur in medium to coarse dolomite grain 
(fine-grained sand size) with cloudy core and clear as seen in the massive and mottled dolostone lithofacies. 
(Fig. 3B & 3C). 
 
3) 
Fracture Porosity: These are laterally extensive features that occur in both macroscopic and 
mesoscopic scale within the Three Forks Formation lithofacies Fractures occurring in mudstones are widely 
distributed and relatively longer while fractures in dolostone are less abundant and relatively shorter.  
Fractures in mudstones are both mineralized and non-mineralized (Fig. 3D). 
 
4) 
Vuggy Porosity: These are secondary solution pores that cuts across grains and cements boundaries 
(Lenoy, 2006). They are relatively larger and wider than all the other pores discussed, circular to elongated 
in shape and mostly interconnected. These pores are widely distributed in the sand-sized dolostone facie 
within the highly fractured brecciated mudstone lithofacies. (Fig. 3E).   
 
5) 
Mudstone microporosity: This group of pores are characterized by their extremely small pore sizes 
(<2um), they are the smallest in size and most widely distributed within the mudstone lithofacies in the 
Three Forks Formation (Fig. 3F).  The extremely small sizes of the dolomite crystals and mudstone matrix 
makes it challenging to classify them into intercrystalline or interparticle pores (Lonoy 2006).

and tan mudstone conglomerate; and H) Grey and tan brecciated mudstone I) Brecciated  mudstone

Porosity

Helium, NMR porosities and XRD mineralogical composition results are displayed in Table 1. The results 
from the helium porosimetry analysis include grain density, bulk density, pore volume and total porosity. 
The massive dolostone is seen to have the lowest porosity (2.32 %), highest grain density (2.82 g/ml) and 
highest bulk density (2.75 g/ml).  The relatively higher grain density is attributed to the abundance of the 
dense dolomite minerals which is 67% of the total composition. Mottled dolostone lithofacies shows a 
relatively lower porosity, grain density and bulk density (5.62%, 2.75 g/ml and 2.59 g/ml respectively). 
Again, these differences in grain density, bulk density and porosity is controlled by the mineralogical 
composition as the dolomite was observed to have decreased relatively from the massive dolostone. The 
massive mudstone lithofacies have relatively low grain density (2.67 g/ml), lowest bulk density (2.42 g/ml) 
and hence the highest porosity (9.63%). This high porosity in the massive mudstone lithofacies is attributed 
to the abundance of low density siliciclastic minerals (clay, quartz and feldspars). Overall, the bulk and 
grain densities are observed to increase from the less dense clean mudstone lithofacies with relatively higher 
porosities into the denser clean dolostone lithofacies with relatively lower porosities.  
 
The results of the NMR transverse relaxation time analysis are displayed in Fig. 4.  The results show the 
incremental porosity in percentage versus transverse time in milliseconds. The peak of the curves 
corresponds to the transverse relaxation time (T2) with the highest porosity. The peak occurs at varying 
time on the T2 time axis depending on the pore distribution within the various lithofacies. T2 distribution in 
rocks with smaller pores have a corresponding shorter relation time (faster) and rocks with larger pores 
have corresponding longer relaxation time (slower) (Kleinberg et. al 1993; Kenyon, 1997). The mudstone 
lithofacies show peaks at faster relaxation with right skewed T2 spectra (the bigger peak on the left and 
smaller peak on the right), this is interpreted as dominance of relative smaller pore sizes (mainly 
mudstone micropores). The T2 spectra in massive dolostone lithofacies is left skewed with their peak 
occurring at longer (slower) relaxation time. This confirms the dominance of larger pore sizes in the 
dolostone dominated lithofacies (intercrystalline, vuggy and interparticle porosity).

NMR porosity values are observed to be greater than the corresponding helium porosimetry values with the 
differences being less than 1% (Fig.5). This difference in porosity values from the two types of 
measurements are attributed mainly to the difference in the operating techniques of both methods. The 
NMR technique can detect both interconnected pores that make up the effective porosity and closed pores 
that host the clay bound water, while helium porosity detects mainly interconnected pores (pores accessible 
to the helium molecules). Yuan and Rezaee (2019) compared the porosity values from helium porosimetry 
and NMR T2 analysis on clay-rich and clay-poor shale samples from different basins in Australia and USA. 
The NMR porosity results were observed to be higher than the corresponding helium porosity values in the 
clay-rich shale and lesser than helium porosity values in clay-poor shales. The authors suggested the higher

NMR porosity is due to the capability of NMR technique in detecting the effective porosity and clay bound 
water (CBW) that is tightly bound to the surface area of the clay minerals. Also, Clarkson et al. (2012) 
compared total porosity in tight-gas shale samples using both Small-angle and Ultra-small-angle neutron 
scattering (SANS and USANS) and helium porosimetry method. Helium porosity was observed to be 
smaller than the corresponding neutron scattering results. The authors suggested the difference is likely 
caused by the capability of neutron scattering to measure both closed and open pores, unlike helium 
porosimetry that measures only accessible (open) pores.
Fig. 4: T2 relaxation time and incremental porosity plot for the studied lithofacies
Fig. 5: Helium and NMR porosity for the studied lithofacies

Conclusion 
 
• 
The reservoir facies identified in the Three Forks Formation are 1) Laminated mudstone and 
dolostone; 2) Massive dolostone; 3) Mottled dolostone; 4) Massive mudstone; 5) Mottled mudstone 
6) Mudstone conglomerates and 7) Brecciated mudstone.  
 
• 
Five major types of porosity were identified and described. They include interparticle, 
intercrystalline, fracture, vuggy and mudstone microporosity. The interparticle and intercrystalline 
porosity are abundant in dolostone dominated lithofacies while the mudstone microporosity are 
abundant in mudstone dominated lithofacies.   
 
• 
The mudstone-rich lithofacies have relatively higher porosities while the dolostone-rich lithofacies 
have relatively lower porosities. This high porosity in the mudstone-rich lithofacies is attributed to 
the abundance of low density siliciclastic minerals (clay, quartz and feldspars). Overall, the bulk 
and grain densities are observed to increase from the less dense clean mudstone lithofacies with 
relatively higher porosity to the denser clean dolostone lithofacies with relatively lower porosity.  
 
• 
NMR porosities values are all greater that the Helium porosimetry method with a difference <1%, 
because Helium porosimetry measures mostly connected pores while NMR detect both connected 
and isolated pores.  
 
• 
Despite the low total porosity values in the dolostone lithofacies, they have the highest distribution 
of large pores sizes as seen from NMR spectra due to the crystal arrangement of the large dolomite 
grains.

ABSTRACT
Exploration of the Taranaki Basin entered a new
phase in 2001 with Astrolabe, a 6,200 km high-quality 2D
seismic survey acquired by TGS-NOPEC that has outlined
a large depocentre containing up to 10 km of sedimentary
fill. This new data has extended the previously-known
Taranaki Basin into deeper water beyond the shelf edge.
Subsequently, the New Zealand Government released an
area of 42,000 km2 for competitive bidding to close in
September 2003.
Sequence analysis shows that a major deltaic system,
comparable to the Golden Beach and Emperor subgroups
of the Gippsland Basin, built into a restricted seaway
during the Late Cretaceous and culminated with
deposition of the Rakopi Formation coal measure
succession. The Rakopi Formation covers an area of at
least 15,000 km2 of the study area and was followed by a
transgression that continued until the Miocene.
Minor Eocene folding created broad structures with
potential to trap large volumes of petroleum. Other
potential trapping structures include drape across
Cretaceous rift blocks and turbidite mounds of Miocene
age.
Modelling shows that much of the Early Cretaceous
delta is thermally mature and should be expelling
petroleum today. Reservoir facies are present at many
horizons, but the primary target is expected to be
sandstones of the Rakopi Formation coal measures.
Many analogies can be drawn between the Taranaki
and Gippsland basins. The deepwater Taranaki basin
appears to be equivalent, however, to the offshore, oil-
prone part of Gippsland while the nearshore Taranaki
and Great South basins together form an analogy for the
more gas-prone nearshore part of Gippsland.
KEYWORDS
Taranaki Basin, Gippsland Basin, Astrolabe 2D seismic
survey, Cretaceous delta.
INTRODUCTION
New Zealand’s Taranaki Basin is named after Mount
Taranaki, a large Pleistocene volcano forming the core of
the Taranaki Peninsula and surrounded by oil and gas
fields (King and Thrasher, 1996). The basin lies partly
onshore but mostly offshore below the broad continental
shelf to the west of central North Island. Taranaki, New
Zealand’s only petroleum producing basin so far, is
separated from the Northland Basin (Isaac et al, 1994)
that occupies the Northland Peninsula and its relatively
narrower shelf, only by an arbitrary east–west line at
about 37oS (Fig. 1). The Astrolabe survey, named after
the ship commanded by an early French explorer of New
Zealand waters, Dumont D’Urville, confirmed that the
Taranaki Basin extended into the head of the New
Caledonia Basin as previously suspected (Uruski and
Wood, 1991; Uruski, 2000). The Taranaki and Northland
Basins, together with the deepwater extension of the
Taranaki Basin, are essentially one large basin system,
referred to in this paper as the greater Taranaki Basin.
On the Australian side of the Tasman Sea (Fig. 1), the
Gippsland Basin, has its onshore, shelf and deepwater
portions that have long been considered part of the same
depositional system. Gippsland is also Australia’s most
productive basin with total reserves, including production
to date, of about 10 trillion (1012) cubic feet (TCF) of gas
and four billion (109) barrels (BBL) of oil. Comparable
figures for Taranaki are 7 TCF of gas and 500 million BBL
of oil.
With locally important petroleum basins on either
side of the Tasman Sea, many authors have sought to
compare the two (e.g. Sutherland et al, 2001), as valid
analogies can clarify poorly-understood factors. Before
the Astrolabe survey, these comparisons could only be
partial and analogies were inconclusive.
The new survey revealed that the thick sediments
lying below the top Cretaceous reflector are laterally
extensive, filling a depocentre about 100 km across and
at least 150 km along the axis of the basin. Seismic
evidence is presented for a Strzelecki Group equivalent
as well as a prograding succession similar to the Emperor
and Golden Beach sub-Groups.
DEVELOPMENT OF THE TARANAKI BASIN AND
COMPARISONS WITH THE GIPPSLAND BASIN:
IMPLICATIONS FOR DEEPWATER EXPLORATION
Background to the Astrolabe survey
A single-channel reconnaissance survey in the head of
the New Caledonia Basin suggested to the authors (Uruski
and Wood, 1991) that the Taranaki Basin extended beyond
the shelf edge, the previous limit for petroleum
exploration. This was  confirmed when, in 1996, the New
Zealand Government acquired a single 1,000 km seismic
line along the axis of the New Caledonia Basin from the
Wainui–1 well on the Taranaki shelf edge as part of a
joint project with AGSO (now Geoscience Australia).
The deepwater Taranaki sector of this line was interpreted
to be underlain by Cretaceous sediments, up to 5,000 m
thick (Uruski, 2000).
In 2001 TGS-NOPEC Geophysical Company, in
collaboration with the Institute of Geological and Nuclear
Sciences (GNS) acquired 6,200 km of new non-exclusive
2D data in the deepwater Taranaki Basin (Fig. 2). The
survey was tied to eight wells on the Taranaki shelf and
the deepwater Wakanui–1 well in the adjacent Northland
Basin.
TGS-NOPEC and GNS planned the Astrolabe 2D
reconnaissance survey of the deepwater Taranaki Basin
on a basic 10 km grid. In water depths beyond 1,500 m and
in the southern sector of the area the grid is much wider.
The survey was acquired to confirm the existence of a
deepwater extension to Taranaki Basin and to investigate
its petroleum prospectivity.
Aims of this paper
First, we investigate comparisons of the Gippsland
and Taranaki Basins possible prior to acquisition of the
new Astrolabe dataset by considering plate tectonic and
tectonostratigraphic evolution of the two basins. We
then show how the new data can improve the analogy.
Finally, implications for petroleum prospectivity of the
two basins are discussed.

PRE-ASTROLABE COMPARISONS
Plate tectonics
Plate tectonics provided a basic control on basin
formation across large regions. If the same event initiated
both the Gippsland and Taranaki Basins, they are by
definition, generically related. Although the New Zealand
mini-continent formed part of the Gondwana margin
until the Late Cretaceous when it was rifted from Australia
and Antarctica (Fig. 3), the known tectonic and
sedimentary history of its basins was thought to have
started later than in Gippsland.
Tasman seafloor spreading started in the Late
Cretaceous (85 Ma) and finished by the end of the
Paleocene (~50 Ma). The New Zealand region then
foundered until the modern Pacific/Australia plate
boundary was initiated near the start of the Miocene. A
complex plate margin then formed with the Pacific Plate
being subducted below North Island and the Australian
plate below the southern end of South Island. Between
the two subduction zones runs the Alpine Fault, a major

Alps have been uplifted some 30 km to provide a

sedimentary basins.
Three basin-forming rift phases are recognised in the
region; the Early Otway, Tasman and Taranaki
(Sutherland et al, 2001). The Early Otway Phase lasted
from 160–100 Ma. This Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous
phase was concurrent with convergence and arc volcanism
along the eastern margin of Gondwana. Volcanism
continued in the New Zealand region until about 130 Ma
(Mortimer et al, 1999). Southern Australia started rifting
away from Antarctica during the Late Jurassic and this
phase is recorded by initial basin formation in the
Gippsland Basin and deposition of the Jurassic Beds and
the Strzelecki Group. Before the Astrolabe survey, there
was little evidence of extensional tectonics in New
Zealand at this time and sedimentary rocks of this age
were unknown in the Taranaki Basin.
The Tasman Rift Phase was essentially a Late
Cretaceous event lasting from latest Albian–Early
Campanian time (100–80 Ma). This phase was recorded
by a change in regional tectonics led up to the  spreading
of the Tasman Sea (Norvick et al, 2001). In the Gippsland
Basin, thick fault-bounded units of clastic sediments, the
Emperor and Golden Beach Groups, were deposited.
Several comparable New Zealand units were present.
The Hoiho Group (Fig 4) was deposited in the Great
South Basin, while the Taniwha Formation (Shell, BP
and Todd, 1986) was deposited in Taranaki and
Northland. Samples of coal measure rocks of late
Cenomanian to Coniacian age (95–86.5 Ma) were
dredged from the flank of the West Norfolk Ridge
(Herzer et al, 1999).
