The Taranaki Rift Phase continued for the rest of the
Late Cretaceous until mid-way through the Paleocene
despite concurrent seafloor spreading in the Tasman
Sea. Extension was widespread in New Zealand through
this time, particularly in Western Southland (Turnbull
et al, 1993), probably in response to the opening of the
Emerald Basin to the south of New Zealand. This phase
does not appear to have affected the Gippsland Basin,
which was separated from the New Zealand mini-
continent by the Tasman Sea.
Although structural inversion is recorded by extensive
erosional channels in a pre-existing seafloor near the
start of the Eocene (Johnstone et al, 2001), little tectonic
activity is apparent in Gippsland later than the middle of
the Late Cretaceous. In contrast, the present-day plate
margin is almost entirely responsible for the presence of
New Zealand, and much of the evolution of New Zealand
and its sedimentary basins took place during the Neogene.
Many spectacular compressional structures were formed at
a variety of scales from petroleum trap-forming folds in
sedimentary basins to uplift of the Southern Alps, which
resulted in the influx of large volumes of clastic sediments
while offshore Gippsland was being starved of clastics.
Stratigraphy
Basement in New Zealand is arranged into a series of
linear terranes about parallel with the ancient Gondwana
margin. Consequently, basement composition in Taranaki
is variable. In the north around the Ariki–1 well (Shell,
BP and Todd, 1984) basement consists of metamorphosed
igneous and volcaniclastic sediments of Mesozoic ages,
correlated with the Median Tectonic Zone (Mortimer et
al, 1997) and the New England Fold Belt of eastern
Australia. The Wainui–1 well stopped in metamorphosed
siliceous sandstone of the Paleozoic Takaka terrane, while
further south in Tane–1 and Kiwa–1 basement is of Early
Cretaceous Separation Point granite.
The oldest sediments in Gippsland Basin (Norvick et al,
2001) are the coal measures and lacustrine facies of the
Jurassic Beds, deposited in extensional basins during the
early stages of the Early Otway Rift Phase. This rift phase
continued through the Early Cretaceous when the Strzelecki
Group was deposited.  Gippsland experienced a mainly
Campanian (100–90 Ma) unconformity followed by
deposition of the Emperor and Golden Bay subgroups in the
Late Cretaceous.
The oldest known unmetamorphosed sedimentary
rocks below the Taranaki shelf are the Cretaceous
Taniwha Formation coal measures (SBPT, 1986) deposited
in extensional basins in variable basement rocks. The
Taniwha Formation is of Latest Albian to Turonian age
(100–90 Ma). This sequence is considerably older than
the Pakawau Group, which forms the bulk of Cretaceous
deposits below the Taranaki shelf, is of Late Campanian
age (80–65 Ma). The Pakawau Group of the Taranaki Shelf
consists of the Rakopi and North Cape formations. The
former is a coal measure succession, while the North Cape
Formation is generally of marine rocks.

On the evidence that existed prior to Astrolabe, Gippsland
has a much earlier inception and contains extensive basal
sediments much older than the Taranaki does.
In broad terms, both the Gippsland and Taranaki
basins experienced an overall Late Cretaceous and
Paleogene transgression followed by Neogene regression
(Fig. 5). Carbonate deposition was widespread in Taranaki
by the Oligocene while onshore in Gippsland, coal
measures and lacustrine rocks were still being deposited.
The Miocene in Taranaki is characterised by widespread
turbidite deposition into a muddy marine background.
During the same time offshore Gippsland remained
relatively starved of clastic sediments except in the
narrow coastal zone. Canyon development in Gippsland
suggested that clastic turbidite fans were probably
distributed into deeper regions. Turbidite deposition is
well documented to be below the present Taranaki
Shelf, where such facies have proven to be petroleum
reservoirs.
RESULTS OF THE ASTROLABE SURVEY
The Astrolabe survey shows that the geology of the
deepwater Taranaki Basin differs from the Taranaki
shelf and onshore in stratigraphy, structural history and
volcanism. The Cretaceous (Fig. 6) and possibly older
succession is considerably thicker in deepwater than
below the shelf. Conversely, the Neogene succession is
considerably thinner. Paleogene sedimentary thicknesses
are more constant and this is also an important feature as
is the relatively gentle post-Cretaceous tectonic regime
documented in the deepwater region.
Extension appears to have been active earlier in the
deepwater region than in the rest of the Taranaki and
Northland region. A relatively gentle tectonic episode
affected rocks in the deepwater region causing long-
wavelength folds and perhaps strike-slip faulting
characterised by flower structures.
Four volcanic episodes are recognised in the deepwater
region. The earliest predates deposition of the prograding
deltaic body described below and the second post-dates
it and is dated from seismic well ties as Late Campanian
(70–75 Ma). A minor volcanic episode appears to have
accompanied Eocene tectonism and is expressed by small
volcanic cones extruded across the flank of the Challenger
Plateau. Finally, Miocene volcanism is expressed in the
large Aotea Seamount.
Cretaceous and older (?) stratigraphy
Between the basement and the top Cretaceous
reflector, which can be readily mapped across the basin
(Fig. 6), is a succession consisting of three megasequences.
Each megasequence is up to one second thickness two-
way time (twt). The basal megasequence (A) is overlain
by a prograding megasequence (B), which in turn is
overlain by an almost parallel-bedded megasequence
(C).

Syn-rift megasequence A
The basal unit is clearly a syn-rift megasequence as it
fills grabens within basement and overtops some horst
blocks (Fig. 6). The top of this unit is marked by downlap
of the overlying megasequence and it does not exist
landward of the present shelf edge. Its internal reflectors
are discontinuous and of variable amplitude. A large
volcanic edifice was extruded onto its top surface. The
age of the syn-rift megasequence is poorly constrained.
The oldest sedimentary rocks encountered in nearby
wells are the Rakopi Formation of Campanian age (about
75 Ma, Fig. 7), but the syn-rift megasequence is clearly
much older. A search for possible analogous rocks yields
the Taniwha Formation of Taranaki and Northland and
the Late Jurassic coal measures of the Huriwai Group
(Ballance, 1988) of the Murihiku Group that were
previously considered as part of the basement terrane.
The Huriwai Formation may be the basal unit of
megasequence A. The Wakanui–1 well drilled by Conoco
in 1998 reputedly penetrated Jurassic coal measures
above basement. If true, this is strong evidence for Jurassic
sediments being present in the deepwater part of the
greater Taranaki basin. A Gippsland equivalent for the
major part of megasequence A is likely to be of Early
Cretaceous making the Strzelecki Group a prime candidate.
Prograding megasequence B
The top of the prograding megasequence is tied to the
Rakopi Formation in Tane–1 (Fig. 7), which dates the
culmination of this prograding succession as Late
Campanian (about 75 Ma). The prograding megasequence
is subdivided into five bodies (Fig. 6) starting with a high-
stand systems tract. This unit is partially fault-bounded
below the present shelf edge zone and thickens to nearly
one second twt before tapering to zero near the basin
centre. This basal unit may include much coarse clastic
material shed from the fault scarps.
The second unit is a more typical slug-model, high-
stand systems tract, thickening from zero on top of unit
one to about 750 milliseconds twt above the toe of unit
one, before thinning to zero again some 50 km to the
northwest. Internally, sinusoidal reflectors onlap the top
surface of the older systems tract and downlap to the
northwest. Together, the two older units are symptomatic
of continuing, if episodic, relative sea-level rise, probably
tectonically driven by extensional of the Tasman Rift
phase 100–80 Ma (King et al, 1999; Norvick et al, 2001).
The third unit is a low-stand wedge with complex
internal reflectors suggesting good development of sea-
bed fan turbidites. The unit thickens to the northwest
from zero at the slope break of unit two to nearly 500
milliseconds twt. Reflectors also onlap the older volcanic
mound.
Unit four is another high-stand systems tract exhibiting
prograding internal reflectors. The topset beds in this
unit are prominent in that they are of high amplitude,
discontinuous reflectors similar to coal measure units
elsewhere in Taranaki. Further, the top surface of this
unit ties to the Rakopi Formation coal measures in
Tane–1.
The final unit that lies below the top Rakopi Formation
reflector is a thin low-stand wedge located to the northwest
of unit four and onlapping its toe.
Together, the prograding reflector geometry and time
isopachs (Fig. 8) of megasequence B, which clearly
illustrates a lobate compound body, are compelling
evidence for deltaic deposition. The evidence suggests
that a river or rivers fed into a restricted seaway at the
head of the New Caledonia Basin. Such seismically-
imaged deltas have been notably absent from the mid-
Cretaceous basins of New Zealand, despite abundant
evidence of fluvial deposition. Much of the Hoiho Group
(Fig. 4) of the Great South Basin, for example, is fluvial,
but no outlet to the sea is apparent. The Great South
Basin was adjacent to Taranaki during this period so the
Taranaki delta may be the outlet for the Hoiho Group
rivers.

Neogene
Wells  at the shelf edge show that carbonate deposition
was not unknown during the Miocene.  The deepwater
Taranaki area remained in relatively deep water
throughout the Neogene.  Miocene depocentres reflect
turbidite deposition, particularly across the paleo shelf
edge to the northwest.  Despite the renewed sediment
supply due to activity at the plate boundary, most Miocene
sediments were deposited closer to shore.  The influx of
sediments associated with renewed Alpine uplift in the
Pliocene formed the present shelf.  The Pliocene within
the study area is up to one second twt thick and is mainly
clastic, consisting of a high proportion of seafloor fan
turbidites.
Petroleum potential of deepwater Taranaki Basin
In deepwater Taranaki, thick coal measure facies at
top Rakopi level cover an area of at least 15,000 km2.
Extensive coals are also likely within the topset beds
of deeper prograding units of the Late Cretaceous
delta, while disseminated coaly kerogen is likely to be
present throughout the foresets and to have been
carried into deeper water by low-stand turbidite fans.
The delta was built into a restricted seaway between
the emergent Challenger Plateau and the West Norfolk
Ridge suggesting that Cretaceous marine mudstones
are also possible petroleum source rocks.  If equivalents
of the Jurassic Huriwai Formation are present in the basin,
a further Jurassic source is also likely along the flanks of the
basin, where it has not been buried too deeply.
Potential petroleum reservoirs in deepwater
Taranaki include the sandstones of the Rakopi coal
measures themselves and marine sandstones of Late
Cretaceous North Cape Formation equivalents as well
as Cretaceous and Paleogene turbidite fans.
Thermal modelling shows that source rocks within the
delta are generally mature today and that maturity is a
low risk for this basin. Two-dimensional thermal maturity
modelling predicts there is up to 1,000 m of mid-
Cretaceous source rock in the oil expulsion window
(Fig. 9). The present day oil generation window is below
about 2,800 m below sea-floor (bsf) for marine source
rocks (Type II kinetics) and 3,200 m for non-marine
source rocks (Type III kinetics). The present day gas
window is below about 5,000 m bsf for non-marine source
rocks (Type III kinetics).
In the centre of the basin, oil expulsion started in the
Cretaceous and Paleogene. A post-Miocene pulse of
sedimentation resulted in the top of the oil expulsion
window climbing a further 200 m to reach much of the
Rakopi Formation equivalent at the present day.  The
gentle Eocene tectonism formed trapping structures as
petroleum was being expelled from source rocks and the
negligible Neogene tectonism that affected the deepwater
Taranaki Basin makes it likely that trap integrity would
have been maintained.

noted in the Taranaki Basin and elsewhere was under-
way and the locus of deposition shifted landward by
about 100 km, resulting in deposition of the mainly

continental shelf and coastal plain was established, so
with this relatively flat topography, minor changes of

and seaward shifts in depositional systems.
Paleogene
The oscillations of depositional systems continued
throughout the rest of the Late Cretaceous and Paleogene.
During this time, the surrounding basement highs of the
Challenger Plateau and part of the West Norfolk Ridge
Basin as well as the more remote New Zealand mainland,
appear to have been emergent and supplying sediments
to the basin. Folding of Eocene age formed large, gentle
anticlines and flower structures as older faults were
reactivated as compressional and strike-slip faults. By
the Oligocene, clastic sediments were in very short supply
and carbonate deposition was widespread.
POST-ASTROLABE COMPARISON WITH
GIPPSLAND
Tectonostratigraphy
The Astrolabe survey provides new data to help
comparisons between the greater Taranaki and Gippsland
Basins.  A direct comparison between the Jurassic Beds
of Gippsland and the Huriwai Formation of Northland is
possible in the deepwater Taranaki Basin.  In both basins
they appear to be essentially coal measures or lacustrine
and their possible presence in Taranaki suggests that
both basins originated during the Late Jurassic in
response to the Early Otway Rift Phase.  The analogy is
strengthened by correlation of the remainder of
Megasequence A with the Strzelecki Group.
The proposed Astrolabe delta of Megasequence B was
deposited in Late Albian to Campanian time (100–75 Ma)
and is a time correlative of the Emperor and Golden
Beach sub-groups.  Megasequence B reflectors downlap
onto the top of Megasequence A, providing evidence for
non-deposition across much of the Strzelecki Group
equivalent in Taranaki. We suggest that this may the
equivalent of the Cenomanian hiatus of Gippsland Basin.
The Kipper volcanics, extruded on top of the Golden
Beach Group, also has its equivalent in Taranaki (Fig.  6).
The Emperor and Golden Beach sub-groups are separated
by a landward shift of facies belts while in Taranaki, the
boundary between the Taniwha equivalent and the
overlying Rakopi Formation is a low-stand followed by a
marked landward shift of facies belts and renewed delta
prograding. In deepwater Taranaki, tectonics appear
to have been waning through Rakopi time as would be
expected, following plate separation and accompanying
opening of the Tasman Sea. This allows a decreasing

Oil or gas?
Following the discovery of the onshore Kapuni gas and
condensate field in the 1950s and the giant Maui gas and
condensate field in the 1970s, the industry tended to the
belief that Taranaki was gas-prone and had therefore not
been a popular exploration venue. Several lines of
evidence suggest that the deepwater Taranaki Basin
should be oil-prone rather than gas-prone.
The first is that the shallow water and onshore Taranaki
Basin is now seen as more oil-prone than previously
thought. This is due to an oil trend in the onshore
overthrust zone, the Kaimiro and Ngatoro oilfields in
northern onshore Taranaki, the Maari discovery in 1999
and the more recent Rimu discovery in 2000.  In addition,
the recent offshore discoveries of an oil leg in the Maui
field and a better understanding of its charge history
enhance the Taranaki Basin’s attraction as an oil basin.
Maui hydrocarbons have a terrestrial source,
predominantly Late Cretaceous coal and coaly sediments
(Sykes, 2001), and a complex charge history
(Funnel et al, 2001). Earliest charge was hot brines with
high CO2 content, followed by several phases of oil
migration and a latest phase of oil and gas charge.
The second line of reasoning is based on the seismic
stratigraphy outlined above. The increased marine
influence implied by the delta interpretation and the
known oil richness of deltas around the world increases
confidence that the deepwater Taranaki Basin is oil-
prone. In addition, the inferred restricted seaway
increases the chances of widespread organic rich shales
being deposited.

one of the basins is poorly known and, while such circular
arguments are not proof, such mutual support may be
beneficial to exploration of both basins.
CONCLUSIONS
1. Before the Astrolabe survey, the Taranaki Basin was a
relatively poor analogue for Gippsland as its oldest
known sediments were much younger than Gippsland’s.
A relatively good comparison could be made between
Late Cretaceous and Paleogene units of both basins,
but the effects of the Neogene plate boundary are
much more marked in Taranaki than in Gippsland.
Taranaki received voluminous Neogene clastic
sediments while Gippsland remained starved of them.
2. The Astrolabe survey provided evidence to suggest
that Taranaki was probably initiated at about the
same time as Gippsland and that correlatives of all of
the main Gippsland sedimentary groups are likely to
be present in the Taranaki Basin. The survey also
revealed the presence of a large Late Cretaceous delta
with extensive associated coal-bearing units, similar
in age and tectonic setting to the Emperor and Golden
Beach sub-groups and effectively linking Taranaki’s
Taniwha and Rakopi Formations to Gippsland
equivalents.
3. Despite being separated by at least 1,000 km for their
entire history, both basins were at the same latitude
for much of their history, so source rocks in Taranaki
should be at least as oil-prone as in Gippsland, assuming
similar climatic controls on deposition and chemistry.
Additionally, the location of Taranaki, at the head of
a restricted marine trough, enhances the possibility
that rich marine source rocks may be present.  About
30% of the world’s known oil reserves were generated
from Cretaceous source rocks.

The Late Cretaceous part of Gippsland’s Latrobe Group
exhibits a seaward shift in facies belts in response to an
apparent marine regression.  By this time, the Taranaki
Rift Phase had commenced below the Taranaki Shelf,
where a mix of coal measure and marine facies were
being deposited in fault-bounded lows. The Pakawau
Group coal measures and North Cape Formation marine
units of Taranaki are equivalents of the Late Cretaceous
Latrobe Group. In deeper water, faulting remained
subdued through the Campanian and Maastrichtian
(84–65 Ma). Reflector patterns are complex and result
from minor relative sea-level changes, the broad shelf
geometry and modest accommodation space.
From the end of the Cretaceous, the Latrobe Group
and Taranaki’s Kapuni coal measures and Moa Group
marine facies are equivalent, even to deposition in a
transgressive environment.  Near the end of the
Paleocene, minor volcanism is recorded across the flank
of the Challenger Plateau synchronous with volcanism in
onshore Gippsland.
Overall patterns are also similar between the two
regions through the Neogene with the exception that
Taranaki received voluminous clastic sediments and
Gippsland was relatively starved of clastics.
Petroleum
Taranaki is New Zealand’s only producing petroleum
basin to date, while Gippsland has been Australia’s most
prolific petroleum region. Although the two basins were
separated by at least 1,000 km at all times since formation
until the Tasman Sea started spreading, both basins were
at similar latitudes and environmental controls on
deposition of coaly source rocks were likely to have been
similar. Much of the petroleum in both Gippsland and
Taranaki was sourced from coal measures of Cretaceous
and Paleogene ages.  In Taranaki, minor volumes were
also generated from Paleocene black marine shale.
Similarly, although coal is the major source rock in
Gippsland, a marine contribution is detected in oils from
the southeastern, oceanward part of the basin (Gorter,
2001).
Reservoir rocks in Gippsland are commonly of
Paleocene age, although accumulations have also been
discovered in Late Cretaceous sediments. Petroleum in
Taranaki has been discovered mainly in Paleocene
reservoirs of the Kapuni Group, but significant discoveries
have also been made in fractured Oligocene limestone
and in Neogene turbidite fans.  The younger reservoirs
are probably symptomatic of Neogene tectonism.
The results of the Astrolabe survey have interesting
implications for both basins.  They show that Cretaceous
plays, particularly Rakopi Formation equivalents, are
valid exploration targets and that marine source rocks
should be considered in the deeper parts of both basins.

Exploration of the Taranaki Basin entered a new
phase in 2001 with Astrolabe, a 6,200 km high-quality 2D
seismic survey acquired by TGS-NOPEC that has outlined
a large depocentre containing up to 10 km of sedimentary
fill. This new data has extended the previously-known
Taranaki Basin into deeper water beyond the shelf edge.
Subsequently, the New Zealand Government released an
area of 42,000 km2 for competitive bidding to close in
September 2003.
Sequence analysis shows that a major deltaic system,
comparable to the Golden Beach and Emperor subgroups
of the Gippsland Basin, built into a restricted seaway
during the Late Cretaceous and culminated with
deposition of the Rakopi Formation coal measure
succession. The Rakopi Formation covers an area of at
least 15,000 km2 of the study area and was followed by a
transgression that continued until the Miocene.
Minor Eocene folding created broad structures with
potential to trap large volumes of petroleum. Other
potential trapping structures include drape across
Cretaceous rift blocks and turbidite mounds of Miocene
age.
Modelling shows that much of the Early Cretaceous
delta is thermally mature and should be expelling
petroleum today. Reservoir facies are present at many
horizons, but the primary target is expected to be
sandstones of the Rakopi Formation coal measures.
Many analogies can be drawn between the Taranaki
and Gippsland basins. The deepwater Taranaki basin
appears to be equivalent, however, to the offshore, oil-
prone part of Gippsland while the nearshore Taranaki
and Great South basins together form an analogy for the
more gas-prone nearshore part of Gippsland.

Taranaki Basin, Gippsland Basin, Astrolabe 2D seismic
survey, Cretaceous delta.

New Zealand’s Taranaki Basin is named after Mount
Taranaki, a large Pleistocene volcano forming the core of
the Taranaki Peninsula and surrounded by oil and gas
fields (King and Thrasher, 1996). The basin lies partly
onshore but mostly offshore below the broad continental
shelf to the west of central North Island. Taranaki, New
Zealand’s only petroleum producing basin so far, is
separated from the Northland Basin (Isaac et al, 1994)
that occupies the Northland Peninsula and its relatively
narrower shelf, only by an arbitrary east–west line at
about 37oS (Fig. 1). The Astrolabe survey, named after
the ship commanded by an early French explorer of New
Zealand waters, Dumont D’Urville, confirmed that the
Taranaki Basin extended into the head of the New
Caledonia Basin as previously suspected (Uruski and
Wood, 1991; Uruski, 2000). The Taranaki and Northland
Basins, together with the deepwater extension of the
Taranaki Basin, are essentially one large basin system,
referred to in this paper as the greater Taranaki Basin.
On the Australian side of the Tasman Sea (Fig. 1), the
Gippsland Basin, has its onshore, shelf and deepwater
portions that have long been considered part of the same
depositional system. Gippsland is also Australia’s most
productive basin with total reserves, including production
to date, of about 10 trillion (1012) cubic feet (TCF) of gas
and four billion (109) barrels (BBL) of oil. Comparable
figures for Taranaki are 7 TCF of gas and 500 million BBL
of oil.
With locally important petroleum basins on either
side of the Tasman Sea, many authors have sought to
compare the two (e.g. Sutherland et al, 2001), as valid
analogies can clarify poorly-understood factors. Before
the Astrolabe survey, these comparisons could only be
partial and analogies were inconclusive.
The new survey revealed that the thick sediments
lying below the top Cretaceous reflector are laterally
extensive, filling a depocentre about 100 km across and
at least 150 km along the axis of the basin. Seismic
evidence is presented for a Strzelecki Group equivalent
as well as a prograding succession similar to the Emperor
and Golden Beach sub-Groups.

DEVELOPMENT OF THE TARANAKI BASIN AND
COMPARISONS WITH THE GIPPSLAND BASIN:
IMPLICATIONS FOR DEEPWATER EXPLORATION

A single-channel reconnaissance survey in the head of
the New Caledonia Basin suggested to the authors (Uruski
and Wood, 1991) that the Taranaki Basin extended beyond
the shelf edge, the previous limit for petroleum
exploration. This was  confirmed when, in 1996, the New
Zealand Government acquired a single 1,000 km seismic
line along the axis of the New Caledonia Basin from the
Wainui–1 well on the Taranaki shelf edge as part of a
joint project with AGSO (now Geoscience Australia).
The deepwater Taranaki sector of this line was interpreted
to be underlain by Cretaceous sediments, up to 5,000 m
thick (Uruski, 2000).
In 2001 TGS-NOPEC Geophysical Company, in
collaboration with the Institute of Geological and Nuclear
Sciences (GNS) acquired 6,200 km of new non-exclusive
2D data in the deepwater Taranaki Basin (Fig. 2). The
survey was tied to eight wells on the Taranaki shelf and
the deepwater Wakanui–1 well in the adjacent Northland
Basin.

TGS-NOPEC and GNS planned the Astrolabe 2D
reconnaissance survey of the deepwater Taranaki Basin
on a basic 10 km grid. In water depths beyond 1,500 m and
in the southern sector of the area the grid is much wider.
The survey was acquired to confirm the existence of a
deepwater extension to Taranaki Basin and to investigate
its petroleum prospectivity.

First, we investigate comparisons of the Gippsland
and Taranaki Basins possible prior to acquisition of the
new Astrolabe dataset by considering plate tectonic and
tectonostratigraphic evolution of the two basins. We
then show how the new data can improve the analogy.
Finally, implications for petroleum prospectivity of the
two basins are discussed.

Plate tectonics provided a basic control on basin
formation across large regions. If the same event initiated
both the Gippsland and Taranaki Basins, they are by
definition, generically related. Although the New Zealand
mini-continent formed part of the Gondwana margin
until the Late Cretaceous when it was rifted from Australia
and Antarctica (Fig. 3), the known tectonic and
sedimentary history of its basins was thought to have
started later than in Gippsland.
Tasman seafloor spreading started in the Late
Cretaceous (85 Ma) and finished by the end of the
Paleocene (~50 Ma). The New Zealand region then
foundered until the modern Pacific/Australia plate
boundary was initiated near the start of the Miocene. A
complex plate margin then formed with the Pacific Plate
being subducted below North Island and the Australian
plate below the southern end of South Island. Between
the two subduction zones runs the Alpine Fault, a major

strike-slip plate boundary, along which the southern
Alps have been uplifted some 30 km to provide a
voluminous source of clastic sediments to New Zealand’s
sedimentary basins.
Three basin-forming rift phases are recognised in the
region; the Early Otway, Tasman and Taranaki
(Sutherland et al, 2001). The Early Otway Phase lasted
from 160–100 Ma. This Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous
phase was concurrent with convergence and arc volcanism
along the eastern margin of Gondwana. Volcanism
continued in the New Zealand region until about 130 Ma
(Mortimer et al, 1999). Southern Australia started rifting
away from Antarctica during the Late Jurassic and this
phase is recorded by initial basin formation in the
Gippsland Basin and deposition of the Jurassic Beds and
the Strzelecki Group. Before the Astrolabe survey, there
was little evidence of extensional tectonics in New

Zealand at this time and sedimentary rocks of this age
were unknown in the Taranaki Basin.
The Tasman Rift Phase was essentially a Late
Cretaceous event lasting from latest Albian–Early
Campanian time (100–80 Ma). This phase was recorded
by a change in regional tectonics led up to the  spreading
of the Tasman Sea (Norvick et al, 2001). In the Gippsland
Basin, thick fault-bounded units of clastic sediments, the
Emperor and Golden Beach Groups, were deposited.
Several comparable New Zealand units were present.
The Hoiho Group (Fig 4) was deposited in the Great
South Basin, while the Taniwha Formation (Shell, BP
and Todd, 1986) was deposited in Taranaki and
Northland. Samples of coal measure rocks of late
Cenomanian to Coniacian age (95–86.5 Ma) were
dredged from the flank of the West Norfolk Ridge
(Herzer et al, 1999).

The Taranaki Rift Phase continued for the rest of the
Late Cretaceous until mid-way through the Paleocene
despite concurrent seafloor spreading in the Tasman
Sea. Extension was widespread in New Zealand through
this time, particularly in Western Southland (Turnbull
et al, 1993), probably in response to the opening of the
Emerald Basin to the south of New Zealand. This phase
does not appear to have affected the Gippsland Basin,
which was separated from the New Zealand mini-
continent by the Tasman Sea.
Although structural inversion is recorded by extensive
erosional channels in a pre-existing seafloor near the
start of the Eocene (Johnstone et al, 2001), little tectonic
activity is apparent in Gippsland later than the middle of
the Late Cretaceous. In contrast, the present-day plate
margin is almost entirely responsible for the presence of
New Zealand, and much of the evolution of New Zealand
and its sedimentary basins took place during the Neogene.
Many spectacular compressional structures were formed at
a variety of scales from petroleum trap-forming folds in
sedimentary basins to uplift of the Southern Alps, which
resulted in the influx of large volumes of clastic sediments
while offshore Gippsland was being starved of clastics.

Basement in New Zealand is arranged into a series of
linear terranes about parallel with the ancient Gondwana
margin. Consequently, basement composition in Taranaki
is variable. In the north around the Ariki–1 well (Shell,
BP and Todd, 1984) basement consists of metamorphosed
igneous and volcaniclastic sediments of Mesozoic ages,
correlated with the Median Tectonic Zone (Mortimer et
al, 1997) and the New England Fold Belt of eastern
Australia. The Wainui–1 well stopped in metamorphosed
siliceous sandstone of the Paleozoic Takaka terrane, while
further south in Tane–1 and Kiwa–1 basement is of Early
Cretaceous Separation Point granite.
The oldest sediments in Gippsland Basin (Norvick et al,
2001) are the coal measures and lacustrine facies of the
Jurassic Beds, deposited in extensional basins during the
early stages of the Early Otway Rift Phase. This rift phase
continued through the Early Cretaceous when the Strzelecki
Group was deposited.  Gippsland experienced a mainly
Campanian (100–90 Ma) unconformity followed by
deposition of the Emperor and Golden Bay subgroups in the
Late Cretaceous.
The oldest known unmetamorphosed sedimentary
rocks below the Taranaki shelf are the Cretaceous
Taniwha Formation coal measures (SBPT, 1986) deposited
in extensional basins in variable basement rocks. The
Taniwha Formation is of Latest Albian to Turonian age
(100–90 Ma). This sequence is considerably older than
the Pakawau Group, which forms the bulk of Cretaceous
deposits below the Taranaki shelf, is of Late Campanian
age (80–65 Ma). The Pakawau Group of the Taranaki Shelf
consists of the Rakopi and North Cape formations. The
former is a coal measure succession, while the North Cape
Formation is generally of marine rocks.

Figure 5. Generalised stratigraphy of New Zealand Basins as
known before the Astrolabe survey. This figure shows the overall
transgression that continued through the Cretaceous and culmi-
nated in the Oligocene, followed by regression resulting from
development of the Neogene plate boundary.

On the evidence that existed prior to Astrolabe, Gippsland
has a much earlier inception and contains extensive basal
sediments much older than the Taranaki does.
In broad terms, both the Gippsland and Taranaki
basins experienced an overall Late Cretaceous and
Paleogene transgression followed by Neogene regression
(Fig. 5). Carbonate deposition was widespread in Taranaki
by the Oligocene while onshore in Gippsland, coal
measures and lacustrine rocks were still being deposited.
The Miocene in Taranaki is characterised by widespread
turbidite deposition into a muddy marine background.
During the same time offshore Gippsland remained
relatively starved of clastic sediments except in the
narrow coastal zone. Canyon development in Gippsland
suggested that clastic turbidite fans were probably
distributed into deeper regions. Turbidite deposition is
well documented to be below the present Taranaki
Shelf, where such facies have proven to be petroleum
reservoirs.

The Astrolabe survey shows that the geology of the
deepwater Taranaki Basin differs from the Taranaki
shelf and onshore in stratigraphy, structural history and
volcanism. The Cretaceous (Fig. 6) and possibly older
succession is considerably thicker in deepwater than
below the shelf. Conversely, the Neogene succession is
considerably thinner. Paleogene sedimentary thicknesses

are more constant and this is also an important feature as
is the relatively gentle post-Cretaceous tectonic regime
documented in the deepwater region.
Extension appears to have been active earlier in the
deepwater region than in the rest of the Taranaki and
Northland region. A relatively gentle tectonic episode
affected rocks in the deepwater region causing long-
wavelength folds and perhaps strike-slip faulting
characterised by flower structures.
Four volcanic episodes are recognised in the deepwater
region. The earliest predates deposition of the prograding
deltaic body described below and the second post-dates
it and is dated from seismic well ties as Late Campanian
(70–75 Ma). A minor volcanic episode appears to have
accompanied Eocene tectonism and is expressed by small
volcanic cones extruded across the flank of the Challenger
Plateau. Finally, Miocene volcanism is expressed in the
large Aotea Seamount.

Between the basement and the top Cretaceous
reflector, which can be readily mapped across the basin
(Fig. 6), is a succession consisting of three megasequences.
Each megasequence is up to one second thickness two-
way time (twt). The basal megasequence (A) is overlain
by a prograding megasequence (B), which in turn is
overlain by an almost parallel-bedded megasequence
(C).

Figure 6. Cretaceous and older (?) stratigraphy of the deepwater part of the Taranaki Basin. For location of line see Fgure 6. 1–4 are the
main bodies forming the Late Cretaceous delta.

The basal unit is clearly a syn-rift megasequence as it
fills grabens within basement and overtops some horst
blocks (Fig. 6). The top of this unit is marked by downlap
of the overlying megasequence and it does not exist
landward of the present shelf edge. Its internal reflectors
are discontinuous and of variable amplitude. A large
volcanic edifice was extruded onto its top surface. The
age of the syn-rift megasequence is poorly constrained.
The oldest sedimentary rocks encountered in nearby
wells are the Rakopi Formation of Campanian age (about
75 Ma, Fig. 7), but the syn-rift megasequence is clearly
much older. A search for possible analogous rocks yields
the Taniwha Formation of Taranaki and Northland and
the Late Jurassic coal measures of the Huriwai Group
(Ballance, 1988) of the Murihiku Group that were
previously considered as part of the basement terrane.
The Huriwai Formation may be the basal unit of
megasequence A. The Wakanui–1 well drilled by Conoco
in 1998 reputedly penetrated Jurassic coal measures
above basement. If true, this is strong evidence for Jurassic
sediments being present in the deepwater part of the
greater Taranaki basin. A Gippsland equivalent for the
major part of megasequence A is likely to be of Early
Cretaceous making the Strzelecki Group a prime candidate.

The top of the prograding megasequence is tied to the
Rakopi Formation in Tane–1 (Fig. 7), which dates the
culmination of this prograding succession as Late
Campanian (about 75 Ma). The prograding megasequence
is subdivided into five bodies (Fig. 6) starting with a high-
stand systems tract. This unit is partially fault-bounded
below the present shelf edge zone and thickens to nearly
one second twt before tapering to zero near the basin
centre. This basal unit may include much coarse clastic
material shed from the fault scarps.
The second unit is a more typical slug-model, high-
stand systems tract, thickening from zero on top of unit
one to about 750 milliseconds twt above the toe of unit
one, before thinning to zero again some 50 km to the
northwest. Internally, sinusoidal reflectors onlap the top
surface of the older systems tract and downlap to the
northwest. Together, the two older units are symptomatic
of continuing, if episodic, relative sea-level rise, probably
tectonically driven by extensional of the Tasman Rift
phase 100–80 Ma (King et al, 1999; Norvick et al, 2001).
The third unit is a low-stand wedge with complex
internal reflectors suggesting good development of sea-
bed fan turbidites. The unit thickens to the northwest
from zero at the slope break of unit two to nearly 500
milliseconds twt. Reflectors also onlap the older volcanic
mound.
Unit four is another high-stand systems tract exhibiting
prograding internal reflectors. The topset beds in this
unit are prominent in that they are of high amplitude,
discontinuous reflectors similar to coal measure units
elsewhere in Taranaki. Further, the top surface of this
unit ties to the Rakopi Formation coal measures in
Tane–1.
The final unit that lies below the top Rakopi Formation
reflector is a thin low-stand wedge located to the northwest
of unit four and onlapping its toe.
Together, the prograding reflector geometry and time
isopachs (Fig. 8) of megasequence B, which clearly
illustrates a lobate compound body, are compelling
evidence for deltaic deposition. The evidence suggests
that a river or rivers fed into a restricted seaway at the
head of the New Caledonia Basin. Such seismically-
imaged deltas have been notably absent from the mid-
Cretaceous basins of New Zealand, despite abundant
evidence of fluvial deposition. Much of the Hoiho Group
(Fig. 4) of the Great South Basin, for example, is fluvial,
but no outlet to the sea is apparent. The Great South
Basin was adjacent to Taranaki during this period so the
Taranaki delta may be the outlet for the Hoiho Group
rivers.

Until the Rakopi unit was deposited, sediment supply
was able to keep up with relative sea-level rise. By the
Late Campanian, the balance had been disrupted by
either an acceleration of relative sea-level rise or a

Figure 7. Seismic line tie to Tane-1 showing main sedimentary
units occupying the shelf area of Taranaki basin.

Wells  at the shelf edge show that carbonate deposition
was not unknown during the Miocene.  The deepwater
Taranaki area remained in relatively deep water
throughout the Neogene.  Miocene depocentres reflect
turbidite deposition, particularly across the paleo shelf
edge to the northwest.  Despite the renewed sediment
supply due to activity at the plate boundary, most Miocene
sediments were deposited closer to shore.  The influx of
sediments associated with renewed Alpine uplift in the
Pliocene formed the present shelf.  The Pliocene within
the study area is up to one second twt thick and is mainly
clastic, consisting of a high proportion of seafloor fan
turbidites.
Petroleum potential of deepwater Taranaki Basin

In deepwater Taranaki, thick coal measure facies at
top Rakopi level cover an area of at least 15,000 km2.
Extensive coals are also likely within the topset beds
of deeper prograding units of the Late Cretaceous
delta, while disseminated coaly kerogen is likely to be
present throughout the foresets and to have been
carried into deeper water by low-stand turbidite fans.
The delta was built into a restricted seaway between
the emergent Challenger Plateau and the West Norfolk
Ridge suggesting that Cretaceous marine mudstones
are also possible petroleum source rocks.  If equivalents
of the Jurassic Huriwai Formation are present in the basin,
a further Jurassic source is also likely along the flanks of the
basin, where it has not been buried too deeply.
Potential petroleum reservoirs in deepwater
Taranaki include the sandstones of the Rakopi coal
measures themselves and marine sandstones of Late
Cretaceous North Cape Formation equivalents as well
as Cretaceous and Paleogene turbidite fans.
Thermal modelling shows that source rocks within the
delta are generally mature today and that maturity is a
low risk for this basin. Two-dimensional thermal maturity
modelling predicts there is up to 1,000 m of mid-
Cretaceous source rock in the oil expulsion window
(Fig. 9). The present day oil generation window is below
about 2,800 m below sea-floor (bsf) for marine source
rocks (Type II kinetics) and 3,200 m for non-marine
source rocks (Type III kinetics). The present day gas
window is below about 5,000 m bsf for non-marine source
rocks (Type III kinetics).
In the centre of the basin, oil expulsion started in the
Cretaceous and Paleogene. A post-Miocene pulse of
sedimentation resulted in the top of the oil expulsion
window climbing a further 200 m to reach much of the
Rakopi Formation equivalent at the present day.  The
gentle Eocene tectonism formed trapping structures as
petroleum was being expelled from source rocks and the
negligible Neogene tectonism that affected the deepwater
Taranaki Basin makes it likely that trap integrity would
have been maintained.

Figure 8. Time isopach map of mega-sequence B, the Late
Cretaceous delta. The red line is the line of figures 6 and 8.

reduction in sediment supply.  The general transgression
noted in the Taranaki Basin and elsewhere was under-
way and the locus of deposition shifted landward by
about 100 km, resulting in deposition of the mainly
marine North Cape Formation.  Previously, an extensive
continental shelf and coastal plain was established, so
with this relatively flat topography, minor changes of
sea-level and sediment supply resulted in large landward
and seaward shifts in depositional systems.

The oscillations of depositional systems continued
throughout the rest of the Late Cretaceous and Paleogene.
During this time, the surrounding basement highs of the
Challenger Plateau and part of the West Norfolk Ridge
Basin as well as the more remote New Zealand mainland,
appear to have been emergent and supplying sediments
to the basin. Folding of Eocene age formed large, gentle
anticlines and flower structures as older faults were
reactivated as compressional and strike-slip faults. By
the Oligocene, clastic sediments were in very short supply
and carbonate deposition was widespread.

The Astrolabe survey provides new data to help
comparisons between the greater Taranaki and Gippsland
Basins.  A direct comparison between the Jurassic Beds
of Gippsland and the Huriwai Formation of Northland is
possible in the deepwater Taranaki Basin.  In both basins
they appear to be essentially coal measures or lacustrine
and their possible presence in Taranaki suggests that
both basins originated during the Late Jurassic in
response to the Early Otway Rift Phase.  The analogy is
strengthened by correlation of the remainder of
Megasequence A with the Strzelecki Group.
The proposed Astrolabe delta of Megasequence B was
deposited in Late Albian to Campanian time (100–75 Ma)
and is a time correlative of the Emperor and Golden
Beach sub-groups.  Megasequence B reflectors downlap
onto the top of Megasequence A, providing evidence for
non-deposition across much of the Strzelecki Group
equivalent in Taranaki. We suggest that this may the
equivalent of the Cenomanian hiatus of Gippsland Basin.
The Kipper volcanics, extruded on top of the Golden
Beach Group, also has its equivalent in Taranaki (Fig.  6).
The Emperor and Golden Beach sub-groups are separated
by a landward shift of facies belts while in Taranaki, the
boundary between the Taniwha equivalent and the
overlying Rakopi Formation is a low-stand followed by a
marked landward shift of facies belts and renewed delta
prograding. In deepwater Taranaki, tectonics appear
to have been waning through Rakopi time as would be
expected, following plate separation and accompanying
opening of the Tasman Sea. This allows a decreasing
Figure 9. Present day maturity model based on Pepper and Corvi (1995) kinetics.  The model was generated using IES Petromod software.

Following the discovery of the onshore Kapuni gas and
condensate field in the 1950s and the giant Maui gas and
condensate field in the 1970s, the industry tended to the
belief that Taranaki was gas-prone and had therefore not
been a popular exploration venue. Several lines of
evidence suggest that the deepwater Taranaki Basin
should be oil-prone rather than gas-prone.
The first is that the shallow water and onshore Taranaki
Basin is now seen as more oil-prone than previously
thought. This is due to an oil trend in the onshore
overthrust zone, the Kaimiro and Ngatoro oilfields in
northern onshore Taranaki, the Maari discovery in 1999
and the more recent Rimu discovery in 2000.  In addition,
the recent offshore discoveries of an oil leg in the Maui
field and a better understanding of its charge history
enhance the Taranaki Basin’s attraction as an oil basin.
Maui hydrocarbons have a terrestrial source,
predominantly Late Cretaceous coal and coaly sediments
(Sykes, 2001), and a complex charge history
(Funnel et al, 2001). Earliest charge was hot brines with
high CO2 content, followed by several phases of oil
migration and a latest phase of oil and gas charge.
The second line of reasoning is based on the seismic
stratigraphy outlined above. The increased marine
influence implied by the delta interpretation and the
known oil richness of deltas around the world increases
confidence that the deepwater Taranaki Basin is oil-
prone. In addition, the inferred restricted seaway
increases the chances of widespread organic rich shales
being deposited.

conclusions to be drawn where knowledge of an aspect of
one of the basins is poorly known and, while such circular
arguments are not proof, such mutual support may be
beneficial to exploration of both basins.

1. Before the Astrolabe survey, the Taranaki Basin was a
relatively poor analogue for Gippsland as its oldest
known sediments were much younger than Gippsland’s.
A relatively good comparison could be made between
Late Cretaceous and Paleogene units of both basins,
but the effects of the Neogene plate boundary are
much more marked in Taranaki than in Gippsland.
Taranaki received voluminous Neogene clastic
sediments while Gippsland remained starved of them.
2. The Astrolabe survey provided evidence to suggest
that Taranaki was probably initiated at about the
same time as Gippsland and that correlatives of all of
the main Gippsland sedimentary groups are likely to
be present in the Taranaki Basin. The survey also
revealed the presence of a large Late Cretaceous delta
with extensive associated coal-bearing units, similar
in age and tectonic setting to the Emperor and Golden
Beach sub-groups and effectively linking Taranaki’s
Taniwha and Rakopi Formations to Gippsland
equivalents.
3. Despite being separated by at least 1,000 km for their
entire history, both basins were at the same latitude
for much of their history, so source rocks in Taranaki
should be at least as oil-prone as in Gippsland, assuming
similar climatic controls on deposition and chemistry.
Additionally, the location of Taranaki, at the head of
a restricted marine trough, enhances the possibility
that rich marine source rocks may be present.  About
30% of the world’s known oil reserves were generated
from Cretaceous source rocks.

sediment supply from New Zealand’s eroding highs to
keep pace with moderate relative sea-level rise enabling
a rich flora to develop across a broad coastal plain.
The Late Cretaceous part of Gippsland’s Latrobe Group
exhibits a seaward shift in facies belts in response to an
apparent marine regression.  By this time, the Taranaki
Rift Phase had commenced below the Taranaki Shelf,
where a mix of coal measure and marine facies were
being deposited in fault-bounded lows. The Pakawau
Group coal measures and North Cape Formation marine
units of Taranaki are equivalents of the Late Cretaceous
Latrobe Group. In deeper water, faulting remained
subdued through the Campanian and Maastrichtian
(84–65 Ma). Reflector patterns are complex and result
from minor relative sea-level changes, the broad shelf
geometry and modest accommodation space.
From the end of the Cretaceous, the Latrobe Group
and Taranaki’s Kapuni coal measures and Moa Group
marine facies are equivalent, even to deposition in a
transgressive environment.  Near the end of the
Paleocene, minor volcanism is recorded across the flank
of the Challenger Plateau synchronous with volcanism in
onshore Gippsland.
Overall patterns are also similar between the two
regions through the Neogene with the exception that
Taranaki received voluminous clastic sediments and
Gippsland was relatively starved of clastics.

Taranaki is New Zealand’s only producing petroleum
basin to date, while Gippsland has been Australia’s most
prolific petroleum region. Although the two basins were
separated by at least 1,000 km at all times since formation
until the Tasman Sea started spreading, both basins were
at similar latitudes and environmental controls on
deposition of coaly source rocks were likely to have been
similar. Much of the petroleum in both Gippsland and
Taranaki was sourced from coal measures of Cretaceous
and Paleogene ages.  In Taranaki, minor volumes were
also generated from Paleocene black marine shale.
Similarly, although coal is the major source rock in
Gippsland, a marine contribution is detected in oils from
the southeastern, oceanward part of the basin (Gorter,
2001).
Reservoir rocks in Gippsland are commonly of
Paleocene age, although accumulations have also been
discovered in Late Cretaceous sediments. Petroleum in
Taranaki has been discovered mainly in Paleocene
reservoirs of the Kapuni Group, but significant discoveries
have also been made in fractured Oligocene limestone
and in Neogene turbidite fans.  The younger reservoirs
are probably symptomatic of Neogene tectonism.
The results of the Astrolabe survey have interesting
implications for both basins.  They show that Cretaceous
plays, particularly Rakopi Formation equivalents, are
valid exploration targets and that marine source rocks
should be considered in the deeper parts of both basins.

text:
New 3-D seismic interpretation techniques such as spec-
tral decomposition and coherency have been shown to
enhance interpretation of stratigraphic features in Tertiary,
poorly lithified rocks, but their use has not been as well
documented on older, more consolidated sediments.
Coherency images seismic discontinuities by calculating
localized seismic trace similarity. Spectral decomposition
uses the discrete Fourier transform to image time thick-
ness variability. In the latter, the amplitude spectrum, com-
puted from a short time window covering the geologic
zone of interest, is tuned by the rock properties within the
analysis window. When applied to 3-D seismic and pre-
sented in map form, these spectral responses image lat-
eral variability within the zone of interest.
In this paper we present a case history where both
spectral decomposition and coherency were used suc-
cessfully to image deep (~10000 ft) and old (Pennsylvanian)
stratigraphic features in the U.S. midcontinent.
The original objective was to generate drilling prospects
in the Middle Pennsylvanian (Desmoinesian) Red Fork
Formation of the Anadarko Basin, Oklahoma. The Red
Fork is a prolific producer throughout the basin, produc-
ing from both marine and valley-fill sands.
The study area is located in the eastern part of the
Anadarko Basin (Figure 1). Pennsylvanian rocks through-
out most of the Anadarko Basin are dominated by shal-
low shelf marine clastics. The Red Fork Formation in the
study area is characterized by three coarsening upward
marine parasequences (Lower, Middle, and Upper Red
Fork), herein referred to as Regional Red Fork, with region-
ally extensive limestones above (Pink Lime) and below
(Inola Lime and Novi Lime). Incised valleys of Lower,
Middle, and Upper Red Fork age have eroded into these
regionally correlative parasequences. This paper will dis-
cuss only Upper Red Fork incised valleys, as they are the
largest and most clearly imaged on the 3-D seismic and
contain the best reservoir rocks in the area.
The Upper Red Fork incised valley system consists of
multiple stages of incision and fill, resulting in a strati-
graphically complex internal architecture. Prior to acquir-
ing 3-D seismic in the area, we followed the conventional
belief that four main stages of valley fill exist, of which the
third, Stage III, is the most abundant producer. Red Fork
incised valleys are generally 0.5-1.0 miles wide and are,
therefore, challenging exploration targets. 3-D seismic tech-
nology was utilized in an attempt to decrease the risk asso-
ciated with drilling for these narrow but prolific objectives.
Acquisition. Amoco acquired three 3-D seismic surveys
over the study area. The first (27 mi2) was shot in 1993. In
1994, 57 mi2 were acquired. Both surveys had primary
objectives below the Red Fork. In 1996, 67 mi2 were
acquired with the main objective of imaging the Upper Red
Fork incised valley system. The three surveys were merged
to produce one 136-mi2 survey (Figure 1). 
Data quality is excellent compared to typical land 3-D
surveys, with a dominant frequency of about 50 Hz and
up to 80 Hz present in the data.
Before the acquisition of the 1996 survey, several wells
in the area were interpreted as penetrating the edge of the
Stage III valley fill. These wells do not produce, but they
do indicate the presence of the Stage III valley. The distri-
bution of wells which produce from Stage III Sand (Figure
1) shows a gap in production in the same part of the 1996
survey. We recognized that this area had good potential
for unpenetrated, and therefore undrained, Stage III reser-
voir sand. This prospective area (Figure 1) was a signifi-
cant objective of the 1996 survey. It was necessary to image
both the edges of the valley and the different stages of fill
within the valley to map the Stage III valley fill and iden-
tify prospects.
Interpretation. Geologically, the Red Fork is bounded
above and below by regionally correlative marker beds
(Pink Lime above and Inola and Novi Limes below) which
have consistent character on electric logs. The same is true
seismically, although the Lower Skinner Shale directly
above the Pink Lime gives a more continuous reflection
than the Pink itself. The Novi Lime provides the most con-

New 3-D seismic interpretation techniques such as spec-
tral decomposition and coherency have been shown to
enhance interpretation of stratigraphic features in Tertiary,
poorly lithified rocks, but their use has not been as well
documented on older, more consolidated sediments.
Coherency images seismic discontinuities by calculating
localized seismic trace similarity. Spectral decomposition
uses the discrete Fourier transform to image time thick-
ness variability. In the latter, the amplitude spectrum, com-
puted from a short time window covering the geologic
zone of interest, is tuned by the rock properties within the
analysis window. When applied to 3-D seismic and pre-
sented in map form, these spectral responses image lat-
eral variability within the zone of interest.
In this paper we present a case history where both
spectral decomposition and coherency were used suc-
cessfully to image deep (~10000 ft) and old (Pennsylvanian)
stratigraphic features in the U.S. midcontinent.
The original objective was to generate drilling prospects
in the Middle Pennsylvanian (Desmoinesian) Red Fork
Formation of the Anadarko Basin, Oklahoma. The Red
Fork is a prolific producer throughout the basin, produc-
ing from both marine and valley-fill sands.
The study area is located in the eastern part of the
Anadarko Basin (Figure 1). Pennsylvanian rocks through-
out most of the Anadarko Basin are dominated by shal-
low shelf marine clastics. The Red Fork Formation in the
study area is characterized by three coarsening upward
marine parasequences (Lower, Middle, and Upper Red
Fork), herein referred to as Regional Red Fork, with region-
ally extensive limestones above (Pink Lime) and below
(Inola Lime and Novi Lime). Incised valleys of Lower,

Middle, and Upper Red Fork age have eroded into these
regionally correlative parasequences. This paper will dis-
cuss only Upper Red Fork incised valleys, as they are the
largest and most clearly imaged on the 3-D seismic and
contain the best reservoir rocks in the area.
The Upper Red Fork incised valley system consists of
multiple stages of incision and fill, resulting in a strati-
graphically complex internal architecture. Prior to acquir-
ing 3-D seismic in the area, we followed the conventional
belief that four main stages of valley fill exist, of which the
third, Stage III, is the most abundant producer. Red Fork
incised valleys are generally 0.5-1.0 miles wide and are,
therefore, challenging exploration targets. 3-D seismic tech-
nology was utilized in an attempt to decrease the risk asso-
ciated with drilling for these narrow but prolific objectives.

Acquisition. Amoco acquired three 3-D seismic surveys
over the study area. The first (27 mi2) was shot in 1993. In
1994, 57 mi2 were acquired. Both surveys had primary
objectives below the Red Fork. In 1996, 67 mi2 were
acquired with the main objective of imaging the Upper Red
Fork incised valley system. The three surveys were merged
to produce one 136-mi2 survey (Figure 1). 
Data quality is excellent compared to typical land 3-D
surveys, with a dominant frequency of about 50 Hz and
up to 80 Hz present in the data.
Before the acquisition of the 1996 survey, several wells
in the area were interpreted as penetrating the edge of the
Stage III valley fill. These wells do not produce, but they
do indicate the presence of the Stage III valley. The distri-

1) shows a gap in production in the same part of the 1996
survey. We recognized that this area had good potential
for unpenetrated, and therefore undrained, Stage III reser-
voir sand. This prospective area (Figure 1) was a signifi-
cant objective of the 1996 survey. It was necessary to image
both the edges of the valley and the different stages of fill
within the valley to map the Stage III valley fill and iden-
tify prospects.

text:
Spectral decomposition provides a
novel means of utilizing seismic data
and the discrete Fourier transform
(DFT) for imaging and mapping tem-
poral bed thickness and geologic dis-
continuities over large 3-D seismic
surveys. By transforming the seismic
data into the frequency domain via the
DFT, the amplitude spectra delineate
temporal bed thickness variability
while the phase spectra indicate lateral
geologic discontinuities. This technol-
ogy has delineated stratigraphic set-
tings (such as channel sands and
structural settings involving complex
fault systems) in 3-D surveys.
Widess pioneered a widely used
method for quantifying thin-bed thick-
ness in 1973. Because it uses peak-to-
trough time separation in conjunction
with amplitude, this method depends
on careful processing to establish the
correct wavelet phase and true trace-
to-trace amplitudes. Although similar
in context, the spectral method pro-
posed here uses a more robust phase-
independent amplitude spectrum and
is designed for examining thin-bed
responses over large 3-D surveys.
The concept behind spectral
decomposition is that a reflection from
a thin bed has a characteristic expres-
sion in the frequency domain that is
indicative of the temporal bed thick-
ness. For example, a simple homoge-
neous thin bed introduces a
predictable and periodic sequence of
notches into the amplitude spectrum
of the composite reflection (Figure 1).
The seismic wavelet, however, typi-
cally spans multiple subsurface lay-
ers—not just one simple thin bed. This
layered system results in a complex
tuned reflection that has a unique fre-
quency domain expression.
The amplitude spectrum interfer-
ence pattern from a tuned reflection
defines the relationship between
acoustic properties of the individual
beds that comprise the reflection.
Amplitude spectra delineate thin-bed
variability via spectral notching pat-
terns, which are related to local rock
mass variability. Likewise, phase spec-
tra respond to lateral discontinuities
via local phase instability. Together,
the amplitude- and phase-related
interference phenomena allow inter-
preters to quickly and efficiently quan-
tify and map local rock mass variabil-
ity within large 3-D surveys.
The difference in frequency
response between a long-window and
a short-window amplitude spectrum
is significant. The transform from a
long trace approximates the spectrum
of the wavelet (Figure 2), but the trans-
form from a short trace comprises a
wavelet overprint and a local inter-
ference pattern representing the
acoustic properties and thickness of
the geologic layers spanned by the
window (Figure 3).
With a few exceptions (e.g.,
cyclothems and sabkhas), long analy-
sis windows encompass many geo-
logic variations that statistically
randomize interference patterns of
individual thin beds. The resulting
long-window reflectivity spectra
appear white or flat. This is the premise
behind multiple suppression via
deconvolution. Given a large enough
window, the geologic stacking of indi-
vidual thin layers can be considered
random. The convolution of a source
wavelet with a random geologic sec-
Interpretational applications of spectral
decomposition in reservoir characterization
GREG PARTYKA, JAMES GRIDLEY, and JOHN LOPEZ, Amoco E&P Technology Group, Tulsa, Oklahoma, U.S.
<image: DeviceGray, width: 885, height: 355, bpc: 8>
Figure 1. Thin-bed spectral imaging.
<image: DeviceGray, width: 858, height: 797, bpc: 8>
Figure 2. Long-window spectral decomposition and its relationship to the
convolutional model. A long temporal window samples random geology
that commonly exhibits a white (flat) amplitude spectrum.
tion creates an amplitude spectrum
that resembles the wavelet.
The response from a short window
is dependent on the acoustic proper-
ties and thicknesses of the layers
spanned by the window. The shorter
the window, the less random the sam-
pled geology. The amplitude spectrum
no longer approximates just the
wavelet but rather the wavelet plus
local layering. In such small windows,
the geology acts as a local filter on the
reflecting wavelet, thereby attenuat-
ing its spectrum. The resulting ampli-
tude spectrum is not white and
represents the interference pattern
within the window.
The short-window phase spectrum
is also useful in mapping local rock
mass characteristics. Because phase is
sensitive to subtle perturbations in the
seismic character, it is ideal for detect-
ing lateral acoustic discontinuities. If
the rock mass within the window is lat-
erally stable, its phase response will
likewise be stable. If a lateral discon-
tinuity occurs, the phase response
becomes unstable across that discon-
tinuity. Once the rock mass stabilizes
on the other side of the discontinuity,
the phase response likewise stabilizes.
Wedge model response. Spectral
decomposition and thin-bed tuning
phenomena can be illustrated by a sim-
ple wedge model (Figure 4a). The tem-
poral response consists of two
reflectivity spikes of equal but oppo-
site magnitude. The top of the wedge
is marked by a negative reflection coef-
ficient and the bottom by a positive
reflection coefficient. The wedge thick-
ens from 0 ms on the left to 50 ms on
the right. Filtering the reflectivity
model (using an 8-10-40-50 Hz
Ormsby filter) illustrates the tuning
effects brought on with a change in
thickness (Figure 4b). The top and bot-
tom reflections are resolved at larger
thicknesses but blend into one reflec-
tion as the wedge thins.
A short-window amplitude spec-
trum was computed for each reflec-
tivity trace. These are plotted with
frequency as the vertical axis (Figure
4c). The temporal thickness of the
wedge determines the period of the
notches in the amplitude spectrum
with respect to frequency (Figure 5a).
Pf = 1/t, where Pf = period of notches
in the amplitude spectrum with
respect to frequency (Hz), and t = thin-
bed thickness (s).
Another viewpoint illustrates that
the value of the frequency component
determines the period of the notches
in the amplitude spectrum with
respect to thin-bed thickness (Figure
5b). Pt = 1/f, where Pt = period of
notches in the amplitude spectrum
with respect to temporal thickness (s),
and f = discrete Fourier frequency.
Even a relatively low-frequency
component such as 10 Hz quantifies
thin-bed variability.
The wedge model (Figures 4 and
5) illustrates the application of this
approach to a very simple two-reflec-
tor reflectivity model. Increasing the
complexity of the reflectivity model
will in turn complicate the interfer-
ence pattern.
The tuning cube. Amoco’s most
common approach to characterize
reservoirs using spectral decomposi-
tion is via the “zone-of-interest tuning
cube” (Figure 6). The interpreter starts
by mapping the temporal and vertical
bounds of the zone-of-interest. Ashort
temporal window about this zone is
<image: DeviceGray, width: 676, height: 619, bpc: 8>
Figure 3. Short-window spectral decomposition and its relationship to the
convolutional model. A short temporal window samples ordered (nonran-
dom) geology that tunes the amplitude spectrum.
<image: Lab, width: 867, height: 763, bpc: 8>
Figure 4. Blocky wedge model. (a) Reflectivity; (b) filtered reflectivity; (c)
spectral amplitudes.
transformed from the time domain
into the frequency domain. The result-
ing “tuning cube” can be viewed in
cross-section or plan view (common
frequency slices).
The frequency slice is typically
more useful because it allows inter-
preters to visualize thin-bed interfer-
ence patterns in plan view from which
he or she can, drawing on experience,
identify textures and patterns indica-
tive of geologic processes. Amplitude
or phase versus frequency behav-
ior/tuning is fully expressed by ani-
mating through the entire frequency
range (i.e., through all frequency
slices).
Tuning cube maps of the earth’s
subsurface are in many ways analo-
gous to satellite imaging maps of the
earth’s surface. Both methods take
advantage of frequency subbands to
map lateral variability in surface prop-
erties.
Removing the wavelet overprint. The
tuning cube has three components:
thin-bed interference, wavelet over-
print, and noise (Figure 7). Since the
geologic response is the most inter-
esting component for the interpreter,
it is prudent to balance the wavelet
amplitude without degrading the geo-
logic information. This reduces the
tuning cube to thin-bed interference
and noise.
Common spectral balancing tech-
niques rely on sparse invariant sta-
tionary statistics. If we assume that the
geologic tuning varies considerably
along any flattened horizon, then we
balance the wavelet spectrum by
equalizing each frequency slice accord-
ing to its average amplitude (Figure 8).
After whitening to minimize the
wavelet effect, the tuning cube retains
two main components: thin-bed inter-
ference and noise. 
In frequency-slice form, thin-bed
interference appears as coherent
amplitude variations. Random noise
speckles the interference pattern in a
similar fashion to poor quality televi-
sion reception. At dominant frequen-
cies, the relatively high signal-to-noise
<image: DeviceGray, width: 418, height: 832, bpc: 8>
Figure 6. Zone-of-interest tuning
cube.
<image: Lab, width: 879, height: 1066, bpc: 8>
Figure 5. Thin-bed tuning of amplitudes versus frequency (a) with respect
to frequency and (b) with respect to thin-bed thickness.
<image: DeviceGray, width: 897, height: 419, bpc: 8>
Figure 7. Prior to balancing the spectrum, the tuning cube consists of thin-
bed interference, the seismic wavelet, and random noise.
ratio (SNR) results in clear pictures of
thin-bed tuning. Movement away
from dominant frequency causes the
SNR to degrade. At frequencies
beyond usable bandwidth, the poor
SNR results in a noise map.
Beyond the zone-of-interest. The tun-
ing cube addresses the tuning prob-
lem on a local zone-of-interest scale.
Characterizing larger seismic volumes
requires a different approach. For
decomposition beyond the single
reflectivity package or zone-of-inter-
est, we recommend “discrete fre-
quency energy cubes” or, with
different data organization, the “time-
frequency 4-D cube.”
“Discrete frequency energy cubes”
(Figure 9) are computed from a single
input seismic volume into multiple
discrete frequency amplitude and
phase volumes. Computation is done
via running window spectral analysis
which calculates the amplitude or
phase spectrum for each sample. The
spectral components are then sorted
into common frequency component
cubes. This method is typically done
only after scoping the zone-of-interest,
horizon-based tuning cube.
For the “time-frequency 4-D cube,”
the spectral decomposition is also com-
puted using a running window
approach. The results are sorted into
common samples with increasing fre-
quency. This volume allows the inter-
preter to exploit conventional
interpretive workstation software and
navigate through the volume at any
depth slice for any frequency. The out-
put is many times the size of the input,
but it allows the interpreter to navigate
and visualize in space, time, and fre-
quency.
Gulf of Mexico example. A case his-
tory from the Gulf of Mexico illustrates
the use of spectral decomposition to
image the Pleistocene-age-equivalent
of the modern Mississippi River delta.
Tuning cube frequency slices (Figure
10) capture the subtleties of inherent
tuning and reveal the various deposi-
tional features more effectively than
full-bandwidth energy and phase
extractions (Figure 11). For example,
compare the north-south delineation
for channel A. The image from 26 Hz
(Figure 10b) is significantly better than
from 16 Hz (Figure 10a). On the other
hand, channel B is better imaged by 16
Hz than by 26 Hz. Neither channel is
adequately delineated by conventional
energy envelope extraction. The
strength of the phase component lies
in detecting discontinuities. The
response in both phase slices (Figure
<image: DeviceGray, width: 919, height: 878, bpc: 8>
Figure 9. Discrete frequency energy cubes.
<image: None, width: 2016, height: 1852, bpc: 1>
Figure 8. Removing the wavelet overprint (balancing the spectrum) without
removing the reflectivity tuning characteristics.
10c,d) is stable away from the faults
but becomes unstable crossing dis-
continuities such as faults. These spec-
tral phase maps provide sharper
definition of faults than a conventional
response phase map (Figure 11b).
Conclusions. Spectral decomposition
can be a powerful aid to the imaging
and mapping of bed thickness and
geologic discontinuities. Real seismic
is rarely dominated by simple blocky,
resolved reflections. In addition, true
geologic boundaries rarely fall along
fully resolved seismic peaks and
troughs. By transforming the data into
the frequency domain with the dis-
crete Fourier transform, short-window
amplitude and phase spectra localize
thin-bed reflections and define bed-
thickness variability within complex
rock strata. This allows the interpreter
to quickly and effectively quantify
thin-bed interference and detect sub-
tle discontinuities within large 3-D sur-
veys.
Suggestions for further reading. The
Fourier Transform and its Applications
by Bracewell (McGraw-Hill, 1965).
“Spectral analysis applied to seismic
monitoring of thermal recovery” by
Dilay and Eastwood (TLE, 1995).
“Identification of deltaic facies with 3-
D seismic coherency and spectral
decomposition cube” by Lopez et al.
(Abstract, Istanbul ‘97). “Interpret-
ational aspects of spectral decomposi-
tion” by Partyka and Gridley
(Abstract, Istanbul ‘97). “How thin is
a thin bed?” by Widess (GEOPHYSICS,
1973).
<image: DeviceGray, width: 668, height: 416, bpc: 8>
Figure 10. Gulf of Mexico (a) 16-Hz energy map, (b) 26-Hz energy map, (c) 16-Hz phase map, (d) 26-Hz phase map.

<image: Lab, width: 668, height: 416, bpc: 8>
<image: Lab, width: 668, height: 416, bpc: 8>
<image: DeviceGray, width: 668, height: 416, bpc: 8>
Figure 11. Gulf of Mexico full-bandwidth (a) conventional energy envelope extraction, (b) conventional response
phase extraction.

General
Well 7220/8-1 was drilled just west of the Polheim Sub-platform and Loppa High in the 
Barents Sea. The main objective was to prove an economical volume of hydrocarbons 
and to establish hydrocarbon contacts in the Stø and Nordmela formations in the 
Skrugard Prospect. The targeted Skrugard fault block is one of several rotated fault 
blocks in the licence and a part of the Bjørnøyrenna Fault Complex.
Operations and results
A shallow 8 1/2" pre-spud well (7220/8-U-1) was drilled and logged to 955 m to check for 
shallow gas due to seismic anomalies around the well location. No shallow gas was 
encountered. After that wildcat well 7220/8-1 was spudded with the semi-submersible 
installation Polar Pioneer on 27 February 2011 and drilled to TD at 2222 m in the Late 
Triassic Snadd Formation. Drilling operations proceeded without significant problems but 
upon intermediate MDT logging the cable broke and about 10 days were lost fishing. The 
well was drilled with spud mud and hi-vis pills down to 850 m and with 
KCl/Polymer/Glycol from 850 m to TD.
The well penetrated Tertiary and Cretaceous Claystones and Sandstones and upper 
Jurassic Claystones above the reservoir. In the reservoir the well penetrated Sandstones 
of Jurassic age, within the Stø, Nordmela and Tubåen Formations, and of Triassic age 
within the Fruholmen and Snadd Formations. The primary target reservoir was 
penetrated with top Stø Formation at 1276 m, and top Nordmela Formation at 1354 m. 
These Formations contained a 37 m thick gas column (GOC at 1312 m) and an 83 m 
thick oil column (OWC at 1395 m). Results from the well indicate that flat spots seen on 
the geo-seismic section represent the gas-oil-contact (GOC) and the oil-water-contact 
(OWC). The Snadd Formation was penetrated at 2122 m TVD, which was 35 m 
shallower than the prognosis.
Very good hydrocarbon shows were seen when drilling the reservoir in the Stø and 
Nordmela Formations. No shows were observed below 1400 m in the core chips and 
cuttings.
A total of five cores were cut in the Stø and Nordmela Formations, in the interval 1292.5 
- 1405.5 m (97.8% recovery). Schlumberger MDT single probe was used for all samples. 
Oil samples were acquired at 1320.6 m, 1336.8 m, and at 1380.5 m in the Stø and 
Nordmela Formations. Due to the broken cable incident no water or gas samples were 
acquired.
The well was permanently abandoned on 2 May 2011 as an oil and gas discovery.
Testing
No drill stem test was performed.

Oil samples were acquired at 1320.6 m, 1336.8 m, and at 1380.5 m in the Stø and
Nordmela Formations. Due to the broken cable incident no water or gas samples were
acquired.
The well was permanently abandoned on 2 May 2011 as an oil and gas discovery.
Testing
No drill stem test was performed.

Wellbore history
General
License 095 was awarded to the Conoco/Statoil/Arco/Tenneco group in 1984 with 
Conoco as operator. The area, known as Haltenbanken, is a promising oil and gas 
province. It straddles two major Mesozoic structural features, the Trøndelag Platform 
and the Vøring Basin and lies along the western flank of the series of NNE-SSW faults, 
which separate them. The well was drilled on the A-prospect and was designed to test a 
major fault block. It was hoped to test oil bearing Middle Jurassic Sandstone at 
approximately 3898 m with a secondary objective at the Early Jurassic level.
The well is Type Well for the Lysing Formation.
Operations and results
Wildcat well 6507/7-1 was spudded with the semi-submersible drilling rig Nortrym on 10 
August 1984 and drilled to TD at a depth of 4825 in the Early Jurassic Tilje Formation. 
The well was drilled with seawater and hi-vis pills down to 906 m, with gypsum/polymer 
mud from 906 m to 3803 m, and with gypsum/lignite mud from 3803 m to TD. Few 
problems were experienced whilst drilling the well. Some time was lost due to gumbo-
associated problems. Mud was lost to formation while cementing the 13 3/8" casing, 
resulting in the top of cement being lower than planned. However this did not affect the 
strength at the shoe, as it was possible to make a good leak off test after drilling out. 
Tight hole problems were experienced on a bit trip from 3716 meters, with over pull 
recorded on the majority of subsequent trips. In addition a gain of 45 bbls of mud at 4360 
meters indicated apparent under balanced conditions. Mud weight was progressively 
raised from 11.2 ppg at 4081 meters to 12.6 ppg by 4360 meters in response to this 
problem. A further increase to 13.1 ppg was made at TD due to logging difficulties 
associated with tight hole. The overall operation took 115 days from spud. Total depth 
was reached in 87 days, while an additional 28 days were used to log, test and abandon 
the well.
Sharp increases in total gas and penetration rates marked the top of the Middle Jurassic 
Sandstone at 4338 m, (Ile Formation). The interval 4340 m to 4370 meters was cored. 
High total gas levels were present in the upper section of this sandstone, however no 
hydrocarbons heavier than propane were recorded. Gas was observed to bleed from the 
core and fluorescence was bright though cut was slow. Log analysis indicated some of 
the sands were possibly gas saturated and it was therefore decided the interval 4338 - 
4374 meters, at the top of the sandstone, should be tested. Core and log derived 
porosities were largely similar. The log derived porosity averaged 6% over the majority of 
the interval with up to 15% indicated in a thin zone at the top and 10% in a 7 meter 
section at the bottom of the sandstone. The core derived permeability data shows an 
average liquid permeability of 0.77 md and an average overall permeability (excluding 
fractures) of 0.3 md. Higher permeabilities in the range 360 md to 673 md were reported 
from a 0.65-meter interval around 4131 meters.
A comprehensive suite of logs was run, including nine RFT runs. A total of seven cores 
were obtained. One was cut in the Early Cretaceous, three in the Ile Formation, one in 
the Ror Formation, and one in the Tilje Formation. The RFT data indicated the tested 
zones had very low permeability. Water and gas was sampled during DST.
The well was permanently abandoned on 1 December 1984 as a dry well with gas 
shows.
Testing
A drill stem test was performed in the upper part of the Ile Formation. Prior to the DST a
