attributes in the reservoir analysis. It begins with the lo-
cation of trap structures, then follows the determination of
accumulation zone parameters, and ends up with the de-
tection of hydrocarbon indicators.
Reminders of reservoir characteristics
Reservoir characterization consists of analyzing the different
reservoir parameters such as porosity, permeability, water sat-
uration, reservoir lithology, and sometimes its size. Reservoirs
are defined in this work as rocks with interconnected voids
that promote the circulation and accumulation of fluids. If we
find the hydrocarbons (oil and/or gas) are found within among
these fluids, reservoirs are called hydrocarbons. The complic-
ity of reservoirs sometimes makes it difficult to better under-
stand these reservoir rocks to the spatial and even temporal
variation of the criteria which conditions the existence of res-
ervoir rocks. Nevertheless, reservoirs can be defined accord-
ing to the petrophysical and geological characteristics.
Petrophysical characteristics
Petrophysics is the study of the physical and chemical charac-
teristics of rocks. According to Cossé (1988), a rock consti-
tutes a reservoir if and only if it has a storage capacity
(porosity) and that fluids can circulate (permeability). The
petrophysical characteristics of the reservoirs are closely de-
pendent on the rock-fluid relations and in particular the inter-
faces between rocks and their contents (fluids). There are two
types of petrophysical properties, namely conventional
petrophysical properties and those derived from rock mechan-
ics (Neau 2009).
Conventional petrophysical properties
It is necessary to take a look at the elements that characterize
the reservoirs notably the porosity, permeability, fluid satura-
tion, and volume of clay.
The porosity (Φ) of a rock is its property to have voids,
pores, or cracks. It is expressed quantitatively by the percent-
age of the pore volume in relation to the total volume of the
rock. Consider a rock sample with its apparent volume or total
volume VT consisting of a solid volume VS and a pore volume
VP. The porosity Φ is presented in the equation: Φ = VVoid−space
VTotal ,
expressed in %.
Reservoir specialists are interested in porosity allowing the
circulation of fluids in the pores. Φe is the effective porosity
which corresponds to the pores connected to each other and
the outside. Thus, we define the total porosity Φt correspond-
ing to all the pores, whether or not related to each other, and
the residual porosity Φr which considers only isolated pores.
The pore structure varies depending on the type of reservoir
rock because the pore system of the carbonate reservoir rock is
different and irregular. Thus, the pore structure has an impact
on the elastic wave velocities. Sun (2004) demonstrates that
by considering the resolution of Zoeppritz’s exact equations
and elastic finite element modeling, it is possible to detect
variations in pore structure in reservoir rocks from seismic
data via an amplitude variation analysis with offset (AVO).
Permeability is a measure of the capacity for fluid move-
ment in porous or fractured media (Rubino et al. 2012). If the
fluid is homogeneous and has no significant action on the
surrounding medium, the permeability is said to be ab-
solute. The unit of measurement of the permeability is
the darcy, and in most cases, the millidarcy is used
(with 1 mD = 10−15m2). The permeability is good if
its value is between 200 and 500 mD.
Saturation can be defined as impregnation of interstitial
voids of a porous or cracked medium by infiltration of fluid
(oil, gas, or water). Thus, the saturation of oil, water, and gas is
defined as the ratio of each of the volume of the fluids to the
total volume and they are denoted as SW, SO and SG for the
water saturation, oil, and gas respectively (1).
SW ¼ VW
VP

where VP is the pore volume, VW is the volume of water, VO is
the volume of oil, and VG is the volume of gas. In the petro-
leum domain, knowledge of the oil and gas volumes requires
knowledge of saturation at all points or at least a satisfactory
approach (Cossé 1988).
Volume of clay The volume of clay is very important for the
study of reservoir rocks. So, we consider the case of simple
clay formations that are formed from a matrix rock sandstone,
limestone, or dolomite, mixed with clay. They contain inter-
stitial fluids such as water, oil, or gas. The distribution of the
clay usually gives dispersed, laminated, and structural clays.
The clay volume VCL comprises bound water ɸB but some-
times the clay index (ICL or Ish) is used instead of clay volume
because of its relation to the effect of the clay only to its
volume. In fact, Vsh consists of clay and the impurities asso-
ciated with it that are silt, limestone, and anhydrite while VCL
is considered as the volume of the pure clay. It is this pure clay
that intervenes during the interpretation.
Petrophysical properties derived from rock mechanics
The indirect or derived petrophysical properties from mechan-
ic rocks are basically related to elastic modules
(incompressibility, shear modulus, Young’s modulus,
Poisson’s ratio). The reservoir is assumed to be a porous iso-
tropic and linearly elastic medium. Thus, the velocities of the
P and S waves are entirely characterized by three parameters,
namely the isostatic modulus of elasticity (bulk modulus), the
shear modulus (shear modulus), and bulk density which is in
grams per cubic centimeter. The rock contains a solid
component and porous component saturated with differ-
ent fluids that represent a continuous real medium with
average elastic properties.
Geological characteristics
Geological characteristics are important in the determination
of layers that constitute accumulation zones. Thus, reservoir
rocks can be grouped into two main types, namely detrital
reservoirs and carbonate reservoirs.
Detrital reservoirs (also known as sandstone reservoirs)
Detrital reservoirs are generally composed of stable elements,
having a fairly homogeneous porosity and permeability, of
intergranular type, controlled by the grain size and the degree
of cementation. The relationships between porosity and per-
meability are generally good and decrease with landfill that
are regular and function with temperature.
Carbonate reservoirs
Carbonated reservoirs are characterized by a very large het-
erogeneity of porosity and permeability. They are often mas-
sive, large pore, and fissured in the case of reefs, finely strat-
ified and laminated in the reef and shoal deposits. They consist
mainly of dolomites and limestones.
Characterization of reservoirs by seismic
attributes
The characterization of the reservoirs by the analysis of the
seismic attributes (Oyeyemi and Aizebeokhai 2015) enables
to build from these attributes so as to make a precise study of
the reservoirs to determine the different models of the reser-
voirs which are precisely geological, stratigraphic, and
petrophysical models. The seismic attributes make it possible
to estimate the permeability, porosity, hydrocarbon indicators,
fluid movement, thickness, lithology, and the monitoring
of hydrocarbon production. This study does not enumer-
ate exhaustively all the attributes used in reservoir char-
acterization but highlights some relevant seismic attri-
butes best suited for reservoir location, property analy-
sis, and hydrocarbon zone detection.
Location of reservoir
Nowadays, there are attributes that can circumscribe areas of
hydrocarbon accumulations. This localization takes place thanks
to the structures that define the delimitation and the location of
the reservoirs because it involves identifying trap structures.
There are summarily three types of traps: structural traps (faults,
anticlines, and synclines); stratigraphic traps (sandstone body,
carbonate reef, and permeability bevel); and mixed traps (salt
dome). Several seismic attributes such as similarity, thinned fault
likelihood, semblance, fault enhancement filter, ridge enhance-
ment filter, curvature, variance, azimuthal AVO, inversion to
anisotropic parameters, fault extraction, instantaneous amplitude,
sweetness attribute, coherence, gradients, and dips are used to
determine the structures for locating the reservoirs. But the cur-
vature, coherence, gradient, and dip are mainly dedicated to the
determination of channel, faults, anticlines, synclines, and salt
dome. To do this, it would be necessary to highlight the most
important attributes in the detection of traps such as coherence,
variance, amplitude gradients, dip azimuth measurements, and
curvature. Coherence attribute can be defined as a measurement
of the lateral continuity of the seismic signal (Backé et al. 2012).
The identification of faults by coherence (Xia et al. 2015) is
undoubtedly a topic that interests specialists in oil exploration
based on publications in this domain (Fig. 1). But the first pub-
lications (Bahorich and Farmer 1995; Marfurt et al. 1998;
Garsztenkorn and Marfurt 1999) played a decisive role in the
use of this method, because it was in their work to highlight
a cross-correlation of the seismic traces, then to conduct a
study of multitrace and finally to implement the algorithm
of similarity obtained thanks to the eigenvalues of a matrix
of covariance on a window of seismic data. For example,
several studies (Roberts 2001; Sigismondi and Soldo 2003;
Chopra and Marfurt 2007a) were conducted to improve
fault detection. With coherence, the location of reservoirs
becomes easy by providing for the determination of geolog-
ical structures (Rezvandehy et al. 2011; Bahorich and
Farmer 1995). Coherence attribute is the method used in
calculating the similarity between seismic traces and is also
the best determinant of anticline structures, faults, deltas,
river channels, dikes, and other stratigraphic anomalies
(Rezvandehy et al. 2011). The identification of faults and
fracture zones by the coherence attribute was first illustrated
by the works of Bahorich and Farmer (1995) on the cross-
correlation of seismic traces, then by a study on a multitrace
semblance of Marfurt et al. (1998) and finally by the analy-
sis of Garsztenkorn and Marfurt (1999) based on the simi-
larity algorithm obtained thanks to the eigenvalues of a co-
variance matrix on a window of the seismic data. Thus, the
detection of faults by the coherence attribute has improved
considerably thanks to the research conducted in recent
years (Randen et al. 2001; Pedersen et al. 2002; Aqrawi
and Boe 2011; Dorn et al. 2012).
Curvature attributes Curvature is an excellent attribute for
detecting fractures and even faults. It is calculated using a very
simple formula (2):

which is also the inverse of the osculating circle with seismic
horizons. According to Roberts (2001), curvature is a 2D property
of a curve and describes how bent a curve is at a particular point on
the curve, i.e., how much the curve deviates from a straight line at
this point (Fig. 2). Therefore, positive or negative curvature values
indicate anticlinal or synclinal structures respectively (Fig. 3).
Thus, there are several types of curvature attributes such as
mean curvature (km), Gaussian curvature (kg), maximum cur-
vature (kmax), minimum curvature (Kmin), intaglio curvature
(Kd), curvature of strike (Ks), contour curvature (kc), and most
positive and negative curvatures (K+ and K−) (Fig. 4). The
utility of curvatures in reservoir analysis varies according to
the structures they emphasize. It is in this sense that the max-
imum curvature is very effective in detecting faults. Similarly,
curvature measurements such as the most positive curvatures
and the most negative curvatures are increasingly used by
specialists because of their significant results in terms of struc-
tural analysis. Thus, the positive curvatures show anticlinal
structures and raised fault blocks, while the most negative

(Chopra and Marfurt 2007). In addition to their effectiveness,
the determination of traps makes it possible to highlight strat-
igraphic characteristics such as channels, lifts, and bars.
The first step in the reservoir study is to locate reservoir
rocks by identifying structures capable of accumulating hy-
drocarbons. To do this, the structural attributes define the oil
system by highlighting the pitfalls that constitute the essential
element in the location of reservoirs. The attributes of curva-
ture, similarity, and spectral decomposition play a large role in
the location of oil deposits. Thus, studies have been conducted
to find out the location of reservoirs (AlBinHassan and
Marfurt 2003; Cohen et al. 2006; Fomel 2007).
Attributes such as instantaneous amplitude, spectral de-
composition, curvature, and coherence enable to deter-
mine geological structures that constitute the zones
where hydrocarbons are trapped. It is clear that these
attributes expose structural, stratigraphic, and even
mixed traps defining the hydrocarbon accumulation
zones. Knowing these areas, it is necessary to make
an analysis of the properties of reservoirs by seismic

Determination reservoir properties
The analysis of reservoir properties is the major step in its char-
acterization. Thus, several attributes analyze reservoir properties
such as lithology, porosity, permeability, thickness, and delimi-
tation of layer. In this case, the analysis of the reservoir parame-
ters is performed using the seismic attributes, mainly accompa-
nied by good data to improve the quality of results. Thus, the
instantaneous amplitude, the instantaneous frequency, the spec-
tral decomposition, the rate of variation of the envelope, the
acoustic impedance, the shear impedance, the shear modulus,
and the instantaneous phase are applied to extract information
relating to lithology, thickness estimation, sequence delineation,
porosity, and permeability. The instantaneous amplitude is wide-
ly used to accurately determine the location of reservoirs through
anomalies such as bright spot, flat spot, and dim spot (Fig. 5).
Thickness and delimitation of layers
The delimitation of layers is carried out by attributes such as
the instantaneous amplitude and the instantaneous phase.
These two attributes highlight the sequences that exist with-
in the reservoir. By referring to regional geology, it
becomes easy to deduce from these sequences the different
layers that constitute the reservoir. After determining the
different layers, it is necessary to estimate the thickness of
the layers of the reservoir. To do this, the instantaneous
frequency and the spectral decomposition are seismic
attributes that make it possible to estimate the thickness
of a layer. Sometimes, the combination of attributes
provides better results in estimating thicknesses (Asim
et al. 2016). It is in this sense that Zhao et al. (2008)
have shown that the association of maximum amplitude
and acoustic impedance illustrates the estimation of
thicknesses (Fig. 6). Spectral decomposition (Castagna
et al. 2003; Naseer et al. 2017; Naseer and Asim
2018) is a seismic attribute that highlights a spectrum
that describes the abnormal low- and high-frequency
effects responsible of seismic traces to change (Fig. 7).
It delineates the reservoir and is very important in the
stratigraphic analysis of reservoirs. It promotes a better
understanding of reservoir heterogeneities and their implica-
tions by analyzing parameters such as seismic geomorpholo-
gy, thickness estimation, lithology, and even direct hydrocar-
bon detection. It is widely used to estimate thickness (Liu and
Marfurt 2006; Dezfoolian et al. 2013; Li et al. 2019).

Lithology
It is very important in the characterization of the reser-
voirs because of the information it contains on the ac-
cumulation zones (Wang and Huang 2016). The nature
of the layers is a determining factor in the quality of the
reservoir. The instantaneous amplitude, instantaneous
frequency, the rate of variation of the envelope, and
the shear modulus are attributes that determine the lith-
ological parameters of reservoirs. The instantaneous at-
tributes (Khan and Akhter 2016) such as amplitude,
frequency, and rate of change of the envelope, through
a good visualization, provide highlight of the different
layers. To do this, it is important to have enough
knowledge of the geology of the study area to better
highlight the different layers. The extraction of the λρ
and μρ attributes of the seismic data provides quality
information on the nature of the rocks and even on
the fluids of the reservoir (Fig. 8). By crossing these
two attributes, the identification of different lithologies
becomes easy. It is the same that the crossing of the
ratio of velocities Vp/Vs by μρ offers good lithological
discrimination. A cross-plot of the natural log of acous-
tic impedance versus Poisson’s ratio is often used for
the identification of layer lithology (Hilterman et al.
1998).
Porosity and permeability
In the study of reservoirs, porosity and permeability are the
most important properties. It is clear that a good knowledge of
these parameters leads to a good understanding of the quality
of the study area but their determination remains difficult.
Thus, the approach used by the seismic (Pride et al. 2003;
Rubino et al. 2012; Naeem et al. 2015) and more precisely
by the seismic attributes would allow the estimation of the
porosity and the permeability through the variation of the
impedance contrast obtained thanks to the reflectivity of the
P and S waves on the reservoir. Thus, Bachrach (2006) uses
three seismic attributes, namely acoustic impedance, shear
impedance, and density, to make a joint estimate of porosity
and saturation (Figs. 9 and 10). Attributes deduced from im-
pedances such as λρ, μρ, and Vp/Vs are widely used to predict
porosity. Similarly, the crossing of the two AVO (amplitude
variation with offset) attributes, namely the gradient and the
intercept, makes it possible to estimate the porosity. Thus,
porosity estimation is most often done using attributes such
as deterministic inversion, neural networks, and rock property
prediction. As regards permeability, the use of the
instantaneous frequency would make it possible to provide
information on the mobility of the fluids. Using linear
regression, Corbeanu et al. (2002) demonstrate that permeabil-
ity is predicted from instantaneous amplitude and frequency at

each point in the data volume (Fig. 11). Thus, Goloshubin
et al. (2006) conducted a study that uses low frequencies to
estimate fluid content and map highly permeable production
zones in reservoirs.
Identifying areas of hydrocarbons
The identification of hydrocarbons through seismic data be-
gan a long time ago when several works have been devoted to
the study of the amplitude of seismic waves in the detection of
areas of hydrocarbon accumulations (O’Doherty and Anstey
1971; Sheriff 1974; Barry and Shugart 1974; Hilterman
1975). Thus, the work of Anstey (1972, 1973a, 1973b) marks
the birth of the seismic attributes which over time have be-
come precious tools of the petroleum industry. For him, the
force of reflection which is a measure of amplitude was the
main attribute for the analysis of bright spots. Afterwards,
researchers’ interest in the notion of attributes is justified by
studies carried out in this domain (Taner et al. 1979;
Robertson and Fisher 1988; Taner et al. 1994; Chen and
Sidney 1997; Barnes 2001; Chopra and Marfurt 2005;
Zhang et al. 2015; Wang et al. 2019). In the literature, several
attributes make it possible to detect hydrocarbons on a volume
or a seismic section (Li and Liu 2018; Negm et al. 2020). The

most common are the AVO attributes, frequency attenuation,

the gas and non-gas zones on the basis of regression analysis
with attributes such as average instantaneous frequency, peak
spectral frequency, average instantaneous phase, and sweet-
ness attributes. The direct detection of hydrocarbons (bright
spot, flat spot, and dim spot) by the instantaneous amplitude
and the instantaneous frequency is not always effective (Fig.
12). Attenuation is defined as any decrease in amplitude of the
wavefront during its propagation and is associated or not with
the velocity dispersion, depending on the physical mechanism
at the origin of the decrease in amplitude (Yao 2013). Also
called the inverse of the quality factor, seismic attenuation is
an attribute sensitive to hydrocarbon accumulation, fluid-
saturated fractures, and roughness (Walls et al. 2003). The
usefulness of this attribute in the characterization of reservoirs
is great because the ratio between compression and shear at-
tenuations is used as an indicator of hydrocarbons for good
data. Also, the variation of frequencies is an indicator of
the detection of hydrocarbons. This is how low frequen-
cies highlight the presence of reservoirs (Castagna et al.
2003). To avoid this doubt, the use of AVO attributes
appears to be a solution in the detection of hydrocarbons.
The AVO attributes as demonstrated by Smith and
Guidlow (1987), Rutherford and Williams (1989),
Hilterman (1990), Castagna and Smith (1994), Castagna
et al. (1998), Disiena et al. (1995), Avseth et al. (2014),
Xiao et al. (2019), and Farfour and Foster (2020) are
involved in all stages of oil exploitation, exploration,
development, and production. On the basis of the
normal incidence reflection coefficient, Rutherford and
Williams (1989) suggest three classes of AVO: I, II, and
III (Fig. 13). The class I refers to sands characterized by
high impedance compared to overlying shales with a pos-
itive intercept (a) and a negative gradient (b). The class II
is composed of sands with low normal incidence reflec-
tivity and the class III is represented by sands with lower
impedance than overlying shales and increasing amplitude
of reflection with offset (intercept (a) and gradient (b) are
negative). The class IV is considered when the reflection
coefficients change more and more from negative sign to
positive sign with an increasing offset (Castagna et al.
1998). Hilterman et al. (2000) demonstrated that class
III and IV anomalies are better at recognizing amplitude
bright spots on seismic data, while class II anomalies are
needed simply to identify potential reservoirs. To do this,
petrophysical parameters such as impedance, P and S
wave velocities, energy conversion elasticity modules,
and wave conversion are extracted to estimate the fluid
content of the diagrams of these parameters. The use of
these attributes for hydrocarbon identification and recog-
nition is very effective. The detection of hydrocarbons by
AVO attributes is a topic of interest to specialists of this
field (e.g., Smith and Guidlow 1987; Fatti et al. 1994;
Veeken and Rauch-Davies 2006).
Discussion
The characterization of reservoirs by seismic attributes is an
interesting technique that provides quality results which al-
lows firstly to locate the accumulation zones, then to analyze
the characteristics of reservoirs, and finally to determine the
distribution of hydrocarbons. The use of seismic attributes to
characterize reservoirs provides information on reservoir char-
acteristics such as porosity, thickness, lithology, direct hydro-
carbon indicators (bright spot, flat spot, and dim spot), and
traps (faults, anticlines, synclines, and salt domes). It should
be emphasized that this approach can be improved by com-
bining it with other methods such as log analysis, seismic
sampling, neural networks, and statistical analysis. However,
the characterization of the reservoirs becomes a multidisci-
plinary study because it integrates geostatistics, geophysics,
petrophysics, seismic coring, and geology.
By associating seismic attributes with good logs, all
petrophysical properties (porosity, permeability, water saturation,
clay volume, and/or shale volume) are taken into account. This
approach provides precise information on the property values of
reservoirs (Sofolabo and Onyia 2017). It becomes very easy to
interpolate the well data with the seismic attributes to know the
distribution of the properties over the whole extent of the reser-
voir. In addition, gamma ray and resistivity logs provide valuable
information on reservoir characteristics (Eshimokhai and
Akhirevbulu 2012). The integration of good logs with seismic
data provides more accurate seismic attributes in the analysis of
hydrocarbon reservoir characteristics.
The statistical approach to reservoir characterization is an
important tool in the analysis of the petrophysical properties of
reservoirs in that it allows the values of each characteristic to
be calculated. As this approach provides local information, it
is important to use the seismic attributes derived from the
integration of statistical data with seismic data. This leads to
a joint analysis of several attributes called multiattribute
(MA). To do this, the multiattribute analysis highlights three
approaches, namely the co-kriging technique, the neural net-
works (Aminzadeha et al. 2000), and the covariance matrix.
These three statistical methods make it possible to predict a
property by using several attributes in order to improve the
results obtained with an attribute.
Conclusion
By revisiting the work related to the application of seismic
attributes in the characterization of reservoirs, it appears that
each attribute gives a particular function and explanation for
the understanding of geological structures and hydrocarbon po-
tentials. This contribution of the attributes is manifested by the
quality of the results obtained and which has been improved
thanks to the combination of several attributes in order to
extract the best information. The variation of inclination and
azimuth provides a rapid and reliable estimation of the conver-
gence, divergence, parallelism, or disorder of the reflectors,
which are the basis of stratigraphic or structural interpretations.
So, the variation of the seismic trace is the consequence of the
change of structures, stratigraphy, porosity, permeability, and
presence of hydrocarbons in geological layers. Despite the
multifunctionality, each attribute is very effective in a specific
field of reservoir characterization. It is therefore important to
specify that the instantaneous amplitude and frequency are
good indicators of the presence of gas. The instantaneous phase
is very effective to determine the configuration of the continuity
of lateral reflector and bedding. The spectral decomposition is
important in estimating bed thickness and finally coherence
while curvature is the best attribute for detecting faults, frac-
tures, and lateral stratigraphic discontinuities. Seismic attributes
play a very important role in identifying potential hydrocarbon
zones. Sometimes, these attributes directly detect hydrocarbons
and refer to direct indicator of hydrocarbons. Among these
attributes, the AVO attribute explains the lithology as well as
the presence of the fluids on a seismic volume (Welsh et al.
2008). This analysis shows that the attributes most commonly
used in the detection of hydrocarbons are those related to the
amplitudes and frequencies of seismic traces.
Single attribute analysis uses a linear or non-linear relation-
ship between a seismic attribute and a property using a single
trace parameter (Guerrero et al. 2010). Generally, it is impor-
tant to combine several attributes in order to improve the qual-
ity of the results obtained during the analysis of reservoirs,
hence the emergence of the notion of multiattributes which
integrates within it all the geostatic methods that use the attri-
butes to characterize the reservoirs. Thus, among these attri-
butes, there is the co-kriging, the neural networks, and the
covariance matrix.

blocks.text: Seismic attributes in reservoir characterization: an overview

Sanda Oumarou1,2 & Djeddi Mabrouk3 & Tabod Charles Tabod4,5 & Jean Marcel1,4 & Simon Ngos III6 &
Jean Marcel Abate Essi7 & Joseph Kamguia1

Received: 31 May 2019 /Accepted: 23 January 2021
# Saudi Society for Geosciences 2021

Abstract
The present study focuses on a literature review using seismic attributes in the characterization of hydrocarbon reservoirs. This
work consists of examining the contribution of seismic attributes in the characterization of reservoirs. With this, it is necessary to
identify and list the attributes involved in analyzing the reservoirs and their degree of involvement in the characterization of the
hydrocarbon accumulation zones. The approach used is to classify attributes according to their levels of intervention as the
attributes that circumscribe hydrocarbon accumulation zones such as instantaneous frequencies. Thus, the attributes which make
it possible to analyze the seismic facies must be enumerated to determine the type of hydrocarbons. The aim of this work is not
only to review the literature on the use of seismic attributes in the characterization of reservoirs but also to expose the limitations
of these attributes in the study of reservoirs to search for the most adapted attributes that have never been used in reservoir
analysis. As a result, several seismic attributes used in reservoir characterization will be evaluated while demonstrating their
strengths and limitations to consider either the combination of certain attributes or the experimentation of new attributes in
deepening the knowledge on the study of reservoirs. This work will contribute to a more sophisticated study in this domain.
Keywords Seismic attributes . Characterization . Reservoir . Hydrocarbon

In general, there are two types of reservoir characteriza-
tions, namely static characterization and dynamic charac-
terization. The static characterization is to determine the
properties of reservoir rocks in a given area. This is an
important step to understand the spatial distribution of
reservoir layer parameters and their environments.
Dynamic characterization involves performing an evolu-
tionary analysis of reservoir properties to evaluate
existing fluids over time. This approach is mainly used
to plan and control production. This article focuses main-
ly on static characterization, which will review the work
done on the use of seismic attributes in the analysis of
reservoir properties. Thus, seismic attributes are special
measures of kinematic, dynamic, geometric, or statistical
characteristics obtained from seismic data and which con-
tribute to structural, stratigraphic, and petrophysical inter-
pretation (Djeddi 2016). In recent years, several attributes
have been used in reservoir characterization to improve
the understanding of reservoir characteristics. The intro-
duction of a multitude of attributes has revolutionized oil
exploration and has extended the application of the

attributes in the reservoir analysis. It begins with the lo-
cation of trap structures, then follows the determination of
accumulation zone parameters, and ends up with the de-
tection of hydrocarbon indicators.

Reservoir characterization consists of analyzing the different
reservoir parameters such as porosity, permeability, water sat-
uration, reservoir lithology, and sometimes its size. Reservoirs
are defined in this work as rocks with interconnected voids
that promote the circulation and accumulation of fluids. If we
find the hydrocarbons (oil and/or gas) are found within among
these fluids, reservoirs are called hydrocarbons. The complic-
ity of reservoirs sometimes makes it difficult to better under-
stand these reservoir rocks to the spatial and even temporal
variation of the criteria which conditions the existence of res-
ervoir rocks. Nevertheless, reservoirs can be defined accord-
ing to the petrophysical and geological characteristics.

Petrophysics is the study of the physical and chemical charac-
teristics of rocks. According to Cossé (1988), a rock consti-
tutes a reservoir if and only if it has a storage capacity
(porosity) and that fluids can circulate (permeability). The
petrophysical characteristics of the reservoirs are closely de-
pendent on the rock-fluid relations and in particular the inter-
faces between rocks and their contents (fluids). There are two
types of petrophysical properties, namely conventional
petrophysical properties and those derived from rock mechan-
ics (Neau 2009).

It is necessary to take a look at the elements that characterize
the reservoirs notably the porosity, permeability, fluid satura-
tion, and volume of clay.
The porosity (Φ) of a rock is its property to have voids,
pores, or cracks. It is expressed quantitatively by the percent-
age of the pore volume in relation to the total volume of the
rock. Consider a rock sample with its apparent volume or total
volume VT consisting of a solid volume VS and a pore volume
VP. The porosity Φ is presented in the equation: Φ = VVoid−space
VTotal ,
expressed in %.
Reservoir specialists are interested in porosity allowing the
circulation of fluids in the pores. Φe is the effective porosity
which corresponds to the pores connected to each other and
the outside. Thus, we define the total porosity Φt correspond-
ing to all the pores, whether or not related to each other, and
the residual porosity Φr which considers only isolated pores.

The pore structure varies depending on the type of reservoir
rock because the pore system of the carbonate reservoir rock is
different and irregular. Thus, the pore structure has an impact
on the elastic wave velocities. Sun (2004) demonstrates that
by considering the resolution of Zoeppritz’s exact equations
and elastic finite element modeling, it is possible to detect
variations in pore structure in reservoir rocks from seismic
data via an amplitude variation analysis with offset (AVO).
Permeability is a measure of the capacity for fluid move-
ment in porous or fractured media (Rubino et al. 2012). If the
fluid is homogeneous and has no significant action on the
surrounding medium, the permeability is said to be ab-
solute. The unit of measurement of the permeability is
the darcy, and in most cases, the millidarcy is used
(with 1 mD = 10−15m2). The permeability is good if
its value is between 200 and 500 mD.
Saturation can be defined as impregnation of interstitial
voids of a porous or cracked medium by infiltration of fluid
(oil, gas, or water). Thus, the saturation of oil, water, and gas is
defined as the ratio of each of the volume of the fluids to the
total volume and they are denoted as SW, SO and SG for the
water saturation, oil, and gas respectively (1).

where VP is the pore volume, VW is the volume of water, VO is
the volume of oil, and VG is the volume of gas. In the petro-
leum domain, knowledge of the oil and gas volumes requires
knowledge of saturation at all points or at least a satisfactory
approach (Cossé 1988).

Volume of clay The volume of clay is very important for the
study of reservoir rocks. So, we consider the case of simple
clay formations that are formed from a matrix rock sandstone,
limestone, or dolomite, mixed with clay. They contain inter-
stitial fluids such as water, oil, or gas. The distribution of the
clay usually gives dispersed, laminated, and structural clays.
The clay volume VCL comprises bound water ɸB but some-
times the clay index (ICL or Ish) is used instead of clay volume
because of its relation to the effect of the clay only to its
volume. In fact, Vsh consists of clay and the impurities asso-
ciated with it that are silt, limestone, and anhydrite while VCL
is considered as the volume of the pure clay. It is this pure clay
that intervenes during the interpretation.
Petrophysical properties derived from rock mechanics

The indirect or derived petrophysical properties from mechan-
ic rocks are basically related to elastic modules
(incompressibility, shear modulus, Young’s modulus,
Poisson’s ratio). The reservoir is assumed to be a porous iso-
tropic and linearly elastic medium. Thus, the velocities of the

P and S waves are entirely characterized by three parameters,
namely the isostatic modulus of elasticity (bulk modulus), the
shear modulus (shear modulus), and bulk density which is in
grams per cubic centimeter. The rock contains a solid
component and porous component saturated with differ-
ent fluids that represent a continuous real medium with
average elastic properties.

Geological characteristics are important in the determination
of layers that constitute accumulation zones. Thus, reservoir
rocks can be grouped into two main types, namely detrital
reservoirs and carbonate reservoirs.
Detrital reservoirs (also known as sandstone reservoirs)

Detrital reservoirs are generally composed of stable elements,
having a fairly homogeneous porosity and permeability, of
intergranular type, controlled by the grain size and the degree
of cementation. The relationships between porosity and per-
meability are generally good and decrease with landfill that
are regular and function with temperature.

Carbonated reservoirs are characterized by a very large het-
erogeneity of porosity and permeability. They are often mas-
sive, large pore, and fissured in the case of reefs, finely strat-
ified and laminated in the reef and shoal deposits. They consist
mainly of dolomites and limestones.

Characterization of reservoirs by seismic
attributes

The characterization of the reservoirs by the analysis of the
seismic attributes (Oyeyemi and Aizebeokhai 2015) enables
to build from these attributes so as to make a precise study of
the reservoirs to determine the different models of the reser-
voirs which are precisely geological, stratigraphic, and
petrophysical models. The seismic attributes make it possible
to estimate the permeability, porosity, hydrocarbon indicators,
fluid movement, thickness, lithology, and the monitoring
of hydrocarbon production. This study does not enumer-
ate exhaustively all the attributes used in reservoir char-
acterization but highlights some relevant seismic attri-
butes best suited for reservoir location, property analy-
sis, and hydrocarbon zone detection.

Nowadays, there are attributes that can circumscribe areas of
hydrocarbon accumulations. This localization takes place thanks
to the structures that define the delimitation and the location of
the reservoirs because it involves identifying trap structures.
There are summarily three types of traps: structural traps (faults,
anticlines, and synclines); stratigraphic traps (sandstone body,
carbonate reef, and permeability bevel); and mixed traps (salt
dome). Several seismic attributes such as similarity, thinned fault
likelihood, semblance, fault enhancement filter, ridge enhance-
ment filter, curvature, variance, azimuthal AVO, inversion to
anisotropic parameters, fault extraction, instantaneous amplitude,
sweetness attribute, coherence, gradients, and dips are used to
determine the structures for locating the reservoirs. But the cur-
vature, coherence, gradient, and dip are mainly dedicated to the
determination of channel, faults, anticlines, synclines, and salt
dome. To do this, it would be necessary to highlight the most
important attributes in the detection of traps such as coherence,
variance, amplitude gradients, dip azimuth measurements, and
curvature. Coherence attribute can be defined as a measurement
of the lateral continuity of the seismic signal (Backé et al. 2012).
The identification of faults by coherence (Xia et al. 2015) is
undoubtedly a topic that interests specialists in oil exploration
based on publications in this domain (Fig. 1). But the first pub-
lications (Bahorich and Farmer 1995; Marfurt et al. 1998;
Garsztenkorn and Marfurt 1999) played a decisive role in the
use of this method, because it was in their work to highlight
a cross-correlation of the seismic traces, then to conduct a
study of multitrace and finally to implement the algorithm
of similarity obtained thanks to the eigenvalues of a matrix
of covariance on a window of seismic data. For example,
several studies (Roberts 2001; Sigismondi and Soldo 2003;
Chopra and Marfurt 2007a) were conducted to improve
fault detection. With coherence, the location of reservoirs
becomes easy by providing for the determination of geolog-
ical structures (Rezvandehy et al. 2011; Bahorich and
Farmer 1995). Coherence attribute is the method used in
calculating the similarity between seismic traces and is also
the best determinant of anticline structures, faults, deltas,
river channels, dikes, and other stratigraphic anomalies
(Rezvandehy et al. 2011). The identification of faults and
fracture zones by the coherence attribute was first illustrated
by the works of Bahorich and Farmer (1995) on the cross-
correlation of seismic traces, then by a study on a multitrace
semblance of Marfurt et al. (1998) and finally by the analy-
sis of Garsztenkorn and Marfurt (1999) based on the simi-
larity algorithm obtained thanks to the eigenvalues of a co-
variance matrix on a window of the seismic data. Thus, the
detection of faults by the coherence attribute has improved
considerably thanks to the research conducted in recent
years (Randen et al. 2001; Pedersen et al. 2002; Aqrawi
and Boe 2011; Dorn et al. 2012).

Curvature attributes Curvature is an excellent attribute for
detecting fractures and even faults. It is calculated using a very
simple formula (2):

which is also the inverse of the osculating circle with seismic
horizons. According to Roberts (2001), curvature is a 2D property
of a curve and describes how bent a curve is at a particular point on
the curve, i.e., how much the curve deviates from a straight line at
this point (Fig. 2). Therefore, positive or negative curvature values
indicate anticlinal or synclinal structures respectively (Fig. 3).

Thus, there are several types of curvature attributes such as
mean curvature (km), Gaussian curvature (kg), maximum cur-
vature (kmax), minimum curvature (Kmin), intaglio curvature
(Kd), curvature of strike (Ks), contour curvature (kc), and most
positive and negative curvatures (K+ and K−) (Fig. 4). The
utility of curvatures in reservoir analysis varies according to
the structures they emphasize. It is in this sense that the max-
imum curvature is very effective in detecting faults. Similarly,
curvature measurements such as the most positive curvatures
and the most negative curvatures are increasingly used by
specialists because of their significant results in terms of struc-
tural analysis. Thus, the positive curvatures show anticlinal
structures and raised fault blocks, while the most negative

curvatures indicate the synclinal and rejected fault blocks
(Chopra and Marfurt 2007). In addition to their effectiveness,
the determination of traps makes it possible to highlight strat-
igraphic characteristics such as channels, lifts, and bars.
The first step in the reservoir study is to locate reservoir
rocks by identifying structures capable of accumulating hy-
drocarbons. To do this, the structural attributes define the oil
system by highlighting the pitfalls that constitute the essential
element in the location of reservoirs. The attributes of curva-
ture, similarity, and spectral decomposition play a large role in
the location of oil deposits. Thus, studies have been conducted

to find out the location of reservoirs (AlBinHassan and
Marfurt 2003; Cohen et al. 2006; Fomel 2007).
Attributes such as instantaneous amplitude, spectral de-
composition, curvature, and coherence enable to deter-
mine geological structures that constitute the zones
where hydrocarbons are trapped. It is clear that these
attributes expose structural, stratigraphic, and even
mixed traps defining the hydrocarbon accumulation
zones. Knowing these areas, it is necessary to make
an analysis of the properties of reservoirs by seismic
attributes

Fig. 4 The use of curvature in the detection of faults. (a) Horizon time surface. (b) Coherence. (c) Mean curvature. (d) Gaussian curvature. (e) Dip
curvature. (f) Strike curvature. (g) Shape index. (h) Most positive curvature. (i) Most negative curvature (modified from Chopra and Marfurt 2007a)

The analysis of reservoir properties is the major step in its char-
acterization. Thus, several attributes analyze reservoir properties
such as lithology, porosity, permeability, thickness, and delimi-
tation of layer. In this case, the analysis of the reservoir parame-
ters is performed using the seismic attributes, mainly accompa-
nied by good data to improve the quality of results. Thus, the
instantaneous amplitude, the instantaneous frequency, the spec-
tral decomposition, the rate of variation of the envelope, the
acoustic impedance, the shear impedance, the shear modulus,
and the instantaneous phase are applied to extract information
relating to lithology, thickness estimation, sequence delineation,
porosity, and permeability. The instantaneous amplitude is wide-
ly used to accurately determine the location of reservoirs through
anomalies such as bright spot, flat spot, and dim spot (Fig. 5).

The delimitation of layers is carried out by attributes such as
the instantaneous amplitude and the instantaneous phase.
These two attributes highlight the sequences that exist with-
in the reservoir. By referring to regional geology, it

becomes easy to deduce from these sequences the different
layers that constitute the reservoir. After determining the
different layers, it is necessary to estimate the thickness of
the layers of the reservoir. To do this, the instantaneous
frequency and the spectral decomposition are seismic
attributes that make it possible to estimate the thickness
of a layer. Sometimes, the combination of attributes
provides better results in estimating thicknesses (Asim
et al. 2016). It is in this sense that Zhao et al. (2008)
have shown that the association of maximum amplitude
and acoustic impedance illustrates the estimation of
thicknesses (Fig. 6). Spectral decomposition (Castagna
et al. 2003; Naseer et al. 2017; Naseer and Asim
2018) is a seismic attribute that highlights a spectrum
that describes the abnormal low- and high-frequency
effects responsible of seismic traces to change (Fig. 7).
It delineates the reservoir and is very important in the
stratigraphic analysis of reservoirs. It promotes a better
understanding of reservoir heterogeneities and their implica-
tions by analyzing parameters such as seismic geomorpholo-
gy, thickness estimation, lithology, and even direct hydrocar-
bon detection. It is widely used to estimate thickness (Liu and
Marfurt 2006; Dezfoolian et al. 2013; Li et al. 2019).

It is very important in the characterization of the reser-
voirs because of the information it contains on the ac-
cumulation zones (Wang and Huang 2016). The nature
of the layers is a determining factor in the quality of the
reservoir. The instantaneous amplitude, instantaneous
frequency, the rate of variation of the envelope, and
the shear modulus are attributes that determine the lith-
ological parameters of reservoirs. The instantaneous at-
tributes (Khan and Akhter 2016) such as amplitude,
frequency, and rate of change of the envelope, through
a good visualization, provide highlight of the different
layers. To do this, it is important to have enough
knowledge of the geology of the study area to better
highlight the different layers. The extraction of the λρ
and μρ attributes of the seismic data provides quality
information on the nature of the rocks and even on
the fluids of the reservoir (Fig. 8). By crossing these
two attributes, the identification of different lithologies
becomes easy. It is the same that the crossing of the
ratio of velocities Vp/Vs by μρ offers good lithological
discrimination. A cross-plot of the natural log of acous-
tic impedance versus Poisson’s ratio is often used for
the identification of layer lithology (Hilterman et al.
1998).

In the study of reservoirs, porosity and permeability are the
most important properties. It is clear that a good knowledge of
these parameters leads to a good understanding of the quality
of the study area but their determination remains difficult.
Thus, the approach used by the seismic (Pride et al. 2003;
Rubino et al. 2012; Naeem et al. 2015) and more precisely
by the seismic attributes would allow the estimation of the
porosity and the permeability through the variation of the
impedance contrast obtained thanks to the reflectivity of the
P and S waves on the reservoir. Thus, Bachrach (2006) uses
three seismic attributes, namely acoustic impedance, shear
impedance, and density, to make a joint estimate of porosity
and saturation (Figs. 9 and 10). Attributes deduced from im-
pedances such as λρ, μρ, and Vp/Vs are widely used to predict
porosity. Similarly, the crossing of the two AVO (amplitude
variation with offset) attributes, namely the gradient and the
intercept, makes it possible to estimate the porosity. Thus,
porosity estimation is most often done using attributes such
as deterministic inversion, neural networks, and rock property
prediction. As regards permeability, the use of the
instantaneous frequency would make it possible to provide
information on the mobility of the fluids. Using linear
regression, Corbeanu et al. (2002) demonstrate that permeabil-
ity is predicted from instantaneous amplitude and frequency at

Fig. 10 a Estimation of porosity from joint inversion. b Comparison to well log data. c Porosity STD associated with the MAP estimator (modified from
Bachrach 2006)

each point in the data volume (Fig. 11). Thus, Goloshubin
et al. (2006) conducted a study that uses low frequencies to
estimate fluid content and map highly permeable production
zones in reservoirs.

The identification of hydrocarbons through seismic data be-
gan a long time ago when several works have been devoted to
the study of the amplitude of seismic waves in the detection of
areas of hydrocarbon accumulations (O’Doherty and Anstey
1971; Sheriff 1974; Barry and Shugart 1974; Hilterman

1975). Thus, the work of Anstey (1972, 1973a, 1973b) marks
the birth of the seismic attributes which over time have be-
come precious tools of the petroleum industry. For him, the
force of reflection which is a measure of amplitude was the
main attribute for the analysis of bright spots. Afterwards,
researchers’ interest in the notion of attributes is justified by
studies carried out in this domain (Taner et al. 1979;
Robertson and Fisher 1988; Taner et al. 1994; Chen and
Sidney 1997; Barnes 2001; Chopra and Marfurt 2005;
Zhang et al. 2015; Wang et al. 2019). In the literature, several
attributes make it possible to detect hydrocarbons on a volume
or a seismic section (Li and Liu 2018; Negm et al. 2020). The

most common are the AVO attributes, frequency attenuation,
energy, sweetness, fluid contact finder, seismic feature en-
hancement, instantaneous amplitude, instantaneous

frequency, gas chimneys, three-term inversion, neural net-
work classification, spectral decomposition, and the apparent
polarity. Thus, the works of Tahir et al. (2016) distinguished

Fig. 13 (a) Illustration of the hydrocarbon detection using the cross-plotting of acoustic impedance and Vp/Vs ratio. (b) Different classes of AVO and
their meanings (modified from Avseth et al. 2008)

the gas and non-gas zones on the basis of regression analysis
with attributes such as average instantaneous frequency, peak
spectral frequency, average instantaneous phase, and sweet-
ness attributes. The direct detection of hydrocarbons (bright
spot, flat spot, and dim spot) by the instantaneous amplitude
and the instantaneous frequency is not always effective (Fig.
12). Attenuation is defined as any decrease in amplitude of the
wavefront during its propagation and is associated or not with
the velocity dispersion, depending on the physical mechanism
at the origin of the decrease in amplitude (Yao 2013). Also
called the inverse of the quality factor, seismic attenuation is
an attribute sensitive to hydrocarbon accumulation, fluid-
saturated fractures, and roughness (Walls et al. 2003). The
usefulness of this attribute in the characterization of reservoirs
is great because the ratio between compression and shear at-
tenuations is used as an indicator of hydrocarbons for good
data. Also, the variation of frequencies is an indicator of
the detection of hydrocarbons. This is how low frequen-
cies highlight the presence of reservoirs (Castagna et al.
2003). To avoid this doubt, the use of AVO attributes
appears to be a solution in the detection of hydrocarbons.
The AVO attributes as demonstrated by Smith and
Guidlow (1987), Rutherford and Williams (1989),
Hilterman (1990), Castagna and Smith (1994), Castagna
et al. (1998), Disiena et al. (1995), Avseth et al. (2014),
Xiao et al. (2019), and Farfour and Foster (2020) are
involved in all stages of oil exploitation, exploration,
development, and production. On the basis of the
normal incidence reflection coefficient, Rutherford and
Williams (1989) suggest three classes of AVO: I, II, and
III (Fig. 13). The class I refers to sands characterized by
high impedance compared to overlying shales with a pos-
itive intercept (a) and a negative gradient (b). The class II
is composed of sands with low normal incidence reflec-
tivity and the class III is represented by sands with lower
impedance than overlying shales and increasing amplitude
of reflection with offset (intercept (a) and gradient (b) are
negative). The class IV is considered when the reflection
coefficients change more and more from negative sign to
positive sign with an increasing offset (Castagna et al.
1998). Hilterman et al. (2000) demonstrated that class
III and IV anomalies are better at recognizing amplitude
bright spots on seismic data, while class II anomalies are
needed simply to identify potential reservoirs. To do this,
petrophysical parameters such as impedance, P and S
wave velocities, energy conversion elasticity modules,
and wave conversion are extracted to estimate the fluid
content of the diagrams of these parameters. The use of
these attributes for hydrocarbon identification and recog-
nition is very effective. The detection of hydrocarbons by
AVO attributes is a topic of interest to specialists of this
field (e.g., Smith and Guidlow 1987; Fatti et al. 1994;
Veeken and Rauch-Davies 2006).

The characterization of reservoirs by seismic attributes is an
interesting technique that provides quality results which al-
lows firstly to locate the accumulation zones, then to analyze
the characteristics of reservoirs, and finally to determine the
distribution of hydrocarbons. The use of seismic attributes to
characterize reservoirs provides information on reservoir char-
acteristics such as porosity, thickness, lithology, direct hydro-
carbon indicators (bright spot, flat spot, and dim spot), and
traps (faults, anticlines, synclines, and salt domes). It should
be emphasized that this approach can be improved by com-
bining it with other methods such as log analysis, seismic
sampling, neural networks, and statistical analysis. However,
the characterization of the reservoirs becomes a multidisci-
plinary study because it integrates geostatistics, geophysics,
petrophysics, seismic coring, and geology.
By associating seismic attributes with good logs, all
petrophysical properties (porosity, permeability, water saturation,
clay volume, and/or shale volume) are taken into account. This
approach provides precise information on the property values of
reservoirs (Sofolabo and Onyia 2017). It becomes very easy to
interpolate the well data with the seismic attributes to know the
distribution of the properties over the whole extent of the reser-
voir. In addition, gamma ray and resistivity logs provide valuable
information on reservoir characteristics (Eshimokhai and
Akhirevbulu 2012). The integration of good logs with seismic
data provides more accurate seismic attributes in the analysis of
hydrocarbon reservoir characteristics.
The statistical approach to reservoir characterization is an
important tool in the analysis of the petrophysical properties of
reservoirs in that it allows the values of each characteristic to
be calculated. As this approach provides local information, it
is important to use the seismic attributes derived from the
integration of statistical data with seismic data. This leads to
a joint analysis of several attributes called multiattribute
(MA). To do this, the multiattribute analysis highlights three
approaches, namely the co-kriging technique, the neural net-
works (Aminzadeha et al. 2000), and the covariance matrix.
These three statistical methods make it possible to predict a
property by using several attributes in order to improve the
results obtained with an attribute.

By revisiting the work related to the application of seismic
attributes in the characterization of reservoirs, it appears that
each attribute gives a particular function and explanation for
the understanding of geological structures and hydrocarbon po-
tentials. This contribution of the attributes is manifested by the
quality of the results obtained and which has been improved
thanks to the combination of several attributes in order to

extract the best information. The variation of inclination and
azimuth provides a rapid and reliable estimation of the conver-
gence, divergence, parallelism, or disorder of the reflectors,
which are the basis of stratigraphic or structural interpretations.
So, the variation of the seismic trace is the consequence of the
change of structures, stratigraphy, porosity, permeability, and
presence of hydrocarbons in geological layers. Despite the
multifunctionality, each attribute is very effective in a specific
field of reservoir characterization. It is therefore important to
specify that the instantaneous amplitude and frequency are
good indicators of the presence of gas. The instantaneous phase
is very effective to determine the configuration of the continuity
of lateral reflector and bedding. The spectral decomposition is
important in estimating bed thickness and finally coherence
while curvature is the best attribute for detecting faults, frac-
tures, and lateral stratigraphic discontinuities. Seismic attributes
play a very important role in identifying potential hydrocarbon
zones. Sometimes, these attributes directly detect hydrocarbons
and refer to direct indicator of hydrocarbons. Among these
attributes, the AVO attribute explains the lithology as well as
the presence of the fluids on a seismic volume (Welsh et al.
2008). This analysis shows that the attributes most commonly
used in the detection of hydrocarbons are those related to the
amplitudes and frequencies of seismic traces.
Single attribute analysis uses a linear or non-linear relation-
ship between a seismic attribute and a property using a single
trace parameter (Guerrero et al. 2010). Generally, it is impor-
tant to combine several attributes in order to improve the qual-
ity of the results obtained during the analysis of reservoirs,
hence the emergence of the notion of multiattributes which
integrates within it all the geostatic methods that use the attri-
butes to characterize the reservoirs. Thus, among these attri-
butes, there is the co-kriging, the neural networks, and the
covariance matrix.

Seismic Facies Analysis: Past, Present and Future
Guoqiang Xu a,b and Bilal U. Haq c
a. 
State Key Laboratory of Oil and Gas Reservoir Geology and Exploitation, Chengdu University of Technology, Sichuan 610059, China.
b. 
College of Energy Resources, Chengdu University of Technology, Sichuan 610059, China.
c. 
Sorbonne University, Institute of Earth Sciences, Paris, France and Smithsonian Institution, Washington DC, USA
Seismic facies and lithofacies analysis, once considered a breakthrough in exploration 
applications, is currently a dynamic field because of the addition of several new 
concepts and interpretive procedures. In terms of basic theory, remarkable 
developments have taken place that encompass refinements in geological and 
geophysical concepts, including several enhancements to sequence-stratigraphic and 
facies distribution models, better knowledge of seismic response mechanism to 
small-scale stratigraphic structures and various rock types, and the emergence of new 
technologies, such as, the restoration of original depositional architecture and spectral 
decomposition. A seismic facies analysis index system has been assembled that 
includes nine independent parameters: position, external form, internal configuration, 
continuity, smoothness, amplitude, frequency, special waveforms, and appearance. 
The sedimentary systems established by traditional seismic facies analysis lack 
detailed lithofacies and hydrodynamic information, however, current further 
subdivision of seismic lithofacies into more detailed categories is now possible, made 
available by the addition of new seismic parameters that are indicative of sedimentary 
structure and rock-type combinations. This enables interpreters to identify lithofacies 
details directly from the seismic data and reconstruct the sedimentary systems with 
greater precision (by superposition of the environment, lithofacies and flow paths). 
The seismic slice image analysis, including seismic geomorphology and seismic 
sedimentology, employs a stratal time slice, 90° phase shift, and spectral 
decomposition techniques to improve the resolution of the slice images, describe 
sedimentary micro-facies and understand sedimentary processes based on the 
geometric features of the time slice. The seismic facies auto-classification techniques 
are still at an early stage of development, but significant possibilities exist for future 
enhancements if the new seismic index system and accumulated knowledge of the 
skilled experts could be utilized advantageously.
Key words: Seismic facies analysis; Seismic lithofacies analysis; Seismic geomorphology；
Seismic sedimentology; Artificial intelligence; South China Sea.
1. Introduction
With the development of rapid digital computing in the 1970s, wavelet side lobes
of seismic data could be suppressed by zero-phase processing (Widess, 1973) leading
to the correlation of sharp seismic reflections with bedding and other physical
Journal Pre-proof
Journal Pre-proof
boundaries that in turn led to the use of seismic data for investigating subsurface
stratigraphic configurations and sedimentary facies (Sangree and Widmier, 1977;
Mitchum et al., 1977; Anstey, 1980). This in turn facilitated the advent of seismic
stratigraphy (e.g., Vail et al., 1977) that was considered a technological revolution in
exploration geology. Seismic stratigraphy involves subsurface geologic interpretations
using seismic data that integrates geophysics and geology (Mitchum et al., 1977;
Bedley, 1985; Sheriff, 1985). One useful aspect of the discipline was seismic facies
analysis (Berg, 1982) accomplished by examining reflection geometries and stratal
architecture and grouping them as depositional sequences to interpret the
paleoenvironment and infer seismic lithofacies (Mitchum et al., 1977; Roksandic,
1978).
At the early stage of this research seismic facies analysis was developed by
geologists and geophysicists working together to ensure that both the kinematic and
dynamic aspects of seismic imaging and geologic features of interest could be
captured and the geological implications of seismic information can be inferred
scientifically (Xu et al., 1990; Chopra and Marfurt, 2012) (Fig. 1). The emergence of
sequence stratigraphy has attracted a large number of geologists to participate in the
geological research related to seismic facies analysis, but reduced the depth of
cooperation between geophysicists and geologists. Geologists independently engaged
in stratigraphy and sedimentology with outcrop, well, and seismic data, while the
geophysicists started employing seismic attributes, such as amplitude and frequency,
to characterize reservoir properties in hydrocarbon exploration (Wang and Shi, 1998).
Over 
the 
last 
three

2. Fundamentals of seismic geological interpretations
Since the early 1970s, when seismic data gathering and processing entered the
digital age, seismic technology has developed rapidly. Modern seismic data contain
an extraordinarily rich amount of information that includes many new precepts and
terms, and now almost all interpretations of seismic data are accomplished through
observations and manipulations on workstations. Currently, by observing the stratal
configurations afforded by seismic reflections patterns, interpreters can obtain
lithological and hydrocarbon-related information offered by seismic attributes, such
as amplitude, frequency, and waveforms (e.g., Meckel and Nath, 1977; Anstey,
1980; Weidess, 1982; Bedley, 1985; Xu et al., 1990; Liu, 1997; Brown, 2011;
Wang et al., 2015, Xu and Pang, 2021). Accordingly, to work effectively with
seismic data various basic features need to be mastered that include
minimum-phase and zero-phase wavelets, positive and negative reflections, polarity
display, phase shifting, amplitude tuning, readable and discernible thickness,
resolution limitations, types of basic waveforms (Anstey, 1980), Boit-Geerstma
equation and the Dominico effect (Domenico, 1977), cumulative thickness effect of
thin interlayers, Fresnel zone, bright spots, American and European polarities, and
spectral decomposition (Brown, 2111). Additionally, appropriate skills are needed
for techniques involving synthetic seismograms, seismic modeling and seismic
slicing, among others (Wang et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021). The
following is a summary of the basic knowledge needed for detailed integration of
seismic geophysical and geological parameters.
2.1. Zero-phase processing
The field wavelet triggered by blasting, gravity hammering, or the use of air gun
is also known as the minimum-phase wavelet (Bedley, 1985; Brown, 2011), which is
composed of multiple phases, where the energy of the head phase is stronger (Fig. 2a)
Journal Pre-proof
Journal Pre-proof
than the energy from the middle to the tail phases where it weakens gradually. After
deconvolving, the minimum-phase wavelet is transformed into a nearly symmetric
waveform wavelet composed of one main lobe and two side lobes (Fig. 2b).
Following displacing and shaping treatments, the main lobe moves to the position of
the geological interface where the corresponding time is zero, the two side lobes
become symmetrical (e.g., Sheriff and Margaret, 1980; Simm and White, 2002), while
the minimum-phase wavelet becomes a zero-phase wavelet (Ricker, 1953) (Fig. 2d).
In seismic profiles that have undergone zero-phase processing, the surface of the
seafloor is often represented by a complete zero-phase wavelet reflection (Fig. 2e).

Over the years, different organizations have defined their own polarity
displays. Because polarity is reversed repeatedly in seismic data, the polarity

sometimes also to the technicians processing the data (Brown, 2011). Many

have been defined to avoid such confusion (Rankey, 2017). In American polarity,

the zero-phase wavelet is used as the center lobe of positive reflection and the peak
as the center lobe of negative reflection (Bedley, 1985). However, as American
polarity is compatible with the pseudo-log display, it has become more popular in
the exploration industry (Brown, 2011).

2.3. The limit of seismic discernibility
The resolution of zero-phase data is one-quarter of the dominant wavelength
(λ) for an interlayer with opposite polarity at the top and bottom (dipolar interlayer,
Fig. 4a) (e.g., Ricker, 1953; Widess, 1973; Anstey, 1977; Anstey, 1980; Brown,
2011). It is λ/4.6 for an interlayer with the same polarity at the top and bottom
(homopolar interlayer, Fig. 4b) (Bedley, 1985). The limit of discernibility is
approximately one-sixtieth (the amplitude of the composite wave is approximately
25% of a single reflection, Figs. 4a) in the most favorable instance for a dipolar
interlayer (Brown, 2011), and it is only λ/4.6 for a homopolar interlayer (e.g.,

2.4. Readable and detectable thicknesses
When the thickness of the interlayer is greater than a quarter of the wavelength,
the seismic top and bottom are consistent with the interlayer top and bottom, and
the time thickness can be read directly from the seismic profile (e.g., Neidell and
Poggiagliolmi, 1977; Anstey, 1980; Brown, 2011; Wang et al., 2015). When the
thickness is less than λ/4, the seismic top is higher than the interlayer top and the
seismic bottom is lower than the interlayer bottom, and the period from the seismic
top to the seismic bottom is greater than the interlayer thickness (Fig. 4a). In this
instance, the interlayer thickness (h < λ/4) can be detected through the composite
wave amplitude as this decreases linearly with the thickness (Anstey, 1980).
2.5. Skew-symmetrical waveform
The low impedance gas-bearing sandstone and high impedance limestone
encased by shale show skew-symmetrical wave with extra-large amplitude (Figs. 5b.
and 5c)，which was defined first by Anstey (1980) as, ''the skew-symmetry is about an
upward-going zero-crossing for gas sandstone and about a downward-going
zero-crossing for limestone. Such a skew-symmetric waveform description
(upward-going or downward-going) starts from the crest generated by the positive
reflection interface, and "zero crossing" is a point where the amplitude is zero, the
dividing line between a trough and a peak. However, this is not easy to use in practice.
Skew-symmetrical waves can be found in seismic data in both low-impedance layer
(such as porous gas sandstone) and high-impedance layers (such as limestone)
encased in shale.
Distinguishing these two waveforms is very important for lithofacies
identification and oil and gas exploration. In order to effectively apply this waveform,
Xu et al. (2015, 2021) redefined the two skew-symmetric waveforms: a combined
wave generated by a low-impedance interlayer known a right-downward
skew-symmetrical wave (RD-wave）because of the right-downward line (marked with

wave generated by a high-impedance interlayer is called the left-downward
skew-symmetrical wave (LD-wave) (Fig. 5c). These two skew-symmetries can be
used to identify large amplitude reflections generated by the high-impedance and
low-impedance layers, respectively. Since the low-impedance interlayer of λ/16 to

2.6. Ninety-degree phase shift
Seismic wavelets can be transformed into various wavelet phases through
phase shifting (Fig. 6a). After phase shifting of 90°, the symmetric waveform
becomes the skew-symmetrical waveform (top of Fig. 
6a), and the
skew-symmetrical waveform becomes symmetric waveform (bottom of Fig. 6a),
and they are the first derivatives of each other (Fig. 6b). The 90° phase shifting
changes the seismic reflection of the thin sandwich from the two main lobes to one,
which allows the thin interlayer to correspond one-to-one to the reflection event.
However, it also changes the waveform from the top or bottom interface of the
thick layer from one main lobe to two main lobes (top of Figs. 6a and 6b), which
confuses the rule that a stratigraphic interface corresponds to a reflection event.
Therefore, the 90° phase data (Fig. 6) is used mainly for thin-layer reservoir study
in a 3d block (Brown, 2011; Miall, 2016; Zeng, 2018).

3. Parameters of seismic facies analysis
3.1. Overview
A seismic facies unit can be defined as a sedimentary unit of which the seismic
signatures differ from those of the adjacent units (Mitchum et al., 1977). In seismic
facies analysis the following parameters should be considered, namely, position
(regional setting), external form, internal configuration, reflection amplitude,
dominant frequency, reflection continuity, interval velocity, areal association of
seismic facies units, abundance of reflections, line direction (dip or strike section),
reflection termination, size, formation thickness, slope break, reflection smoothness,
special waveform pattern, appearance, reflection polarity, acoustic impedance, bright
spots, amplitude variation with offset (AVO) and AVO-derived attributes, arc length
and loop area (amplitude-derived attributes), curvature, plane geometry of seismic
slice, and the like (e.g., Mitchum et al., 1977; Sangree and Widmier, 1977; Roksandic,
1978; Anstey, 1980; Sheriff and Margaret, 1980; Brown et al., 1982; Bedley, 1985;
Liu, 1997; Chopra and Marfurt, 2007; Brown, 2011; Miall, 2016; Xie et al., 2017;
Verma et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021). There are dozens of seismic
signatures and hundreds of derived attributes for seismic facies recognition (Brown,
2011); however, only nine main independent seismic parameters and one geological
parameter can be readily used for seismic lithofacies analysis (Fig. 7).
Position, external form, internal configuration, amplitude, frequency and
continuity are six independent parameters most commonly used since the emergence
of seismic facies analysis (Fig. 7). In addition to this, interval velocity was used
widely to interpret lithology in the early years. However, this lost favor in the 1990s
because of its low precision (Bedley, 1985; Liu, 1997), and was replaced by acoustic
impedance inversion and wave pattern analysis (Brown, 2011). Reflection smoothness,
waveform (special pattern), and seismic profile appearance are three newly added
common elements in seismic lithofacies analysis (Xu et al., 2021). Wave pattern
Journal Pre-proof
Journal Pre-proof
contains two parameters, namely, reflection polarity and acoustic impedance. In terms
of their geological and geophysical meaning, the external form and internal
configuration of a seismic facies unit and reflection continuity are classified as
broader geometric attributes, whereas reflection smoothness and seismic profile
appearance are considered as smaller scale geometric attributes. Amplitude, frequency,
and wave pattern are dynamic attributes, whereas position and relationship with other
units have spatial and geological connotations. Provenance is a very important
geological parameter, which is mainly used to determine whether the deep-water fan
sand body is sandstone or siltstone. As seismic data cannot distinguish the grain size
of siliceous clastic rocks, the sandstone seismic lithofacies obtained by enhanced
seismic lithofacies analysis include conglomerate, sandstone, and siltstone. The grain
size of deep-water fan sandstone is the same as that of its parent rock, so the grain size
can be determined from its parent rock. Therefore, this parameter can only be used
after the depositional system has been reconstructed (Xu et al., 2021).

3.2.1. Position
Position is a spatial indicator for sedimentary facies interpretation and is a
parameter for seismic facies analysis, as many sedimentary bodies exist in specific
locations (Fig. 8). For example, large reefs are usually found at the edge of platforms
or continental shelf margins (Bubb and Hatlelid, 1977), deep-water fans are found on
slopes and in deep-sea basins, and a large number of volcanic cones are found in the
transitional ocean-continental crust. Based on the interpretation of the regional
seismic profile, the position of the seismic facies unit can be determined roughly, after
which the sedimentary facies can be inferred according to existing sedimentary facies
models (e.g., Berg, 1982; Vail et al., 1991; Catuneanu et al., 2009; Matenco and Haq,
2020; Xu and Pang, 2021) and other indicators.

3.2.2. External form
In the 1970s and 80s, the external form of a seismic facies unit was observed
mainly by means of seismic profiles.  External structures can now be observed
directly through slices and three-dimensional visualization. The external form of the
units can be divided roughly into seven categories, i.e., sheet, wedge, bank, lens,
mound, fan, and concave (Mitchum et al., 1977; Sangree and Widmier, 1977). In the
modified scheme shown here, three aspects of the previous classification have been
modified: (1) Sheet drape is classified as a secondary type of the sheet form; (2) Fan
shape is classified as a first-order external form because the fan is hilly only in the
strike section, wedge-shaped in the dip section, and fan-shaped in the plane and
three-dimensional view; (3) Fill shape has been renamed concave shape because the
filling emphasizes sedimentary features, whereas the concave surface emphasizes the
external geometry. The concave shape of incised valley is a very important shape of
sedimentary body, which includes river channel, gully, channel, canyon and trough,
which can be filled or unfilled.

emphasizes the basinward syn-sedimentary thickening of the strata caused by an
increase in the accommodation space, whereas the latter emphasizes the basinward
syn-sedimentary thinning of the strata caused by a decrease in the sediment supply.
(2) In the early classification diagrams, the scale of the five oblique
configurations was incongruous. Height of clinoforms in parallel and shingled
configurations is reduced because they are formed in shallow-water environments
(e.g., the middle to outer continental shelf). However, the height of clinoforms in
oblique, sigmoid, and complex sigmoid–oblique configurations is increased because
they are formed when rivers flow into deep-water environments (e.g., the edge of the
continental shelf). After the modification above, the five oblique configurations is
more reasonable and the scale is coordinated with each other, which is more
beneficial to fully understand the geological implications of oblique configurations.

plane (Mitchum et al., 1977) to the inclined plane toward the basin (Catuneanu,
