blocks.text: The impact of reservoir scale on amplitude variation with offset
Chao Xu, Jianxin Wei∗ and Bangrang Di

State Key Laboratory of Petroleum Resources and Prospecting and CNPC Key Laboratory of Geophysical Prospecting, China University
of Petroleum (Beijing), Beijing, 102249, China

ABSTRACT
To investigate the vertical and horizontal impact of reservoir scale on the amplitude-
versus-offset characteristics, we conduct seismic numerical simulations on models
containing spatially confined lithologic units with different scales. We find that the
reservoir scale has a nonlinear effect on the amplitude-versus-offset intercepts and
gradients. As the reservoir width increases, amplitude-versus-offset intercept and gra-
dient both first increase, then decrease, and finally remain stable. The amplitude-
versus-offset intercept is maximum when the reservoir width is 80% larger than
the Fresnel zone radius, whereas the amplitude-versus-offset gradient peaks at 1.5
times the Fresnel zone radius. Both amplitude-versus-offset intercept and gradient are
approximately proportional to the reservoir width prior to reaching their maxima.
When the lateral extent of the reservoir is more than three times the Fresnel zone
radius, the amplitude-versus-offset attributes are constant. Modelling the reservoir
thickness shows that intercept and gradient behave in a manner similar to that of
tuning of thin beds. Both the amplitude-versus-offset intercept and gradient first in-
crease and then decrease with the thickness, peaking at the tuning thickness. The
thickness contribution to amplitude-versus-offset variations is negligible when the
thickness is larger than 1.6 times of the tuning thickness. Considering the magnitude
of the changes in amplitude-versus-offset intercept and gradient caused by reservoir
scale, the width causes a maximum 433% intercept increase and a 344% gradient
increase, whereas the thickness causes a maximum 100% intercept increase and a
73% gradient increase. Cross-plotting the amplitude-versus-offset intercept and gra-
dient shows the reservoir scale change gives rise to an anti-clockwise spiraling effect.
In conclusion, the lateral and vertical extents of the reservoir both play an important
role in amplitude variation with offset. Our analysis shows that the lateral reservoir
extent has a larger impact on the amplitude variation with offset than the vertical
tuning effect.
Key words: AVO, Seismic amplitude, Resolution.

Since Ostrander (1984) pointed out that amplitude increased
with offset in gas sands, amplitude variation with offset or
angle (AVO or AVA) has been studied by many geophysi-
cists and is widely applied to the discrimination of lithology

and fluid (Smith and Gidlow 1987; Rutherford and Williams
1989; Fatti et al. 1994; Castagna and Swan 1997; Foster,
Keys, and Lane 2010). AVO has also been extensively ap-
plied to prospects with finite reservoir scale, such as the karst
reservoir in the Tarim basin in China, which is famous for its
numerous cavernous fractured reservoirs (Zeng et al. 2011;
Yang et al. 2012; Sun et al. 2012; Zhao et al. 2014). Tra-
ditional AVO analysis is based on the Zoeppritz equations

(Zoeppritz 1919) whose derivation is based on the assump-
tion of a single interface between two elastic half-spaces. It is
therefore in principle not suitable to the analysis of pre-stack
amplitudes and AVO responses in finite-scale settings. How-
ever, in our opinion, AVO can be extended to arbitrary inter-
faces through diffraction theory. Based on Huygens’ principle,
Trorey (1970) showed that a subsurface reflector can be rep-
resented as an ensemble of diffractors, with each diffraction
point as the source of a secondary wave. The seismic signal
measured at the receivers placed on the surface is thus the sum
of all diffraction responses. The single interface, as used by
the Zoeppritz equations, is a simple special case of Trorey’s
diffraction theory. This leads us to conclude that AVO can
also be analysed in the case of a diffracting reservoir.
We believe the reservoir scale plays a crucial role in AVO
characteristics, particularly for reservoirs at seismic scale. For
reservoirs at finite scales, both laterally and vertically, the
identification of lithology and fluid through AVO could be
contaminated by the effect of the reservoir scale. For quanti-
tative AVO analysis, and in particular the analysis of lithology
and fluid content, reservoir scale and resolution, both later-
ally and vertically, needs to be understood, in order to avoid
misinterpretation. A common approximation of the spatial
resolution is the Widess resolution L (Widess 1973):

where λ is the wavelength. According to Widess, the infor-
mation on the layer thickness is encoded in the amplitude of
the composite reflection. The tuning thickness λ/4 is twice
the spatial resolution. Lateral resolution is usually estimated
as the Fresnel zone radius, given by (Sheriff 1977):

where h is the target depth and λ is the wavelength. The
boundary of the (first) Fresnel zone corresponds to the posi-
tion of maximum energy build-up (Br¨uhl, Vermeer, and Kiehn
1996). The first Fresnel zone is often used as an indicator of
the region that contributes energy (constructively) to the total
reflection energy, whereas energy returning from areas outside
this region interferes destructively.
For the thickness effect, previous researchers have con-
ducted a large number of AVO tuning studies (Bakke and
Ursin 1998; Liu and Schmitt 2003). The AVO response of a
thin layer is dependent upon the thickness of the layer and dif-
fers significantly from the AVO response of a simple interface
(Almoghrabi and Lange 1986; Juhlin and Young 1993). Swan
(1988) pointed out that AVO distortions due to tuning might

be larger than the underlying lithologic AVO effect. Vertical
tuning analysis is closely related to Widess’s analysis (1973).
However, we should not analyse the thickness impact without
considering the width impact. Actually, the AVO of a reservoir
is the compositive result of both thickness and width impacts.
Few well-developed conclusions about the effect of the reser-
voir width on AVO have been published. Wu et al. (2006)
demonstrated significant effects of wave diffractions due to
lateral changes in the overburden properties on AVO. Wang
et al. (2002) suggested to decompose the structural amplitude
effect (focusing and defocusing) from the AVO attributes. The
study conducted by Sun et al. (2012) showed the AVO re-
sponses of karst caves with different diameters and suggested
AVO intercept and gradient were affected by the cave size. Xu,
Di, and Wei (2014) pointed out that both reservoir thickness
and width exerted considerable effects on AVO. However,
the reservoir scale in their study is so limited to be systematic
enough, and it is mostly less than one wavelength in particular.
In this paper, our objective is to demonstrate the impact
on AVO of reservoir scale, by which we mean the combined
effect of reservoir width and thickness. Rather than gener-
ating AVO angle gathers using the Zoeppritz equations, we
conduct finite difference modelling of the elastic seismic wave
equation. We model reservoirs over a large range of scales al-
lowing us to map out the lateral and vertical tuning effects of
AVO intercept and gradients. We will show that the reservoir
scale has a considerable impact on the AVO behaviour.

We performed 2D numerical simulations of the elastic wave
equation with staggered-grid finite-difference method on
models including reservoirs with extensive scale ranges. Since
our goal was to demonstrate the impact of reservoir scale on
amplitude variation with offset (AVO), all parameters other
than the scales of the reservoir were held fixed in all numerical
simulations. A Ricker wavelet was employed with the domi-
nant frequency of 30 Hz. The calculating grid was 10 m. For
each model, 220 shots gathers were calculated, and there were
120 receivers within each shot, meaning the maximum offset
was 2,400 m. The receiver interval was 20 m, whereas the
source interval was 40 m. There were 3,600 sampling points
within each trace and the sampling interval was 0.5 ms.
To investigate the impact of the reservoir width on AVO,
we first designed two three-layer models containing reservoirs
with a wide range of widths (100 m, 200 m, 300 m, 400 m,
500 m, 600 m, 700 m, 800 m, 900 m, 1,000 m, 1,100 m, and
1,200 m) within the second layers as shown in Fig. 1(a, b).

Figure 1 Three-layer models containing reservoirs with different widths: (a) ranging from 100 m to 600 m, (b) ranging from 700 m to 1,200 m,
(c) infinite width, and (d) single interface.

Figure 2 Three-layer models containing reservoirs with different
thicknesses: (a) ranging from 10 m to 60 m and (b) from 70 m to
140 m.

Considering the extreme situation, we designed a model with
an infinite-width reservoir similarly located at the middle of
the second layer, shown in Fig. 1(c). The reservoir width is
the same as the layers (9,000 m). The reservoir thickness
in these models is held constant at 100 m. In addition, we
also designed a model of a single interface at the middle of
the second layer, as given in Fig. 1(d). The elastic parame-
ters of the top and base media of the single interface are the

same as that of the surroundings and reservoirs in the above
models.
Similarly, to demonstrate the impact of the reservoir
thickness on AVO, we designed two three-layer models con-
taining reservoirs with a wide range of thicknesses (10 m,
20 m, 30 m, 40 m, 50 m, 60 m, 70 m, 80 m, 90 m, 100 m,
120 m, and 140 m) within the second layers, as shown in
Fig. 2. For these models, the lateral reservoir extent is held
constant at 100 m. The parameters within our models origi-
nate from the real karstic reservoir strata from Tarim Basin,
China. It is deeply buried, more than 5,500 m, and the ve-
locity and density are very high (Zhao et al. 2014; Xu et al.
2016). Field data from the area show that the P-wave velocity
is more than 6,000 m/s.
3.1 Modelling gathers in offset and angle domain

Based on the raw seismic data, we obtained from seismic
simulations with the above parameters, we conducted a
conventional processing procedure including amplitude com-
pensation, noise filtering, removing multiples, deconvolution,
normal movement correction, and stack. Figure 3(a) is an ex-
ample of one of the processed shot gathers. The waveforms of
the reservoir top and base interfere with each other and appear
between 680 ms and 800 ms. To get the amplitude-versus-
offset (AVO) variation in the angle domain, we transformed
the shot gather from the offset domain to the angle domain,

Figure 3 Shot gather in (a) offset domain and (b) angle domain for the midpoint of the 400-m-wide reservoir, corresponding to CMP 179,
within the model in Fig. 1(a). The waveforms of the reservoir top and base interfere with each other and appear from about 680 ms to 800 ms.

as shown in Fig. 3(b). The transform process needs a well, in-
cluding information of interfaces and elastic parameters. We
used an artificial well that was generated based on Fig. 1(a).
The angle transform process is based on the ray parameter
equation reported by Bale, Leaney, and Dumitru (2001):

where θ is the incidence angle, x is the offset, Vint is the interval
velocity of one layer, Vrms is the root mean square (RMS)
velocity, and t is the two-way time at offset x. From Fig. 3(b),
we can see an obvious waveform truncation for far angles
after 33°. That is because the angle of incidence for a constant
offset trace decreases with the depth. The maximum incidence
for the reservoirs near 2,000 m deep, which is about 33°, is
less than that for the above interface, which is more than 42°.
In addition, the incidence range for the 3,000 m interface is
much narrower.
Similar to Trorey’s (1970) work, we illustrate in Fig. 4a
zero offset section near the 400-m-wide reservoir in Fig. 1(a)
to show the diffractions. The reservoir ranges from CDP 160
to CDP 199. As mentioned above, the artificial well, Well_1, is
located at the middle of the reservoir (CDP 179). As reported
by Sun and Bancroft (2003), when the reservoir width is large
enough, we can get a good image of the reservoir except at

the reservoir edges, where the diffractions are not properly
collapsed. We can see uncollapsed diffractions at the left side
of the section. In agreement with Trorey’s report, we find that
the diffraction amplitude is much less than the reflections of
the reflector. The events at the right of CDP 240 are responses
for the 500-m-wide reservoir. It is hard to find diffractions
between the two reservoirs. That is because the two reservoirs
are so close that the diffractions destructively interfere with
each other.

In our experiment, the wavelength computed using the ve-
locity of the reservoirs is estimated to be about 154 m. The
spatial resolution is calculated as about 19 m, and the lateral
resolution is calculated as about 394 m through equations (1)
and (2). In the above models, all reservoir thicknesses, ranging
from 10 m to 140 m, are comparable to the spatial (vertical)
resolution. Similar to a thin bed, the reflections of the top and
base of a finite-scale reservoir interfere with each other. With
different reservoir scales, the interference between the top and
base of reservoirs is different. Thus, the apparent amplitude
of a finite-scale reservoir is controlled by the top and base
reflection coefficients and the reservoir scale. Different from
Figure 4 A part of the zero-offset section for the model in Fig. 1(a).

Figure 5 Waveforms for the 400-m-wide reservoir from Fig. 1(a). The
first trough around 705 ms, as marked with a dashed line, in each
trace is extracted as the amplitude during AVO extraction.

conventionally extracted reflection amplitudes of the top in-
terface during AVO analysis, we can only get the composite
reflections of the top and base for a finite-scale reservoir.
From the angle gathers at the common midpoints (CMPs)
of reservoirs, we extract the amplitudes of different incident
angles to investigate the impact of width and thickness on
AVO. Figure 5 illustrates the amplitude extraction process.

The first troughs of the composite waveform of the reservoirs
are extracted for AVO analysis. Least-squares fitting is used to
extract AVO intercepts and gradients based on Shuey’s two-
term approximation of the Zoeppritz equations (Shuey 1985):

where θ is the incidence angle, A is the AVO intercept, and B
is the AVO gradient. Then, we can demonstrate the impact of
the width and thickness on AVO characteristics.
3.3 Impact of reservoir width on AVO

AVO curves of reservoirs with different widths are shown
in Fig. 6. AVOs of these reservoirs belong to class IV. As
Castagna, Swan, and Foster (1998) explained, class IV AVO
frequently occurs when a low-velocity sand is overlain by a
high-velocity unit. This coincides with the situation in our
models. We can see that AVO dramatically varies with the
reservoir width. To be more precise, the magnitude of the
amplitude first increases with the width when the width ranges
from 100 m to 700 m, and then decreases with the width
when the width ranges from 800 m to 1,200 m. Noticeably,
the ordinate ranges of Figs. 6(a) and (b) are different. In fact,
the amplitude decrease in Fig. 6(b) is very slight in comparison
with the amplitude increase in Fig. 6(a). In Fig. 6(b), the AVO
curve of the 1,200 m almost overlaps with that of the infinite
width. Eventually, the AVO curve tends to the infinite-width

Figure 6 AVO curves of reservoirs with different widths: (a) ranging from 100 m to 700 m, and (b) from 800 m to 1,200 m. Empty circles
indicate amplitude samples from AVO extraction.

situation. The magnitude of amplitudes peaks at 700 m, which
is about 1.8 times of the Fresnel zone radius.
To show the width impact more clearly, we extract the
intercepts (A) and gradients (B) of the AVO curves in Fig. 6,
given in Table 1, and illustrate them in Fig. 7. Intercept and
gradient clearly both depend on the reservoir width, ranging
from 100 m to 1,200 m. Given that the intercept measures the
amplitude at normal incidence, the intercept variation is in
accordance with the amplitude variation discussed in the last
paragraph. The magnitude of the intercept shows an approxi-
mately linear increase from 0.044 at 100 m to 0.233 at 700 m,
which is an increase of about 430%. Then, it is followed by
a slight drop until 1,000 m, which is almost 2.5 times of the
Fresnel zone radius. Beyond a reservoir width of 1,000 m,
the intercept is constant. By comparison, the gradient behaves
quite differently. In particular, it varies beyond the 1,000-m
reservoir width, at which the intercept becomes stable. The
gradient shows a slight rise from 0.12 at 1,000 m to 0.16 at
1,200 m. When it is less than 1,000 m, the magnitude of the
gradient also shows an approximately linear increase from

Table 1 AVO intercepts (A) and gradients (B) of reservoirs with dif-
ferent widths and the same thickness of 100 m from Fig. 6

0.057 at 100 m to 0.258 at 600 m, which is an increase of
about 353%. Then, it is followed by a decrease until 1,000 m
(0.116). The gradient peaks at 6,000 m, which is about 1.5
times of the Fresnel zone radius.

Figure 7 AVO intercept (A) and gradient (B) versus reservoir width
from AVO curves in Fig. 6.
3.4 Impact of reservoir thickness on AVO

AVOs for different thicknesses are shown in Fig. 8. From
Fig. 8(a), it is easy to see AVO curves of different thicknesses

dramatically deviate from that of the single interface. That is
because the widths of the former are only 100 m, whereas
that of the latter is infinite (large compared with the seismic
wavelength). As discussed above, the amplitudes generally in-
crease with the reservoir width. Therefore, the amplitudes of
the single interface are much larger than that of the reservoirs
in Fig. 1(c). We can also see the variation of AVO curves
with the thickness is much less pronounced than that with the
width. AVO curves corresponding to thicknesses ranging from
60 m to 140 m almost overlap with each other. That means
the thickness scarcely contributes to the AVO variation when
the thickness is more than 60 m. To see the variation with
thicknesses from 10 m to 70 m more clearly, we magnify their
AVO curves in Fig. 8(b). The magnitude of the amplitudes
first increases and then decreases with the thickness, peaking
at the thickness of 30 m. The curve of the 60 m almost over-
laps with that of the 70 m. The thickness change will not cause
obvious AVO changes when it is more than 60 m.
Table 2 gives the extracted the intercepts (A) and gradi-
ents (B) of the AVO curves in Fig. 8(a), and we illustrate them
in Fig. 9 to show the thickness impact more clearly. There is

Figure 8 AVO curves of reservoirs with different thicknesses (a) ranging from 10 m to 140 m. AVO curves from 10 m to 70 m are magnified
in (b). Empty circles indicate amplitude samples from AVO extraction.

Table 2 AVO intercepts (A) and gradients (B) of reservoirs with dif-
ferent thicknesses and the same width of 100 m from Fig. 8(a)

a rise in the magnitude of the intercept from 0.029 at 10 m
to 0.058 at 30 m, which is an increase of about 100%. Then,
the magnitude of the intercept gradually decreases to 0.42 at
60 m. The magnitude of the intercept remains at this level
when the thickness ranges from 60 m to 140 m. The variation
of the gradient is similar to that of the intercept, except that
there is some fluctuation between 60 m to 90 m. However, the
overall trend is almost the same. The gradient peaks at 30 m
(0.071), which is close to the tuning thickness, and remains
almost stable when the thickness is larger than 60 m, which
is 1.6 times of the tuning thickness. The maximum change of
the gradient due to the thickness is about 73% (from 0.041
at 10 m to 0.071 at 30 m). The impact of reservoir thick-

Figure 9 AVO intercept (A) and gradient (B) versus reservoir thick-
ness from AVO curves in Fig. 8.

ness could be explained by Widess theory (Widess 1973). As
pointed out by Chopra, Castagna, and Xu (2009), in Widess’
theory, the reflection coefficients of the thin bed top and bot-
tom are exactly equal and opposite. In our study, the above
and laying backgrounds of reservoirs are the same medium.
Therefore, the Widess limit applies in our situation.

As mentioned above, the amplitude-versus-offset (AVO) in-
tercepts, the amplitudes at zero offset, first increase with the
width (from 100 m to 700 m), followed with a slight decrease
(from 700 m to 1,000 m), and finally remain stable. The pro-
cess is similar to the tuning effect for a thin bed. We conjecture
that there is a tuning effect in the lateral direction. The tun-
ing width is 1.8 times of the Fresnel zone radius, which is
700 m here. The waveform energy increases with the width
before the tuning width and decreases after the tuning width.
When the width is larger than 3 times of the Fresnel zone, the
waveform energy will remain stable.
The AVO curve of a reservoir 1,200 m wide almost over-
laps with that of the infinite width as shown in Fig. 6(b).
The largest width that contributes to AVO change, which is
1,200 m here, is about three times of the Fresnel zone radius.
That is because the reservoir width would not contribute to
seismic energy change when it is beyond the lateral resolution.
Consequently, as the width increases, the AVO curve tends to
the infinite-width situation. The AVO curves of the reservoir
with infinite width and of a single interface are clearly identi-
cal. These reservoirs differ only in thickness, the former being
100 m and the latter infinitely thick. However, as discussed,
AVO attributes are not affected by vertical tuning beyond a
thickness of 60 m (using our model parameters).
It is worth noting that reservoir scale can cause con-
siderable variations on cross-plots of AVO intercepts and
gradients. Cross-plotting AVO intercepts and gradients is a
common approach during AVO analysis. As pointed out by
Castagna et al. (1998), gas sands tend to plot to the lower
left of the brine sands on cross-plots of A and B, meaning
A and B of gas sands are more negative than that of brine
sands. The deviation of gas sands from brine sands is the
basis for many hydrocarbon detection methodologies. How-
ever, we see here that the deviation may also be caused by
non-petrophysical factors such as the reservoir scale. This is
illustrated in Fig. 10, which cross-plots AVO intercepts and
gradients of different widths and thicknesss for reservoirs in
the above models. Since AVO in this study belongs to class Ⅳ,
samples fall in quadrant Ⅱ. The reservoir scale change, both

Figure 10 Cross-plots of AVO intercepts and gradients of (a) different widths ranging from 100 m to 1,200 m and (b) different thicknesses
ranging from 10 m to 140 m. Note that numbers are widths and thicknesses in metres.

the width and thickness, gives rise to a spiraling effect on the
intercept-gradient cross-plot. Samples in Fig. 10(a, b) both
move in an anti-clockwise direction along with the increase
in reservoir scale. This phenomenon coincides with Simm and
Bacon’s report (Simm and Bacon 2014). In this paper, we
studied class Ⅳ AVO, whereas in Simm and Bacon’s (2014)
report, they studied class Ⅲ AVO. In both situations, points
in the intercept and gradient cross-plot rotate in the anti-
clockwise direction. This phenomenon reflects the impact of
reservoir scale, which is a non-petrophysical factor, no matter
which quadrant points fall in. It is reasonable to conjecture
that this phenomenon applies for other AVO classes (Ⅰ and Ⅱ).
Moreover, the magnitude of the deviation caused by width is
larger than that caused by thickness. Noticeably, the devi-
ation caused by reservoir scale is comparable to, sometimes
even larger, that caused by hydrocarbons, which was reported
by Castagna et al. (1998). Therefore, it is reasonable to believe
the validity of hydrocarbon detection without considering the
impact of reservoir scale is questionable. The reservoir scale
is an important factor to be taken into consideration during
AVO analysis for reservoirs at finite scale.

We have presented an analysis of the impact of lateral and
vertical scales on the amplitude-versus-offset (AVO) intercept
and gradient. This is a single-factor analysis, in the sense that
only the size of the reservoir was varied, and all modelling
parameters were held constant throughout. Clearly, there are
other factors that need to be analysed, and we hope to do this

in the future. This includes the frequency bandwidth, sam-
pling grid, noise, and acquisition density during the modelling
process.
Trorey (1970) showed that, at a diffracting edge, the am-
plitude of the reflection is halved. Similarly, Sun and Bancroft
(2003) pointed out that the edge impact on AVO was signifi-
cant if the reflector was comparable to the Fresnel zone. How-
ever, for a large reflector, the diffraction effect is insignificant,
particularly in the middle of the reflector that is the furthest
point from the edge. As Fig. 4 shows, when the reservoir width
is large enough, we can get a good image of the reservoir, ex-
cept there is serious diffraction near the edge. Therefore, to
avoid the edge diffraction unreliability, all the above AVO
analysis is conducted on seismic gathers for the middle point
of each reservoir. We can extract AVO for reservoirs with
higher reliability from the properly collapsed diffractions far
from the reservoir edges.
Our conclusions are drawn from a numerical model and
have yet to be verified with experimental data. Xu et al. (2014)
conducted physical modelling experiments to understand the
reservoir scale impact. However, the range of reservoir size
analysed is too small for us to be able to verify if their results
match ours.
The seismic response of spatially confined units is mainly
dominated by wave diffraction, instead of simple reflections at
a single interface. Diffractions will no longer interfere when
the unit is large enough. Compared with previous research,
we extend the reservoir scale to a wider range and get a more
extensive understanding of the impact of reservoir scale on
AVO. It is noticeable that there are both disadvantages and

advantages of the impact of the reservoir scale on AVO. On
one hand, it brings about contamination to fluid discrimina-
tion. On the other hand, the relationship between the reservoir
scale and AVO responses may be useful in quantitative inter-
pretation of reservoirs. We suggest that we could make the
best of it to achieve reserve estimation. The impact of reser-
voir scale on AVO we propose in the paper is essential for
researchers of AVO technology.

For reservoirs with finite scale, the reservoir scale plays an im-
portant role in amplitude variation with offset (AVO) and has
a nonlinear impact on AVO intercept and gradient. AVO in-
tercept and gradient are linearly proportional to the reservoir
scale only when it is less than some certain values. Based on
the data in our numerical simulations, we find AVO intercept
achieves its maxima at a width of 1.8 times of the Fresnel zone
radius, whereas AVO gradient peaks at a width of 1.5 times
of the Fresnel zone radius. The AVO did not change with the
width if it is larger than three times of the Fresnel zone ra-
dius. Both the AVO intercept and gradient first increase and
then decrease with the thickness, peaking at the tuning thick-
ness. The thickness contribution to AVO variations is negligi-
ble when the thickness is larger than 1.6 times of the tuning
thickness. Compared with the reservoir thickness, the reser-
voir width is much more dominant in contributing to AVO.
On cross-plots of AVO intercept and gradient, the reservoir
scale change causes a spiraling effect. Samples move in an anti-
clockwise direction along with the increase in reservoir scale.

This work was supported by the China National Petroleum
Corporation (CNPC) and National Science & Technol-
ogy Major Project (Grant No. 2011ZX05007-006) and
by The National Natural Science Foundation of China
(No. 41474112). Special thanks to the editor and reviewers
for their comments which significantly improve the paper.

FULL LENGTH ARTICLE
Use of spectral decomposition technique
for delineation of channels at Solar gas discovery,
oﬀshore West Nile Delta, Egypt
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 87, height: 84, bpc: 8>
Adel A.A. Othman a, M. Fathy a, Ali Maher b,*
a Geophysics Department, Faculty of Science, Azhar University, 1 El-Mokhayam El-Daem Street, Nasr City, 11884 Cairo, Egypt
b Rashid Petroleum Company (RASHPETCO), Building 18 Road 293, New Maadi 1073, Cairo, Egypt
Received 20 January 2015; revised 1 March 2015; accepted 3 March 2015
Available online 7 December 2015
KEYWORDS
Spectral decomposition;
WDDM concession;
Offshore West Nile Delta;
Solar gas discovery
Abstract
This paper presents a case study of spectral decomposition of seismic data and how it
aids in seismic data interpretation. It is also known as time–frequency analysis where non-
stationary signals in time/space are from time/space domain to time/space vs. frequency domain.
The frequency domain representation illustrates many important features that are not apparent
in time domain representation. Spectral decomposition is a non-unique process for which various
techniques exist and newer modiﬁed techniques are being discovered. Over the years, spectral
decomposition of seismic data has progressed from being a tool for stratigraphic analysis to helping
as a Direct Hydrocarbon Indicator (DHI); a potential weapon for reducing dry well drilling. In the
coming years, it is expected that spectral decomposition may be able to play a signiﬁcant role in
analyzing time lapse seismic data.
In this paper, spectral decomposition technique is applied to the imaging and mapping of bed
thickness, geologic discontinuities and channel delineation at Solar discovery. From the study,
two distinctively different channels (gas bearing ‘‘Red channel” and water bearing ‘‘Yellow chan-
nel”) were delineated in the area, and are proven by the drilled well, and some stratigraphic features
are identiﬁed.
� 2015 The Authors. Production and hosting by Elsevier B.V. on behalf of Egyptian Petroleum Research
Institute. This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/
licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
1. Introduction
Seismic data, being non-stationary in nature, have varying
frequency content in time. Time–frequency decomposition
(also called spectral decomposition) of a seismic signal aims
to characterize the time-dependent frequency response of sub-
surface rocks and reservoirs. Spectral decomposition unravels
the seismic signal into its constituent frequencies. This allows
the interpreter to see amplitude and phase tuned to speciﬁc
wavelengths, just as a radio can pick out a single station or a
prism a single color. Since the stratigraphy resonates at wave-
lengths dependent on the bedding thickness, the interpreter can
image not only subtle thickness variations and discontinuities,
* Corresponding author.
E-mail address: Ali.Maher@Rashpetco.com (A. Maher).
Peer review under responsibility of Egyptian Petroleum Research
Institute.
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 268, height: 293, bpc: 8>
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 284, height: 359, bpc: 8>
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.ejpe.2015.03.005
1110-0621 � 2015 The Authors. Production and hosting by Elsevier B.V. on behalf of Egyptian Petroleum Research Institute.
This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
but also accurately predict bedding thickness quantitatively [7].
In addition, since the high-frequency response of a reﬂector
can be attenuated by the presence of compressible ﬂuids, spec-
tral decomposition can also assist in the direct detection of
hydrocarbons [1]. These approaches, applied alone to a seismic
dataset, can be very enlightening but the results can also be
somewhat cryptic. Seismic modeling gives the interpreter a
critical insight into tuned attribute maps, and also allows
him or her to predicting what a particular bed geometry or
thickness trend will look like. Volume visualization and
interpretation can enhance the interpretation further still, sig-
niﬁcantly reducing exploration risk.
2. General geological setting
Egypt is divided into three main petroleum provinces which
are Gulf of Suez, Nile Delta and Western Desert. The Nile
Delta province is rapidly emerging as a major gas province,
highly proliﬁc, with signiﬁcant Yet To Find (YTF) estimates
[3,5,9].
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 1654, height: 2116, bpc: 8>
Figure 1
Satellite image showing the location of West Delta Deep Marine (WDDM) concession, offshore Egypt (upper) and an index
map showing Solar channel location (lower).
Solar is a Pliocene gas discovery in the West Delta Deep
Marine concession (WDDM) located 100 km north off the
present day shoreline of Egypt (Fig. 1) in water depths between
800 and 1000 m. WDDM concession is located in the Mediter-
ranean Sea around 110 km NE of Alexandria [4,10]. Two
channels have been identiﬁed in Solar discovery. In this paper,
they are referred to as the Red channel and Yellow channel.
Both channels exhibit a combined stratigraphic/structural
trapping style and were deposited in a conﬁned deep marine
turbiditic environment (Fig. 2). Laterally both channels are
stratigraphically side sealed (pinch out). The overall northward
dipping nature of the channel creates dip closure to the north.
To the south, stratigraphic closure is interpreted at the head of
the channel, this is the highest risk section of the trap. The ver-
tical seal is El-Wastani claystone with some risk of seal capa-
bility due to the thinning of the overburden. The well
location was optimized to penetrate a relatively high ampli-
tude, thick section at the intersection of the two channels.
The Red channel is about 10–12 km long, 400–500 m wide
and 40 m average thickness.
3. Conventional data interpretation
The whole ﬁeld was surveyed during 2006, and its high quality
three-dimensional (3D) seismic cube was later processed in
2007. No multiple reﬂections, or even small multiplicative
events, were seen on stacked–migrated seismic sections, partic-
ularly in the vicinity of the target reservoir zone.
Data were extensively visualized, colored-contoured and
conventionally interpreted using the integrated Petrel reservoir
characterization
software
(Schlumberger
Limited,
USA).
Three time horizons, within which ﬂuid-bearing channels can
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 1300, height: 1512, bpc: 8>
Figure 2
Sum of positive amplitude attribute map (over Solar top Red channel) showing the NE–SW trending Solar channel.
<image: DeviceRGB, width: 957, height: 621, bpc: 8>
Figure 3
Amplitude spectrum for the full stack seismic data
within the interval 2200–3000 ms.
exist, were obviously interpreted in terms of main reﬂectors;
namely, ‘Top Red Ch Gas Sand’, ‘Base Red Ch Gas Sand’
and ‘Base Red Channel’.
4. Spectral decomposition history
Castagna [1] used matching-pursuit decomposition for instan-
taneous spectral analysis to detect low-frequency shadows
beneath hydrocarbon reservoirs. Peyton [8] used spectral
decomposition and coherency to interpret incised valleys.
Partyka [7] used windowed spectral analysis to produce
discrete-frequency energy cubes for applications in reservoir
characterization. Hardy [2] showed that an average frequency
attribute produced from sine curve-ﬁtting strongly correlates
with shale volume in a particular area. Spectral decomposition
transforms the seismic data into the frequency domain via
mathematic methods such as Discrete Fourier Transform
(DFT), Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT), and other
methods. The transformed results include tuning cubes and a
variety of discrete common frequency cubes.
Spectral decomposition has proved to be a robust approach
for seismic interpretation. It is used for mapping temporal bed
thickness [7], to indicate stratigraphy traps [6], and to delineate
hydrocarbon distribution [1].
5. Methodology and results
From the 3D seismic dataset, we know that there are two
channels for Solar discovery (Red channel and Yellow chan-
nel). The Red channel appears clearly on the seismic and
could easily be interpreted. It is sinuous and has a discontinu-
ity in its central part in the form of a dim part of the channel
which is attributed to late stage mud-ﬁlled channels that
mask the seismic amplitudes. The southern part of the chan-
nel has two branches and the channel fairway could not be

range in the seismic dataset) in Red color, 25 Hz (the dominant

on the AAA map appear to coincide with the low frequency
range in the spectral decomposition map (in Red color). This
means that the channel seems to be connected. The southern
part of the channel coincides with the high frequency range

deﬁnes the channel fairway. Some parts of the channel appear

features of the lower channel (Yellow channel). AAA map

channels.

stacked channels for the Yellow channel which does not
stand out very well in the normal time attribute (AAA
map).
The color blending display helps to optimize the well loca-
tion in terms of targeting the thickest and high quality part of
the channel which appears as the white color (a mix of the
three RGB frequencies) on the display.
The spectral decomposition provides substantially more
detail and ﬁdelity than full bandwidth conventional attributes.
It reveals stratigraphic and structural edges as well as relative
thickening and thinning. It allows viewing subsurface seismic
interference at discrete frequencies.

Use of spectral decomposition technique
for delineation of channels at Solar gas discovery,
oﬀshore West Nile Delta, Egypt
Adel A.A. Othman a, M. Fathy a, Ali Maher b,*

a Geophysics Department, Faculty of Science, Azhar University, 1 El-Mokhayam El-Daem Street, Nasr City, 11884 Cairo, Egypt
b Rashid Petroleum Company (RASHPETCO), Building 18 Road 293, New Maadi 1073, Cairo, Egypt

Received 20 January 2015; revised 1 March 2015; accepted 3 March 2015
Available online 7 December 2015

Abstract
This paper presents a case study of spectral decomposition of seismic data and how it
aids in seismic data interpretation. It is also known as time–frequency analysis where non-
stationary signals in time/space are from time/space domain to time/space vs. frequency domain.
The frequency domain representation illustrates many important features that are not apparent
in time domain representation. Spectral decomposition is a non-unique process for which various
techniques exist and newer modiﬁed techniques are being discovered. Over the years, spectral
decomposition of seismic data has progressed from being a tool for stratigraphic analysis to helping
as a Direct Hydrocarbon Indicator (DHI); a potential weapon for reducing dry well drilling. In the
coming years, it is expected that spectral decomposition may be able to play a signiﬁcant role in
analyzing time lapse seismic data.
In this paper, spectral decomposition technique is applied to the imaging and mapping of bed
thickness, geologic discontinuities and channel delineation at Solar discovery. From the study,
two distinctively different channels (gas bearing ‘‘Red channel” and water bearing ‘‘Yellow chan-
nel”) were delineated in the area, and are proven by the drilled well, and some stratigraphic features
are identiﬁed.

Seismic data, being non-stationary in nature, have varying
frequency content in time. Time–frequency decomposition

(also called spectral decomposition) of a seismic signal aims
to characterize the time-dependent frequency response of sub-
surface rocks and reservoirs. Spectral decomposition unravels
the seismic signal into its constituent frequencies. This allows
the interpreter to see amplitude and phase tuned to speciﬁc
wavelengths, just as a radio can pick out a single station or a
prism a single color. Since the stratigraphy resonates at wave-
lengths dependent on the bedding thickness, the interpreter can
image not only subtle thickness variations and discontinuities,

In addition, since the high-frequency response of a reﬂector
can be attenuated by the presence of compressible ﬂuids, spec-

hydrocarbons [1]. These approaches, applied alone to a seismic
dataset, can be very enlightening but the results can also be
somewhat cryptic. Seismic modeling gives the interpreter a
critical insight into tuned attribute maps, and also allows
him or her to predicting what a particular bed geometry or
thickness trend will look like. Volume visualization and

interpretation can enhance the interpretation further still, sig-
niﬁcantly reducing exploration risk.

Egypt is divided into three main petroleum provinces which
are Gulf of Suez, Nile Delta and Western Desert. The Nile
Delta province is rapidly emerging as a major gas province,
highly proliﬁc, with signiﬁcant Yet To Find (YTF) estimates
[3,5,9].

Solar is a Pliocene gas discovery in the West Delta Deep

channels have been identiﬁed in Solar discovery. In this paper,
they are referred to as the Red channel and Yellow channel.

Both channels exhibit a combined stratigraphic/structural
trapping style and were deposited in a conﬁned deep marine
turbiditic environment (Fig. 2). Laterally both channels are
stratigraphically side sealed (pinch out). The overall northward

To the south, stratigraphic closure is interpreted at the head of
the channel, this is the highest risk section of the trap. The ver-

location was optimized to penetrate a relatively high ampli-

The Red channel is about 10–12 km long, 400–500 m wide

The whole ﬁeld was surveyed during 2006, and its high quality

Data were extensively visualized, colored-contoured and
conventionally interpreted using the integrated Petrel reservoir
characterization
software
(Schlumberger
Limited,
USA).

PR4
Well Logging in Support for Seismic Reservoir
Characterization
A. Bovykin* (TNK-BP), V. Matusevich (TNK-BP), N. Bachurin (TNK-BP), N.
Chikina (TNK-BP) & S. Klarner (TNK-BP)
SUMMARY
For the successful application of quantitative seismic interpretation techniques, namely the prediction of
lithology, porosity and potentially pore fluid from seismic data, reliable calibration well data is key.
Usually, the acquisition of a sophisticated logging suite involves higher costs, and we need hard facts for
their legitimation. To prove the value of a modern logging suite, a pilot project over several wells in the
Orenburg area has been conducted, where the results of domestic standard logging runs with extended
measurements using foreign tools were compared. In this paper, we discuss both approaches and highlight
what additional information we gain from the extended measurements. Using only the standard logging
suite, it is very difficult to obtain accurate lithology, porosity and acoustic impedance values. For high
quality reservoir characterization, in addition to the p-wave velocity, the shear wave and the Stoneley
provide extremely useful information, especially for lithology estimation and the definition of permeable
reservoir intervals. We show that in order to make use of the full potential of seismic inversion techniques,
the complex of modern logging curves has to be acquired at least in a number of key wells for exploration
and production.

Introduction
Over the last years, the industry has undertaken serious efforts to move from qualitative seismic 
interpretation – basically structural mapping and amplitude maps – to quantitative seismic 
interpretation, namely the prediction of lithology, porosity and potentially pore fluid from seismic 
data. The results help to mitigate the exploration risk and optimize the well pattern in the field 
development phase. However, for a successful prediction of the rock properties the access to reliable 
well data is key, to calibrate amplitude variations to physical effects of changes in the reservoir. 
Usually, the acquisition of a sophisticated logging suite involves higher costs, and we need hard facts 
for their legitimation. To prove the value of a modern logging suite, a pilot project over several wells 
in the Orenburg area has been conducted, where we compared the results of domestic standard 
logging runs with extended measurements using foreign tools. In this paper, we discuss both 
approaches and highlight what additional information we gain from the extended measurements.
Geological setting
The area under consideration is located on the south-eastern slope of Volga-Ural anticlise within the 
Volga-Ural oil and gas bearing basin, European South-East. The sedimentary cover of the area is 
composed of Riphean siliciclastic graben fill, Middle Devonian to Lower Permian (Artinskian) mixed 
siliclastic-carbonate complexes, Kungurian sulfite-halogen complex and Upper Permian to 
Quaternary siliciclastics.
More than 20 reservoir intervals within the Middle Devonian - Lower Permian succession have been 
proved to be oil bearing and involved into development. Some gas discoveries were made in the 
Upper Permian Ufimian deposits. Major productive reservoirs vary from field to field, but as whole 
they are represented by Middle Devonian (D2) clastic and carbonate deposits (D7-D3), Upper 
Devonian (D3p) Pashian clastics (D0-D2), Frasnian-Famennian (D3f-fm, clinoforms of the so called 
Kalganski formation –Dkt), Frasnian to Tournaisian (D3f-C1t) carbonates including reefs (Df, Dzl, 
T1-T2), Visean ( C1v) clastics (B2), Visean (C1v) Oksky carbonates (O6-O2).
Acquired well log data
Our usual logging program for an exploration or appraisal well in the Orenburg area so far comprised 
a set acquired with domestic tools, consisting of Acoustic log, Density log, Resistivity logs (lateral 
logging, micro-laterolog, contact logging, mud resistivity log), Conductivity logging (induction log), 
GR & Spectral Gamma-Ray, Neutron logging, Calliper and Spontaneous Potential (SP). The quality 
of the data was deemed to be sufficient for the evaluation of lithology, porosity and saturation of the 
reservoir section.  
 
To tie well and seismic data correctly and make use of the advantages of simultaneous angle stack 
inversion, however, reliable shear information is required. So far there is no domestic tool for high 
quality shear data acquisition available - this represents a serious obstacle for utilizing the well data in 
quantitative interpretation of seismic data. Within the frame of a pilot program “Well logging in 
support for seismic”, in several wells over the section of interest in addition to the local logging 
standards a suite of modern western tools has been acquired by the same contractor. This program 
includes Cross-dipole acoustic measurements (P-wave velocity, S-wave velocity, Stoneley wave, 
azimuthal anisotropy as well as a complex including GR, Density, PEF, Neutron-porosity, and 
Calliper.

Comparison of Domestic and Western logging suites
The analysis of the data made clear that the domestic sonic log tool delivers a high quality p-wave 
velocity, meeting the requirements of quantitative seismic interpretation (Fig.1). But in view of the 
importance of Vp/Vs for lithology definition, the lack of a local tool for reliable shear wave 
measurements is a big disadvantage. Moreover, only shear waves measurements will give us 
indications of potential azimuthal anisotropy (fracture detection). In addition, without the Stoneley 
wave it is not possible to analyze the permeability intervals. The analysis of the extended pilot 
program revealed that the Stoneley derived permeability shows a very good match with the results of 
the well testing and core analysis, so it is considered as a very good tool to identify effective reservoir 
intervals. Therefore, for advanced reservoir characterization the necessity of using foreign equipment 
arises.

While analyzing, we observed a number of significant downsides for density/porosity measurements 
using the standard tools. The provided density logs are of poor quality and show a nonsystematic 
nonlinear shift along the borehole (Fig. 2). This is not only of relevance for the calculation of acoustic 
impedance as one of the key parameters derived from seismic data. Density is also one of the most 
important input parameters for porosity calculation, and if the porosity is wrong, the volumes and 
hence the reserves may not be correct. This critical issue led us to the conclusion that the standard 
density tool has to be exchanged for a modern, more reliable tool.

(“standard”) and foreign (“extended”) logging tools.
The analyzed standard data also suffer from the poor quality of the neutron log (Fig.3). Often, the 
Neutron log is still acquired in counts per second and needs to be transferred to porosity by the 
interpreter using empirical relationships. Much more accurate results are received, when the Neutron 
tool is already calibrated and the measurements are delivered in porosity units. The cross plots on 
figure 3 also demonstrate that the modern tools show a sharper separation by lithology and better 
correlation of porosity for both, limestones and dolomites. The standard tools exhibit a large scatter of 
values and hence, a larger uncertainty range.

logging suite (a and b –Calibrated Neutron, c and d – acoustic impedance), vertical axis: porosity 
data from “standard” tools (a and c) versus data from extended logging suite (b and c). Note the 
large uncertainty in lithology and porosity definition for the standard tools.
Conclusions
Using only the standard logging suite, it is rather difficult to obtain accurate lithology, porosity and 
acoustic impedance values. Intervals with fractured reservoirs may be overlooked. Especially the 
provided density measurements with older tools proved to be extremely unreliable, and this may have 
a direct impact of the reserves evaluation. In addition, the data are – due to the inherent blurring – 
applicable for property prediction from seismic data only in a qualitative manner. In view of the 
importance of the porosity estimation these standard tools have to be substituted by modern tools.
For high quality reservoir characterization, in addition to the p-wave velocity, the shear wave and the 
Stoneley provide extremely useful information, especially for lithology estimation and the definition 
of permeable reservoir intervals. To make use of the full potential of seismic inversion techniques, the 
complex of modern logging curves has to be acquired at least in a number of key wells for exploration 
and production.

PR4
Well Logging in Support for Seismic Reservoir
Characterization

A. Bovykin* (TNK-BP), V. Matusevich (TNK-BP), N. Bachurin (TNK-BP), N.
Chikina (TNK-BP) & S. Klarner (TNK-BP)

For the successful application of quantitative seismic interpretation techniques, namely the prediction of
lithology, porosity and potentially pore fluid from seismic data, reliable calibration well data is key.
Usually, the acquisition of a sophisticated logging suite involves higher costs, and we need hard facts for
their legitimation. To prove the value of a modern logging suite, a pilot project over several wells in the
Orenburg area has been conducted, where the results of domestic standard logging runs with extended
measurements using foreign tools were compared. In this paper, we discuss both approaches and highlight
what additional information we gain from the extended measurements. Using only the standard logging
suite, it is very difficult to obtain accurate lithology, porosity and acoustic impedance values. For high
quality reservoir characterization, in addition to the p-wave velocity, the shear wave and the Stoneley
provide extremely useful information, especially for lithology estimation and the definition of permeable
reservoir intervals. We show that in order to make use of the full potential of seismic inversion techniques,
the complex of modern logging curves has to be acquired at least in a number of key wells for exploration
and production.

Over the last years, the industry has undertaken serious efforts to move from qualitative seismic 
interpretation – basically structural mapping and amplitude maps – to quantitative seismic 
interpretation, namely the prediction of lithology, porosity and potentially pore fluid from seismic 
data. The results help to mitigate the exploration risk and optimize the well pattern in the field 
development phase. However, for a successful prediction of the rock properties the access to reliable 
well data is key, to calibrate amplitude variations to physical effects of changes in the reservoir. 
Usually, the acquisition of a sophisticated logging suite involves higher costs, and we need hard facts 
for their legitimation. To prove the value of a modern logging suite, a pilot project over several wells 
in the Orenburg area has been conducted, where we compared the results of domestic standard 
logging runs with extended measurements using foreign tools. In this paper, we discuss both 
approaches and highlight what additional information we gain from the extended measurements.

The area under consideration is located on the south-eastern slope of Volga-Ural anticlise within the 
Volga-Ural oil and gas bearing basin, European South-East. The sedimentary cover of the area is 
composed of Riphean siliciclastic graben fill, Middle Devonian to Lower Permian (Artinskian) mixed 
siliclastic-carbonate complexes, Kungurian sulfite-halogen complex and Upper Permian to 
Quaternary siliciclastics.

More than 20 reservoir intervals within the Middle Devonian - Lower Permian succession have been 
proved to be oil bearing and involved into development. Some gas discoveries were made in the 
Upper Permian Ufimian deposits. Major productive reservoirs vary from field to field, but as whole 
they are represented by Middle Devonian (D2) clastic and carbonate deposits (D7-D3), Upper 
Devonian (D3p) Pashian clastics (D0-D2), Frasnian-Famennian (D3f-fm, clinoforms of the so called 
Kalganski formation –Dkt), Frasnian to Tournaisian (D3f-C1t) carbonates including reefs (Df, Dzl, 
T1-T2), Visean ( C1v) clastics (B2), Visean (C1v) Oksky carbonates (O6-O2).

Our usual logging program for an exploration or appraisal well in the Orenburg area so far comprised 
a set acquired with domestic tools, consisting of Acoustic log, Density log, Resistivity logs (lateral 
logging, micro-laterolog, contact logging, mud resistivity log), Conductivity logging (induction log), 
GR & Spectral Gamma-Ray, Neutron logging, Calliper and Spontaneous Potential (SP). The quality 
of the data was deemed to be sufficient for the evaluation of lithology, porosity and saturation of the 
reservoir section.  
 
To tie well and seismic data correctly and make use of the advantages of simultaneous angle stack 
inversion, however, reliable shear information is required. So far there is no domestic tool for high 
quality shear data acquisition available - this represents a serious obstacle for utilizing the well data in 
quantitative interpretation of seismic data. Within the frame of a pilot program “Well logging in 
support for seismic”, in several wells over the section of interest in addition to the local logging 
standards a suite of modern western tools has been acquired by the same contractor. This program 
includes Cross-dipole acoustic measurements (P-wave velocity, S-wave velocity, Stoneley wave, 
azimuthal anisotropy as well as a complex including GR, Density, PEF, Neutron-porosity, and 
Calliper.
Comparison of Domestic and Western logging suites

The analysis of the data made clear that the domestic sonic log tool delivers a high quality p-wave 
velocity, meeting the requirements of quantitative seismic interpretation (Fig.1). But in view of the 
importance of Vp/Vs for lithology definition, the lack of a local tool for reliable shear wave 
measurements is a big disadvantage. Moreover, only shear waves measurements will give us 
indications of potential azimuthal anisotropy (fracture detection). In addition, without the Stoneley 
wave it is not possible to analyze the permeability intervals. The analysis of the extended pilot 
program revealed that the Stoneley derived permeability shows a very good match with the results of 
the well testing and core analysis, so it is considered as a very good tool to identify effective reservoir 
intervals. Therefore, for advanced reservoir characterization the necessity of using foreign equipment 
arises.

Figure 1 Example of a well showing the good match of p-wave for both, the domestic (“standard”) 
and foreign (“extended”) logging tools and the importance of advanced acoustic measurements for 
reservoir evaluation.

While analyzing, we observed a number of significant downsides for density/porosity measurements 
using the standard tools. The provided density logs are of poor quality and show a nonsystematic 
nonlinear shift along the borehole (Fig. 2). This is not only of relevance for the calculation of acoustic 
impedance as one of the key parameters derived from seismic data. Density is also one of the most 
important input parameters for porosity calculation, and if the porosity is wrong, the volumes and 
hence the reserves may not be correct. This critical issue led us to the conclusion that the standard 
density tool has to be exchanged for a modern, more reliable tool.

Figure 2 Example of differences in density measurements and porosity evaluation using domestic 
(“standard”) and foreign (“extended”) logging tools.

The analyzed standard data also suffer from the poor quality of the neutron log (Fig.3). Often, the 
Neutron log is still acquired in counts per second and needs to be transferred to porosity by the 
interpreter using empirical relationships. Much more accurate results are received, when the Neutron 
tool is already calibrated and the measurements are delivered in porosity units. The cross plots on 
figure 3 also demonstrate that the modern tools show a sharper separation by lithology and better 
correlation of porosity for both, limestones and dolomites. The standard tools exhibit a large scatter of 
values and hence, a larger uncertainty range.

Figure 3 Cross plot analysis using five wells. Horizontal axis: measured data from “extended” 
logging suite (a and b –Calibrated Neutron, c and d – acoustic impedance), vertical axis: porosity 
data from “standard” tools (a and c) versus data from extended logging suite (b and c). Note the 
large uncertainty in lithology and porosity definition for the standard tools.

Using only the standard logging suite, it is rather difficult to obtain accurate lithology, porosity and 
acoustic impedance values. Intervals with fractured reservoirs may be overlooked. Especially the 
provided density measurements with older tools proved to be extremely unreliable, and this may have 
a direct impact of the reserves evaluation. In addition, the data are – due to the inherent blurring – 
applicable for property prediction from seismic data only in a qualitative manner. In view of the 
importance of the porosity estimation these standard tools have to be substituted by modern tools.

For high quality reservoir characterization, in addition to the p-wave velocity, the shear wave and the 
Stoneley provide extremely useful information, especially for lithology estimation and the definition 
of permeable reservoir intervals. To make use of the full potential of seismic inversion techniques, the 
complex of modern logging curves has to be acquired at least in a number of key wells for exploration 
and production.

Introduction
Six seismic reflection lines from Mountrail County,
N. Dak., were acquired to document the relation between 
mapped surface lineaments and to interpret structure related to 
oil and gas production. The longest line, 100-14W/100-14E, 
extends east–west over the Parshall producing area (fig. 1), 
which produces from the Bakken Formation. Line 100-14E is 
an eastern extension of line 100-14W and extends over Plaza 
and Wabek fields that produce from the Mississippian Mission 
Canyon Formation. Both lines were merged during reprocess-
ing (fig. 1). Line 100-9 is a north–south line that ties with lines 
100-14E and 100-14W. Lines NEW-228, GR-414, and 100-13 
(fig. 1) were used to supplement structural and stratigraphic 
interpretations of the study area.
Interpretation
The history of the Precambrian basement of the Williston 
Basin is critical to understanding the basin’s evolution, struc-
tural configuration, and sedimentation and thermal patterns. 
Geophysical methods used to map Precambrian structures 
include gravity and magnetic surveys, which define large- 
scale Precambrian fault blocks (Brown and Brown, 1987; 
Anna, 1986) including their orientation and block length that 
are important attributes to help interpret structural and sedi-
mentation trends. Seismic data were used to refine the gravity 
and magnetic interpretations. Interpretation of the six, two-
dimensional (2-D) seismic lines included the delineation of the 
Red River Formation, Bakken Formation, Madison Group, and 
Spearfish Formation (figs. 2–7), and the mapping of numerous 
faults, most of which are thought to be rooted in Precambrian 
basement. These faults were interpreted as approximate or 
inferred because net offsets are small and are difficult to map 
at the seismic scale. There is also uncertainty as to how far the 
faults propagate upward through the stratigraphic section. A 
minor number of structural anomalies may be attributed to salt 
dissolution.
The positions of the Stanley and Lonetree-Glenburn 
lineaments (fig. 1) (Anna, 1986) are interpreted from seis-
mic lines, as well as the location of two major producing 
areas in Mountrail County, N. Dak. (North Dakota Oil and 
Gas Commission, 2009). Although the Parshall and Sanish 
producing areas straddle the two lineaments, it is unclear if the 
lineaments create an area of enhanced reservoir quality. Later-
als from horizontal wells trend northwest–southeast, which 
indicates that operators are attempting to intercept northeast–
southwest structural features.
Seismic Reflection Data Acquisition 
and Processing
Data Acquisition
The seismic data consist of six multichannel seismic 
reflection lines that the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 
purchased by contractual agreement from Seitel Data, Ltd., 
in 2007. Two of the lines (100-14W and 100-14E) were 
combined during reprocessing and interpreted as a single 
line (line 100-14W/100-14E; fig. 3). The data were originally 
acquired between 1974 and 1984 by Pacific West Exploration 
Company, Kemp Geophysical Corp., and Sefel Geophysical, 
Ltd. (table 1). The lines form a loose network covering a large 
part of Mountrail County, N. Dak. In total, 67 line-miles of 
data were purchased. The acquisition agreement for these data 
by the USGS included limited publication rights. Table 1 gives 
the field acquisition parameters for all of the lines.
Data Processing
The seismic reprocessing by the USGS was conducted 
to emphasize reflectors in the sedimentary column and to 
convert the seismic time structure into depth coordinates. This 
reprocessing consisted of a standard sequence of (1) auto-
matic gain-control scaling, single-design window-spiking

(2) a second velocity analysis; (3) normal move-out and stack; 
(4) shift to a horizontal datum equal to the average elevation 
of the line; (5) migration using a smoothed stacking velocity 
field and automatic gain control scaling; and (6) second-zero-
crossing predictive deconvolution, and bandpass filter. Depth 
conversion was performed using the same smoothed stacking 
velocity field used for migration. After depth conversion, all 
seismic lines were shifted to an elevation datum of 2,100 ft 
above sea level.
Because the seismic lines were recorded by different 
companies, using different energy sources and recording 
parameters, the processing parameters used for each line 
were data dependent and were selected based on exten-
sive testing. For example, the seismic energy sources were 
Vibroseis, dynamite, and land airgun (table 1), which made 
it necessary to vary deconvolution and bandpass filter 
parameters significantly. Another problem we encountered 
was that, although lines 100-14W and 100-14E overlapped, 
they were recorded in different years using a different
geophone group interval, which resulted in different horizontal 
trace spacing. Migration requires constant trace spacing, so to 
solve this problem each line was processed separately up to 
the point of migration and then combined. Before combining 
the lines, the trace spacing of line 100-14E was adjusted to 
match that of 100-14W by means of a Fourier trace interpola-
tion algorithm. This allowed us to migrate the combined lines 
as a single line.
Identification of Reflectors
To tie the seismic data to well data, we created a synthetic 
seismogram using a sonic log recorded in Lear Petroleum, 
#1 School District, located in T. 152 N., R. 90 W., sec. 3. The 
location of this well is about 52,800 ft east of the west end 
of line 100-14W and a few feet north of the line at the loca-
tion shown on figure 1. We were able to identify reflectors 
with a high degree of confidence between 3,500 and 12,500 ft 
depths. The synthetic seismogram was embedded in line 
100-14 Synthetic (figs. 1 and 2), a shortened version of line 
100-14W/100-14E (figs. 1 and 3).

County, North Dakota, chap. 6 of U.S. Geological Survey Williston Basin Province Assessment Team, Assessment of

1. Seismic lines, major producing areas, and major lineaments ..............................................2
2. Seismic line 100-14 Synthetic and includes synthetic seismogram .....................................3
Six seismic reflection lines from Mountrail County,

N. Dak., were acquired to document the relation between 
mapped surface lineaments and to interpret structure related to 
oil and gas production. The longest line, 100-14W/100-14E, 
extends east–west over the Parshall producing area (fig. 1), 
which produces from the Bakken Formation. Line 100-14E is 
an eastern extension of line 100-14W and extends over Plaza 
and Wabek fields that produce from the Mississippian Mission 
Canyon Formation. Both lines were merged during reprocess-
ing (fig. 1). Line 100-9 is a north–south line that ties with lines 
100-14E and 100-14W. Lines NEW-228, GR-414, and 100-13 
(fig. 1) were used to supplement structural and stratigraphic 
interpretations of the study area.

The history of the Precambrian basement of the Williston 
Basin is critical to understanding the basin’s evolution, struc-
tural configuration, and sedimentation and thermal patterns. 
Geophysical methods used to map Precambrian structures 
include gravity and magnetic surveys, which define large- 
scale Precambrian fault blocks (Brown and Brown, 1987; 
Anna, 1986) including their orientation and block length that 
are important attributes to help interpret structural and sedi-
mentation trends. Seismic data were used to refine the gravity 
and magnetic interpretations. Interpretation of the six, two-
dimensional (2-D) seismic lines included the delineation of the 
Red River Formation, Bakken Formation, Madison Group, and 
Spearfish Formation (figs. 2–7), and the mapping of numerous 
faults, most of which are thought to be rooted in Precambrian 
basement. These faults were interpreted as approximate or 
inferred because net offsets are small and are difficult to map 
at the seismic scale. There is also uncertainty as to how far the 
faults propagate upward through the stratigraphic section. A 
minor number of structural anomalies may be attributed to salt 
dissolution.

The positions of the Stanley and Lonetree-Glenburn 
lineaments (fig. 1) (Anna, 1986) are interpreted from seis-
mic lines, as well as the location of two major producing 
areas in Mountrail County, N. Dak. (North Dakota Oil and 
Gas Commission, 2009). Although the Parshall and Sanish 
producing areas straddle the two lineaments, it is unclear if the 
lineaments create an area of enhanced reservoir quality. Later-
als from horizontal wells trend northwest–southeast, which 
indicates that operators are attempting to intercept northeast–
southwest structural features.

Seismic Reflection Data Acquisition 
and Processing

The seismic data consist of six multichannel seismic 
reflection lines that the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 
purchased by contractual agreement from Seitel Data, Ltd., 
in 2007. Two of the lines (100-14W and 100-14E) were 
combined during reprocessing and interpreted as a single 
line (line 100-14W/100-14E; fig. 3). The data were originally 
acquired between 1974 and 1984 by Pacific West Exploration 
Company, Kemp Geophysical Corp., and Sefel Geophysical, 
Ltd. (table 1). The lines form a loose network covering a large 
part of Mountrail County, N. Dak. In total, 67 line-miles of 
data were purchased. The acquisition agreement for these data 
by the USGS included limited publication rights. Table 1 gives 
the field acquisition parameters for all of the lines.

The seismic reprocessing by the USGS was conducted 
to emphasize reflectors in the sedimentary column and to 
convert the seismic time structure into depth coordinates. This 
reprocessing consisted of a standard sequence of (1) auto-
matic gain-control scaling, single-design window-spiking

Williston Basin Province—Interpretation of 2-D Seismic 
Data, Mountrail County, North Dakota
By Lawrence O. Anna, John J. Miller, and Ofori N. Pearson
2  Williston Basin Province—Interpretation of 2-D Seismic Data, Mountrail County, North Dakota

Figure 1. Seismic lines, major producing areas, and major lineaments. Inset 
map is the Williston Basin Province. Line 100-14 Synthetic is a shortened version 
of line 100-14W/100-14E as shown by the brace.

deconvolution, datum statics using smoothed surface eleva-
tions, velocity analysis, and surface-consistent residual statics; 
(2) a second velocity analysis; (3) normal move-out and stack; 
(4) shift to a horizontal datum equal to the average elevation 
of the line; (5) migration using a smoothed stacking velocity 
field and automatic gain control scaling; and (6) second-zero-
crossing predictive deconvolution, and bandpass filter. Depth 
conversion was performed using the same smoothed stacking 
velocity field used for migration. After depth conversion, all 
seismic lines were shifted to an elevation datum of 2,100 ft 
above sea level.
Because the seismic lines were recorded by different 
companies, using different energy sources and recording 
parameters, the processing parameters used for each line 
were data dependent and were selected based on exten-
sive testing. For example, the seismic energy sources were 
Vibroseis, dynamite, and land airgun (table 1), which made 
it necessary to vary deconvolution and bandpass filter 
parameters significantly. Another problem we encountered 
was that, although lines 100-14W and 100-14E overlapped, 
they were recorded in different years using a different

geophone group interval, which resulted in different horizontal 
trace spacing. Migration requires constant trace spacing, so to 
solve this problem each line was processed separately up to 
the point of migration and then combined. Before combining 
the lines, the trace spacing of line 100-14E was adjusted to 
match that of 100-14W by means of a Fourier trace interpola-
tion algorithm. This allowed us to migrate the combined lines 
as a single line.

To tie the seismic data to well data, we created a synthetic 
seismogram using a sonic log recorded in Lear Petroleum, 
#1 School District, located in T. 152 N., R. 90 W., sec. 3. The 
location of this well is about 52,800 ft east of the west end 
of line 100-14W and a few feet north of the line at the loca-
tion shown on figure 1. We were able to identify reflectors 
with a high degree of confidence between 3,500 and 12,500 ft 
depths. The synthetic seismogram was embedded in line 
100-14 Synthetic (figs. 1 and 2), a shortened version of line 
100-14W/100-14E (figs. 1 and 3).

Induced seismicity observed in Hellisheiði is found to be highly temperature dependent. Thermal stressing is significantly promoted by cooling-induced fracture permeability enhancement, controlling the stability conditions of the fractures. The spatial and temporal evolution of the sesimic events can only be numerically reproduced by considering a significant contribution of thermal permeability enhancement. Calibration of numerical models against field injectivity data shows that injectivity is governed by the injected fluid temperature. The colder the injected fluid, the higher the injectivity.

High-positive amplitude anomalies interpreted to be flows of sediment out of high flux vent sites on steep slopes. They either 1) contained hydrocarbons and were subsequently partially lithified, 2) attracted chemosynthetic clams which consumed what hydrocarbon was available (and since they were not located at the active seep site, subsequently died), or 3) are made up of acoustically faster sediment (i.e., sand). The flows that have been visited by submersibles are often a combination of two or more of the above.

The flows that have been visited by submersibles are often a combination of two or more of the above.

High-positive amplitude anomalies interpreted to be flows of sediment out of high flux vent sites on steep slopes. They either 1) contained hydrocarbons and were subsequently partially lithified, 2) attracted chemosynthetic clams which consumed what hydrocarbon was available (and since they were not located at the active seep site, subsequently died), or 3) are made up of acoustically faster sediment (i.e., sand). The flows that have been visited by submersibles are often a combination of two or more of the above.
